en: [Page 1] [The First Consolation] [The Genealogy of the Lineage]
I bow to the slayer of Madhu, whose feet are unincreased yet lofty, uncontracted yet wide,
unbent yet deep, not light yet smooth, and who makes manifest the supreme truth that is beyond decay.
(Setubandha 1) Upon which [feet] the spreading radiance of the sky flashes, clinging to the blood of the lord of the Danus...
Like the fortune of the great Asuras, trembling, helpless, and fallen upon her breasts;

his life, which had passed away with difficulty, was held fast by the cruel grasp of his arms—arms as difficult to overcome as their fullness—and his neck, twisted in agony, was like that of the demon Rīṭṭha. (Sētubandha 2–3)
By him, who has gained a firm footing through the roots of his virtues that have taken root across the expanse of the earth,
the fame of Mahendra was uprooted like a tree whose sprouts are being torn out. (Sētubandha 4,
Ākulaka)
Salutations to Him whose face, with its clearly visible curved eyebrows, appears like the quarters of the sky where the flames of the fire of His eyes meet the shadows of His throat;

it flashes with a radiant smile that seems to consume the darkness entirely. He whose playful glance, turning with a frown, desires to embrace the slopes of His own breasts which are bristling with horripilation.
His left side, which is indifferent to the nature of affection and longing to go to the dwelling of Ambikā—

[upon that side] the waves of moonlight, white as a blooming lily, reflected from the edge of the horizon and echoing against the sky, cling like playful smiles on nights bright with the moon. (Sētubandha 6–7)
When the ocean begins its dance, the seas become like the submarine fire belching smoke, with their waters agitated by the blows of fish leaping in fear. (Sētu 8)
Even when stumbling through the errors of newly composed royal panegyrics,
poetic discourse— like a friendship that has been broken and then restored— is difficult to sustain without the joy of its initial inspiration.
(Sētu 9) Knowledge increases, fame is cultivated, and virtues are acquired.
The deeds of great heroes are heard; why then do poetic compositions not captivate us?

(Sētubandha 10) Like wealth obtained through desire, or like prosperity acquired through youth, a new path of meaning is perceived with difficulty through the shadow of the connection [between words]. (Sētubandha 11)

Listen to that slaying of the Ten-faced one, which brought liberation to the captive gods, which extracted the thorn from the hearts of the three worlds, and which destroyed the suffering of Anurādhā and Indrasīlā. (Sētu 12) Then,
by Rāvaṇa, who had accepted the arrows of Kāma as his own adversaries, [his pride] was further increased...
When Sugrīva had pursued the beauty of Rāvaṇa’s heart,

which had been pierced [by Rāma], the rainy season somehow passed away for the son of Daśaratha, who was like a lion among men, as if it were a heavy chain of firm iron links forged from the twilight of his resolve and the fury of his passion. (Sētubandha 13–14)

The sky was filled with clouds as dark as blue lotuses, and the sound of thunder was heard; yet even so, there was no hope for his life. [He was] the first hand of support for the life of Rāvaṇa, who was fierce in his enmity toward the glory of Hari’s foe (Rāma). *Setu-bandha* 15.20.
Autumn has arrived, the day of execution for the swarms of female cranes afflicted by the onset of cold winds.
(Sētu 16) The surface of the sky shines like a thousand white lotus petals, resembling a mass of hair on the head of Rati’s lover [the moon];
it is fit for the sight of Madhumathana [Viṣṇu] and appears like the birth-lotus of Pitāmaha [Brahmā]. (Sētu 17)
The rainbow is the sun-gem’s fluttering veil, the jeweled girdle of the cloud-goddess,
the arrow-case for the moon-lover’s shafts, and the fresh filaments of the celestial *mandāra* tree. (Sētubandha 18) [The raindrops] fall,
released from the clouds that have descended as if drawn up by the swarm of bees that are the vanished clouds.
The quarters of the sky have returned to their own places, like branches of the tree of heaven;
fresh drops of water are seen falling in showers upon regions still moist with dew. (Setubandha 19)
The days seem to bear a complexion like that of a king who has just finished his bath and is dressed in fresh garments.

(Sētu 20) The Destroyer of Madhu, though not yet awake, is served by the Fortune of Dawn who has first awakened; she is filled with longing for him who crossed the ocean while suffering from the pangs of separation, having been comforted by sleep during her time of happiness. (Sētu 21)

The moon shines in the ocean of the sky, its pure rays reaching the shore of night; it is released from the shell-like cavity of clouds, which have been shattered by the gushing spray of starry pearls.
(Setu 22) The fragrance of the *saptacchada* trees clings [to the air], while the pollen of the *kadalī* flowers stirs within the heart.
The sweet warbling of the kalahamsas does not compare to the mature cry of the peacock;
clinging to her full breasts, the fresh rainbow—the first sign of good fortune bestowed by the sky at the onset of the rainy season—shines forth. (Sētubandha 23–24)
In the expanse of the sky, rendered stainless by the washing of abundant rainwater,
the lunar orb stands as if very close at hand, its true splendor revealed after casting off its previous pallor. (Setu 25) The quarters of the sky,
swirling with the pollen of night-lotuses that have long since returned from their journey, are made fragrant.

The flock of swans, eager to behold the lotus-pool but finding it unattainable, wanders about in distress. (Sētubandha 26) In the gentle month of Śarad, the nights—white as the moon and possessing a beauty enhanced by the shimmering rays of the sun—bear the charm of strings of pearls upon the breast of the moon. (Sētubandha 27)
The lotus, its stalk resting in the water, awakens as if from sleep—its petals released from the obstruction caused by the contact of bees and the sun’s rays, and delightful to the touch;
it is like the sound of the tinkling anklets of the Goddess Lakṣmī as she stumbles through the forest of lotuses, which resounds with the roar of Cupid’s bow. (Setubandha 28)
The retreat of the lotuses, driven away by the cries of the kalahamsas and the humming of the bees, is heard.

(Sētu 29) Having seen the lotus stalk broken and fallen, as if it were a beloved with her girdle loosened, the bee seizes the lotus—its face intoxicated with honey—as if it were the face of a woman uttering sweet cries. (Sētu 30)
The forest breeze wafts along, heavy with its own fragrance, carrying the pollen of fresh *kumuda* lilies that are closing as they are moistened by the honey-scented dew from full-blown lotuses,
and is irresistible to the wandering bees. (Sētu 31)
With her limbs bent by the thorns and her natural innocence lost through the exhaustion of her efforts,
the lotus does not withdraw its face— which is being kissed by the bee of Rati— just as a woman does not turn away from her lover.
[Sētu 32] It is sprinkled with the white pollen of *saptacchada* flowers that have fallen after being tossed about.

The swarm of bees, like chowries on the ears of an elephant that has arrived for a moment, fans the crooked trunk of the gift; thus, in this world where the moonlight is at odds with the lotus-faces of the soldiers in the lake of blooming lilies.
*Sētubandha 33* [Couplet] Thus, in this world where the moonlight is at variance with the lotus-faces of the warriors in the lake of blossomed lilies—
In the autumn, when there is a fresh twilight accompanied by the embrace of the shimmering star-eyed Lakṣmī,
Rāma’s face— though already withered— wells up again as if weeping, as if Hanumān had returned after a long absence to restore his bonds of hope. (Sētubandha 34–35)

But then he beheld the son of the Wind-god, whose radiance was emerging from the completion of the task exactly as it had been envisioned, like a mental desire brought to fruition through the attainment of happiness. (Sētu.
36) At first, with a face whose eyes were overflowing with joy at the sight of Māruti...
Afterwards, the news regarding Janaka’s daughter was related by Vāyudeva in its entirety.
[Rāma] did not believe that she had been seen; he sighed slowly with tears, saying "She is wasted away";
he wept, saying "You are grieving"; and Māruti embraced him, saying "She lives. (Sētubandha 37–38)
She offers him a jewel that seems to have its luster extinguished by anxiety, as if seated there out of exhaustion,
soiled by the binding of her braid, and weary from the sorrow [of separation]. (Sētubandha 39) That jewel,
with its rays flashing upward, is struck by the staff-like arms held in the hollow of his cupped palms.
Beheld by the descendant of Daśaratha with his own eyes, was he drunk in, or was he questioned for news?

(Sētubandha 40) And the Lord of the Raghus weeps for him, as if pouring out a handful of water from within his face—which possesses a stainless luster—through a stream of rays trickling from his slender fingers. (Sētubandha 41)
Even on that part of his body which was not touched by Rāghava— though it had been rubbed by Sītā—
a continuous horripilation arose from that very touch. (Setubandha 42)
Then his face, though soiled by tears, became a world of suffering—its indignation expanding through sweat, sighs, and anxiety; it was like the orb of the sun growing old and dimming.
Then, on him who had long been indifferent, there appeared a frown resembling a row of angry eyebrows.
His gaze, as if it were the single-pointed tip of an arrow, rested upon his own bow.
(Sētubandha 44) By Rama’s glance, the bow—though not even bent—became as if ready for action, like a bow whose string has been fixed for a moment and which is being drawn smoothly. (Sētubandha 45)
Even Sugrīva’s heart, disregarding the pride of the Ten-faced one, heaved a sigh at that moment as if bearing a burden supported by Rāghava’s embrace;
it was like an object found after being sought, its essence of indignation indicated by the knitting of his brows. (Setu 46)

The departure [of Rāma] was like poison placed within the heart of Rāvaṇa, which robs the life of the Rākṣasa. (Sētubandha 47) His gaze clings to the face of Lakṣmaṇa as if to the moon, to the broad chest of the Lord of Monkeys as if to a forest garland, and to the son of the Wind-god as if to his own fame or his own strength. (Sētubandha 48)
With the earth compressed beneath him, the forest regions agitated by the monkey army,
and facing the ocean that was being churned, he moved like Mount Mandara at the commencement of the churning of the sea.
(Setu 49) And when he had moved, the monkey host moved as well, shining with the brilliance of its swaying manes.
Like the shimmering mass of rays of the sun that has grasped the expanse of the directions,
that host of monkeys— kindled by the fire of enmity and fanned by the wind of wrath—
increases as it follows the path, like a forest fire through the groves of Laṅkā’s woods. (Sētubandha 50–51)

And it flows forth like an ocean surrounded by monkeys in the form of the bright masses of flickering filaments, crowded with mountains ablaze with the fire of universal destruction drawn toward it from every direction. (Setubandha 52)
The directions—spotless, their forms revealed by the shimmering sun, and displaying the path even within the sea of mist—are being whirled about.
And he gazes upon the Vindhya mountain, which is capable of supporting the weight of the ocean that has the form of a bow. (Sētubandha 53)
As if it were a life-line fashioned by the dwelling places of the Sarayū river flowing through the mountain clefts at twilight;

though its peaks were smoothed and its broad slopes revealed by the forests on its wide flanks, the Vindhya mountain—its caves filled and its winds blowing with ease—could not be endured even by the monkeys. (Sētubandha 54–55)
They have reached the mountain where the night-fires rest upon the surfaces of stone slabs cooled by the mineral ores of the *asībhara* river;
they reach that place where the wine of *vaula* flowers, emerging from the mouths of caves laughing with waterfalls, provides intoxication.
And they proceed, beholding masses of white clouds reflected in their own images.
Like a river’s current stalling upon a path strewn with solid crystal rocks (Sētu 57);

the currents of the great rivers became like the sites of great battle-roads, where the waters, having fallen into the netherworld as they were forced back by the weight of the banks, have become desolate (Sētu 58).

Having reached Malaya, which is dark with foul weather and where the sandalwood trees sleep in the coolness of the forest thickets like clouds sleeping at night, she has attained the mountain whose sandalwood sap flows down broken by the wind.
(Sētubandha 5.9) There, the fragrance of the creepers that have burst open and clung to the sandalwood trees spreads its shade.
They gaze upon the paths where great serpents are entangled and unable to extricate themselves;

they frequent the mountain river currents, which are smeared with sandalwood paste oozing from the banks and rendered bitter by the ichor of elephants whose rut-shedding is intensified by their delight. (Sētubandha 60–61)

Then she reached the shore, fragrant with the ichor flowing from the temples of the young elephants, where a multitude of pearls had been placed in the water after being opened from their fresh shells. (Setubandha 62)
Dark as a blooming *tamāla* tree, repeatedly polished by the hands of its restless waves,
and fragrant with forests of blossoming *elā* plants, it stands like the streak of ichor from the ocean-elephant—
its body smeared unevenly with foam, its face-like expanse marked by the scars of coral teeth. (Setubandha 63)
Carrying the fragrance of the Malaya forest flowers that has spread throughout the ocean, her eyes are closed by the shells of oysters;
within the interiors of the caves on Mount Laṅkā, she seems to be listening to the sound of the Kinnaras’ song, which increases her passion and is offered with devotion. (Sētubandha 64–65)
Thus ends the first canto in the great poem *Daśamukhavadha*, composed by Śrī Pravarasena.
[The second act, the consolation;
Ākula 35] Then the son of Raghu beholds that which is flickering, difficult to traverse due to hundreds of faults and sorrows.
The ocean is like youth for the undertaking of tasks that are heavy with the essence of nectar;

it is like a reflection of the sky, the source of the earth, and the abode of the quarters; it is like a jeweled floor for the world, and like the remaining mass of water from the dissolution of the mountain [Mandara]. (Setubandha 1–2)
The ocean, with its surging and formidable waves, has the faces of the quarters darkened by its massive waters;
it is perpetually agitated in many ways by the moon that travels through the directions, as if by a constant wind.
(Setubandha 3) Its water-waves rise and crash against the groves of coral trees that have been submerged.
Even now, it flows as if red with blood from the wounds inflicted by the Mandara mountain;
spreading out through the gaps between the clouds, filling the entire expanse of heaven and earth, and overflowing at its mouths, it appears like his own fame issuing forth. (Sētubandha 4–5)
Like the moonlight clinging to the moon, like fame to a great hero, like radiance to the sun,

or like a great river that has long since departed clinging to a mountain— it was not leaving him, even though he had passed away. (Sētubandha 6) It was being struck by the wind as it subsided after having sustained life for some time.
Like a broad arrow lodged in the body, or like the submarine fire of the Vāḍava mouth consuming [the ocean], [the mountain]—
which was once comforted by the friction against the breasts of Mount Mahendra, whose palm-like rays had washed away the rows of forest trees—
is now, as if embracing the shore, pressing against the earth with its waters receding due to the ebbing tide. (Sētubandha 7–8)

Even though he occupies a single spot, his presence is manifold; though he cannot be contained even within the circle of the earth, he bends his body as he bows, filling the worlds with the weight of his form—like Hari when he assumed the dwarf’s shape. (Sētu. 9)

Though appearing delightful and being heard as such, it possesses qualities that are neither pleasant nor sorrowful; like the ripening of sugarcane, though it is being consumed, it bears the fruit of eternal happiness.
Like a mountain from which trees have been uprooted, or like a lotus pond abandoned by Fortune, [it is desolate]. (Sētubandha 10)
Like a wine-cup filled with intoxicating liquor, like the gentle moon separated from the thick clouds;
like a mass of jewels being drawn out slightly by the sun, which has grasped its hand, standing within the interior of pure water, providing a vision of perfected bliss. (Sētu 11–12)

It carries a mass of water that is free from the fear of the submarine fire, a multitude of flames whose shackles have been severed, flowing like a discharge from the mouth of the ocean, heaped within the cavity of the submarine fire’s mouth; it is like a steady body of water containing a multitude of whales, or like a mountain range with its wings intact. (Setubandha 13)
Carrying [the people] like waves in the stream of a river, or like jewels in a heavy net of ropes;
making himself go and come through the three worlds—deep as the netherworld, vast as the earth, and supportless as the sky—just as the Lord of Love does for himself. (Setu 14–15)
The path was being entreated by rivers who, with faces turned away in shame, had retreated after touching him, yet now followed him with glances trembling with affection;
they trembled and turned back as he departed, while he, heavy with life, still tasted the full flavor of the pleasure of his desire even today. (Setubandha 16) May he protect me.

Though it is produced from the salt-water ocean, it is not fickle like wine; though it is unstable, it is made firm by its stability; though it is surpassed by the jewels cast up by the gods, it is superior in essence; though it is great, it is not overflowing; and though its water is salty, it is a distillation of the nectar of immortality. (Setubandha 17–18)
Carrying within her womb a treasure like the god of wealth himself— whose sprout-like arms rest upon the orb of the moon, which is filled with abundant jewels—
just as the treasure is deposited in the mountain within the interior of the earth.
(Setubandha 19)
When the moonlight—whose flickering nature has now subsided after having once enveloped all—has returned, it is like the bliss of union with Kāmandakī in fresh youth;
it fills the mouths of shells tumbling from oyster shells slightly opened, with heaps of pearls. (Sētu 20)
[The mountain] where the clouds, having returned from their paths after being half-filled with water tossed far away by the wind;
where the old sprouts and young shoots are turned green by the radiance of emerald gems;
and where the elephants, intoxicated by the scent of celestial flowers, give rise to clouds as they sit near them. (Setu 21–22)
The Setu, with its jeweled embankments, beautiful with the laughter-like splendor of the groves of trees on its shores;

dense with water, restless through the embrace of the tide, and capable of leaping over the earth; its waters agitated by the moonbeams pushing against them, and its mountain ranges shaken as they move across it. (Setu 23)
It is constantly being struck by clouds that move swiftly, and it is scorched by the powerful submarine fire.
(Setu 24) There, venomous serpents are agitated by heaps of pearls scorched by their own submarine fire;
and the masses of jewel-stones are darkened by moss, revealing the paths through which the fish swim. (Setu 25)

The lineage of the Mahī, beloved by the god of love, was filled with *saris* (reeds) and resembled the essence of *lakṣmī*; it was like a woman whose girdle (*velā*) was tucked away at the mouth of the river.
(Setu 26) It resounded with the cries of peacocks descending from the thousands of rivers, and its roar was as unbearable as the thundering of clouds at the time of universal dissolution.
By the gentle breeze, the honey-like essence was wafted forth, as if it were flowing out while stumbling under the weight of soft intoxication.
(Sētubandha 27) With foam overflowing upon its surface, colored by the hue of the juice of black gems...
The ocean, its vast whirlpools produced by the sighs of the remaining serpents who stumbled over the rows of Hari’s horses,

possessing the hue of deer and the shimmering radiance of coral sprouts, shines like the surface of the earth colored by the sun after it was tossed far away by the churning of Mount Mandara. (Sētubandha 28–29)
The causeway, a gateway of pearls granted by the gods, a gateway of joy for those who have attained life;
vast, it is made wide by the play of waters surging over it;
its surface adorned with ancient, moss-covered rocks, it resounds with the harsh noise of timber shattered by the wind. (Setu 30)
At the time of Mahāmuṣa’s sleep, it was like a forest fire extinguished and cooled by the rain of a lull in the monsoon;

[it was] a mass of earth heated by the water gushing forth from the fissures torn open by the descent of the Asura, with fragments of Mount Mandara clinging to the intervals between the islands, which had been shattered and scattered by the churning. (Setu 31–32)
Thinking, "This has arisen from the essence of nectar," it was conceived by him as if to fill the four quarters with darkness;

it is the protector of the earth, a treasury of his own fame, and a repository of the ocean’s waters—possessing a wealth of virtues, its forested shores resonant and struck by the masses of water droplets driven by the wind. (Sētubandha 33)
Its sandy banks were washed by waters increased by the moon, mountains, clouds, and mountain torrents;
its surface was filled with water released from the swans that were the digits of the moon scattered by the Mandara-like clouds;
and pairs of fish lay silent upon emerald moss. (Setu 34–35)
In its midst, fish and whales are perceived moving within waters resembling the currents of a full river;
the netherworld (pātāla) is blackened by masses of soot emerging from the mouths of serpents.
(Setubandha 36)

The ocean was weighed by Rāvaṇa with his own eyes— having overflowed the earth as it was pressed down by the force of the uprooted trees at its base, and having been seen to possess a substance that could be measured. [Sētubandha 37] Even though he saw his own bed upon the great ocean abandoned for a long time...
With his heart captivated by Janaka’s daughter, he did not remember Śrī, the wife of the Destroyer (Śiva).

(Sētu 38) Even though Lakṣmaṇa was not visible, the Ocean did not let go of its steady gaze, as it seemed to be smiling with eyes slightly moistened by tears while exchanging words with the Lord of Monkeys. (Sētu 39)
The lord of the monkeys too beheld Hanumān, who had half-risen with his body held firm, his broad upper torso clearly visible as he was lifted up by the force of his joy.
The army of monkeys was gazed upon like a pair of wings spread out for the flight of descent;
[Sētu 41]. Terrified at the sight of the ocean, their bodies recoiling and trembling, the hosts of monkeys stood as if suddenly painted, motionless with eyes devoid of luster; [Sētu 42].
Beholding the ocean, the multitude of eyes of the monkeys—though naturally restless—fell upon Hanumān with profound respect, stunned by the unprecedented rasa of wonder;
for they had seen the son of the Wind-god return from having crossed the ocean, which was otherwise impossible to traverse. (Setubandha 43)
Their enthusiasm wanders hidden within their hearts, obscured by the enemy of delusion.
(Sētu 44) Then, the fickleness of their husbands—even that which was previously painted as a portrait lamp, with its extinguished luster and fixed gaze—has vanished.
(Sētu 45)
In some places, the monkeys steady themselves, their own selves bewildered by the sorrow of seeing the ocean,

their passion for moving lost, and their eyes turned back from the path ahead. (Setubandha 46) Thus ends the second canto in the great poem *Daśamukhavadha* composed by the illustrious Pārśvadeva, based on the work of Kālidāsa.
[The Third Chapter] [p.
13] [The Third Consolation]
Then you two, intoxicated by the wine of grief arising from the separation from the beloved, sat down with arms flung over the stone slabs that served as hitching posts for elephants. (Sētubandha 1)
Sugrīva laughs with a roar like the thundering of clouds, a sound clearly resonating with his spreading fame;
his speech is profound, heavy with essence, pure in meaning, and radiant with the luster of his teeth.
(Setu 2) When the earth was being lifted by his arm alone as if it were a mountain, the gods and demons were crushed, and the oceans were swallowed up.
"Alas! While the Ten-faced one is to be slain, you here are merely companions to the Destroyer of Madhu.

(Sētubandha 3) "Do not disparage your fame—which is like a well-born hero who, having turned back from some cause, has planted his foot facing the enemy, yet, having advanced and faltered, is now retreating like a kinsman who has been abandoned.
(Sētubandha 4)

The undertaking of this difficult task, which involves crossing the ocean and carrying the burden of the Rākṣasas, has collapsed like the very weight that was first weighed upon the heart of the Lord of the Raghus—so heavy with the crossing of the sea and so hard to abandon due to the slaughter of the demons.
(Setubandha 5) This title of "Lordship" bears fruit merely as a command for you; it is this very burden [of responsibility] that has been cast off.
The dawn, the bearer of shadows, causes the lotus-pools to blossom by itself.

(Sētu 6) It is not merely for crossing that you are all capable of holding this ocean in the hollows of your hands—this ocean fragrant with the scent of the *vaula* flowers in the groves on its shores at this hour—but even to drink its fruit-like water. (Sētu 7)

This is indeed the occasion for those who have long desired [liberation], whose fetters are falling away as they are being shaken off, and whose heads are bound together in a manner suited to the moment—just as the heads of two oxen are joined when the yoke is applied. (Setubandha 8) Those virtuous men are rare who, without speaking, bring about the accomplishment of their tasks. (Setubandha 9)
Even those two trees, whose emergence of flowers remains unnoticed, give fruit so soon; [just as] the hand is weary from long-pending labor, and the mind is impatient with longing.
(Setubandha 9) [p.
14] The hand is exhausted by the long delay in work, and the mind is filled with indignation due to its longing.
Do not, O Lord, cast your gaze, heavy with tears, toward the arrows of Rāhu’s son (Rāvaṇa).

Let your fame encompass the harem of the sky— whose girdle is the agitated ocean and whose palace is the firmament— and the multitude of the quarters as its brides, all of which are protected by the kings who are the dust from the soles of Daśaratha’s feet.
One who does not commit violence while giving up his life is indeed called a giver;

he who, even though he has abandoned all virtuous efforts, is counted as one who is "dead while living" in this world—do you not know that this matter, though seemingly fragile, will result [in such a state]? (Setubandha 12)

It bestows supreme delusion, like a flower upon a poison tree that withers away. (Sētubandha 13) Even when failing, it carries a man’s effort—difficult for others to traverse—to the other shore of the world, just as the sun carries a chariot with one broken wheel across the expanse of the sky. (Sētubandha 14)
Behold! In this matter, the ministers have become like palm trees [bending] together;
the royal assembly has become discordant, yet the royal assembly of the adversary remains tranquil.
(Sētubandha 15) The world of Rākṣasas was seen with eyes rolling, agitated by the roar of the ocean as it was churned.
Even as they are being swept away by the tide, the son of the Wind-god does not laugh at them in his heart.
(Sētubandha 16) The enthusiasm of the great warriors, spreading without interruption and flashing with the brilliance of the sun, rises up in their hearts;
though checked by the uneven terrain, it is like the current of great rivers. (Sētubandha 17)

The innate luster of the enemy, which was maintained by pride through a succession of unyielding efforts and could not even be conceived of by others, has been surpassed by those whose martial envy was provoked by his ever-increasing prowess; thus, its excellence remains unattained. (Sētubandha 18)

The reputation of being a hero is difficult to maintain when one is dragged away by the crocodile of hope. (Sētubandha 19) In times of both calamity and festival, those whose minds remain equanimous toward victory and defeat are truly steadfast;
even in the face of danger, they alone are capable of remaining composed. (Sētubandha 20)

[15] O you who are thirsty for the nectar of resolve, how is it that they do not attain the glory already held in their own hands? Like serpents at the risk of their lives, they vomit forth their indignation. (Sētubandha 21)
Lions endure captivity; venomous serpents with upraised fangs survive for a long time;

yet those whose resolve remains unshaken even when thwarted are not merely capable, but are able to prevail even for a moment. (Setubandha 22) O you who have turned back from your purpose, how is it that you have retreated merely upon seeing me?
You shall behold your own sorrow reflected in the faces of your beloveds, as if in the surfaces of mirrors.
(Sētubandha 23) The currents of rivers, though deep as the ocean and long accustomed to flowing forward, can be turned back;
but noble men, having not yet fulfilled their mission, cannot be made to turn back. (Sētubandha 24)
The ocean is leaped over by Jāmbavat; it is even drunk many times over by the fire of his stomach.
How then can that sea, which has been rendered impassable by his power, be called "difficult to cross" by monkeys?
Let this first be considered: while they carry a fame worthy of their lineage and conduct... [Sētubandha 25]

What is difficult for both the ocean and the moon to accomplish out of shame? [To cross over]. (Sētu 26) O mountain, do not release the thunderbolt of your rays, which is indeed the destroyer of the happiness of Rāhu’s son; otherwise, having defeated you, the cloud that is the essence of the moon will become the showerer of water upon you. (Sētu 27)

Even a stranger, when served with humility, becomes a kinsman through the bonds of affection; how much more so, then, for Dāśarathi, who is a devoted kinsman by his very nature and whose deeds are performed without ulterior motive?
He lingers like a fig tree that has grown long ago, its shade spreading wide like the wind of the rainy season.

Even now, Fortune does not even show the fruit of this [union] to me; how much longer will she remain thus deceived? Having been born from the lotus, why does Lakṣmī not abandon Rāma during the nights? (Sētu 29–30)

Just as the shadow of a tree, even when it has fallen upon the ground, does not remain for long upon the sun that illuminates the entire expanse of the world with its pervasive radiance, so too does infamy not endure long among virtuous men, even if it has descended upon them. (Sētubandha 31)
Whether it was actually done by Rāghava against us or not, that first act of treachery toward a virtuous man was committed by him;
what then need be said of what he did not do?
(Sētubandha 32) For how much longer shall the ten-faced Rāvaṇa appear as one who is being sought after by Rāghava?
Like a forest tree struck by a massive thunderbolt falling from a towering cloud, it was difficult to behold from afar;
like a mass of ripe mangoes falling from a young mango tree, the monkey army—shrouded in the darkness of the multitude of Rākṣasa troops—was unbearable even to look upon. (Sētubandha 33–34)
Even when faced with a formidable adversary, warriors become even more resolute and turn back the enemy;
like elephants whose rutting ichor is checked by the upraised goads of their drivers, they restrain their own fury.
Even in adversity, only the true leader remains undaunted and bears the burden.
What support does the day have when the sun has set? The lunar orb [is its refuge].

(Sētu 36) Clouds that have released their waters, rows of trees that have bestowed new fruit, and arms that have been drawn back at the front of battle—even though they are light, they become heavy. (Sētu 37)
The great mountains do not tolerate pride, for they are easily moved by the task of uprooting them with their arms;
why then does the enemy, who occupies the vast expanse of the sky, display such heaviness?
Only the truly brave bear even a heavy burden while guarding their fortitude. (Setubandha 38)
The rays of the sun destroy the entire three worlds while remaining in their very place;

likewise, great heroes first conquer their own army—which has cast off its burden and has its shoulders already overstepped the starting line—and only afterwards do they strike the enemy. (Sētubandha 39–40)
When a great hero has resolved upon the ardor for battle and set out to uproot his adversaries, auspicious omens arise, fortune and fame increase, and he stands at the forefront.
(Sētubandha 41) As he advances to the extreme limit, drawing along the ranks of warriors whose hands are encased in the sheaths of their swords...
Only the sons of Rāhu do not tremble, like mountains with their wings clipped, bound by their enemies.
Therefore,
the son of Raghu sleeps, while Sītā likewise sleeps with her face buried in his hand.
The Ten-faced one shall maintain his composure only so long as he is compared with you in dejection.
(Sētu 43) Furthermore, you two do not know each other’s minds;
I am distressed as I observe this Hanumān, whose body is covered with scars from the mountain peaks. (Sētu 44)

For a man who has not fulfilled his purpose, death is better than a long life lived without having achieved his goal—death while hoping for the fortune of an adversary and hoping for the glory of one's own lineage; not a life lived without such accomplishment. (Sētu 45) Moreover, by this very Fortune, whose eyes are straight, the beauty of the filaments was brought near to her lotus-hand.

Those possessed of true knowledge are immersed in me—who am equal in passion and pride—as if in a battle where passion and pride are equal, while I speak thus. (Sētu 46 [Yugalaka]) Let the sorrowful Sītā not be grieved for by the world, like a withered lotus crushed by the heat of the cold season. (Sētu 47)

When Rāghava’s heart was pained, it was like the moon when soiled by clouds; when his life was fading, it was like the night when its essence has vanished. When Rāghava’s heart was distressed, it was like a lotus scorched by frost;
when his life-breath was exhausted, it was like a flower withered and devoid of bees. (Sētubandha 47–48)
[The Couple] When indeed will they cast off their ornaments— the very remedies for the exhaustion caused by separation?

We shall behold our beloved wives, their broad cheeks soiled by long locks of hair tossing in the force of their sighs; their creeper-like arms hanging down, loosened by the slipping of their girdles from their broad hips; and feeling ashamed because they have been sent on an errand praised by their attendants. (Sētubandha 49–50)
When the word "juggaaṃ" (halt!
was thus spoken, the monkey army—its bodies sinking under the weight of anxiety, motionless as if being dragged, like a herd of elephants mired in mud—did not stir. (Sētubandha 51)

The Lord of the Monkeys, his mouth filling the mountain caves and forests with the loud sound of his roar, laughs again and says, unable to endure the enemy's prowess: "What expectation can there be for one whose power is so unstable, even among his own retinue? (Setu 52) Thus, what hope is there for one whose strength is unsteady, even regarding his attendants?
Even there, indeed, this army of mine stands ready against the son of Daśamukha.

(Sētubandha 53) Until the flood of the ocean, whose waters are driven by my great hands and teeth as it seeks an outlet during the ebb-tide, has not turned back, let the monkey host remain submerged in the sea. (Sētubandha 54)
Laughing at the Malaya mountain, which bears the weight of the Tōsala forest, I shall,

with my arm, lift up the army of a hundred yojanas— an army heavy with the burden of its great mass— just as a single person, when meeting another face-to-face in a moment of imminent danger, becomes a helper to one another.
(Sētubandha 5.55) In a situation of imminent danger, each one who meets another face-to-face indeed becomes a helper.
As long as the sight is not given, it remains as if carried away for a long time.

(Sētu 56) Or rather, for me who set out toward the great ocean, the vast sky was not enough; having slain [my enemies] who were like blood, fat, and flesh, I dwell in satisfaction, having reached my goal. (Sētu 57)

"Do not be bewildered by the serpent being crushed; as soon as the surface of the earth bows down when struck by my feet in fury, then indeed let the entire ocean flow forth. (Sētubandha 58) [With arms held like twin pillars, in the midst of the great ocean...]
By him who has uprooted Mount Maināka, the army of monkeys has crossed the Vindhya range— [a crossing] where serpents are fleeing,
aquatic creatures are overturned, and mountain peaks are shattered. (Sētubandha 59)
Behold, I shall turn the city of Rājagṛha—its waters agitated by the wind from my mouth—into dry land.

(Sētubandha 60) I shall turn the ocean into such a state that its remaining shores are whirled about as their arms are broken and uprooted in the middle, with Mount Suvela on this side and Mount Malaya on that side. (Sētubandha 61)
Or rather, behold Lanka today— clinging to the edge of the dawn like a creeper, its Rākṣasa-tree broken,
with only the sprout of Sītā remaining, as if it were a vine uprooted by my arm. (Sētubandha 62) Behold Lanka,
where the tree of the Rākṣasas has been shattered, where the lions— the Daśānanas— have been struck down, and where there is the joy of safe passage.

Intoxicated by his passion for Rāma, I regard Laṅkā as a forest clearing, like a wild elephant. (Sētubandha 63) Thus ends the third Āśvāsa in the epic poem *Daśamukhavadha*, composed by the great poet Kālidāsa and written down by Śrī Pravarasena.
[The Fourth Consolation] Then the army of monkeys,
silent at the first word and subsequently heated with shame, [remained still].
Like a forest of lotuses fast asleep at the sight of the moon, [the world] has awakened at the arrival of day.

But now, the single enthusiasm for departure has climbed upon many mountain peaks together with the monkeys' hearts, which were vast and shrouded in the darkness of sorrow, just as the dawn climbs the mountains.
Then, the joy of their hearts, which had begun as a smile on their faces,

spread forth like a companion to the hand placed upon the path of valor in battle— its radiance laughing at those [enemies] who were struck by the mountain of dust raised thickly by the trampling of the horses.
(Setubandha 3) [The faces] whose cheeks were struck by streams of sweat shaken from the profuse exertion.
The blue-necked one (Nīla) sprinkles with water the chest of the mountain peak—its left arm shattered, its crest uprooted and bent, its fame destroyed;
its surface rough and dark with the thrill of joy, resembling a cloud split by the moon placed within its heart. (Setu 4–5)
The water-lily, with its petals of parted lips, its mass of filaments of shimmering teeth,
and its outburst of fragrant scent, smiles with a joyous glance of the moon.
(Sētubandha 6) With its branches trembling and agitated by the movement of arms that have broken the bonds of the earth...
The sandalwood tree on the shore, which was like a venomous serpent falling upon uneven ground, was shaken by the lord of elephants.

(Sētu 7) The glance of the serpent-like sun—blazing and difficult to behold—is like the smokeless flame of a fire; though it overflows with joy, it does not attain gentleness, just as the gaze of a venomous serpent does not. (Sētu 8)

Sarasvatī too releases her speech, which causes the mass of the Malaya mountains to resound with the echoes from the mouths of the frightened [serpents], and she purifies her own body, which had been afflicted by the poison of anger. (Setubandha 9) She possesses the beauty of a lotus that has just awakened for a mere moment, its hue like the dawn’s crimson glow.
Anger blazed clearly even upon the face of Nīlāñjaṇa, like the sun upon the face of a cloudless day.
Adorned within the space between his broad lips by the laughter of his wrath, Susena’s anger shone forth clearly. (Sētubandha 10)
His face was like the orb of the moon bursting forth from the midst of the rising blood of dawn;

by him, whose face was turned forward with its lower part beginning to appear, who was reddened by joy and possessed the luster of the rising sun’s orb, the son of Vālin was made manifest like the day itself. (Sētubandha 11–12)
Having fulfilled his burden, the son of the Wind does not desire a lightness born of pride;
he desires to preserve only his dignity and his reputation as one who has executed his mission.
(Setubandha 13) [He is] being dragged by the fangs protruding from lips parted by the roar of the ocean, as he is rebuked.
Sugrīva laughed, his eyes reddening with a wrath that had been calmed by pride in his own prowess.

(Setubandha 14) Then the son of Sumitrā, disregarding both his teacher’s [Rāma’s] and his own strength, neither reflected nor spoke; he regarded the ocean and the ten-faced Rāvaṇa as mere blades of grass. (Setubandha 15)

Even from Rāvaṇa, the lord of the monkeys of his own vision, a speech with quivering coral-red lips was taken away by Sītā’s words—speech that was like a lotus with trembling bees—as if a swarm of bees had departed from a lotus. (Sētubandha 16;
Antyakulaka 3)
The flash of his gaze, obstructed by the folds of his brow lowered through the transformation of his form,
was like a mountain whose medicinal herbs are stumbling against the nearby white sands,
while the brilliance of his eyes was bestowed upon the monkeys who had raised their necks to ward him off with their hands. (Sētubandha 17)
Like a forest fire that has turned the great mountains tawny with sparks from the masses of trees caught in its net, the lord of the bears speaks,
having raised up the Vatsa ridge— which lies upon the surface of the earth and reveals its broad, thick forest caves through its stumbling folds and crevices. (Sētubandha 18–19)

I remember the heaven devoid of the Parijata tree, the chest of Indra bereft of the splendor of the Kaustubha gem, and the slope of Shiva’s forehead, innocent of the frontal globes of the elephant [that was Mahisha].
(Setu 20) The fresh heart of the great Asura, shattered by the claws of the lion in the hand of Indra...
[She was seen] running after Śrī, who had been cast off like her own lotus-hand. And I remember that [jewel], which belonged to Hiraṇyākṣa and was split by the tusk of the Great Boar. (Setubandha 21)
The mountain-fastening of the uplifted heart has been loosened, as if the entire circle of the earth had been weighed down;
O child, despondency carries away even fortitude, the intoxication of youth takes away modesty, and old age, seizing the armpits, establishes one in a state of extreme shame. (Setubandha 22–23)

Do not disregard the lamentations of one aged by old age— though their words may be scattered with disjointed and harsh syllables, their meaning is well-composed— as if they were the idle chatter of those deluded by youth.
(Sētubandha 24) Seated upon your two arms, the army of the enemies of the gods was powerful even in battle against the Suras.
Even the dust of the earth, its strength gained from the wind, follows the sun;

how much more so, then, do the undertakings of those who have gathered together with essential weight, though they be difficult to turn back, fall apart like the ocean when its course is obstructed by the violation of established order? (Sētubandha 25–26)

"Set aside what is beyond your perception; even if it were established by the scales of logic, purified by scripture, and made unshakable by experience—even such [knowledge] is not as weighty as my own sacred tradition (śruta).
(Sētu 27) "That which is adorned by all-encompassing, incomparable, essential prowess does not manifest [as such] when it is not yet fully developed."
A single cloud may rain heavily, yet the suns, joined together, consume the three worlds.
(Sētubandha 28) Enthusiasm, seized by indignation, overcomes the pride of even an adversary;
it does not grant such fear as that which is produced by an arrow released from a bow whose joints are devoid of strength. (Sētubandha 29)
"You must not abandon it, even if you are moving very swiftly; for as the sun hastens through the course of the steadfast kings, its footfall on the southern face [of the mountain] is delayed.
(Setu 30) "What is the use of haste? Enough with these stories conceived in the joy of battle upon this path! (Setu 31)
O Goddess Jayalakṣmī, you appear dejected as if by the stumbling of the moon’s rays upon your face, which has been cast down in derision.
(Sētu 31) Do not take pleasure even in the moon that rises in haste;
for the fame produced by the night-lotus groves, whose sole essence is its manifest excellence, has long since vanished from the day-lotuses. (Sētu 32)
What is the use of one’s own retinue, or another’s retinue? O friend, it is the rival who shines when being solicited by living beings.
What is the use of grasping at birth even in this world for one whose pride has been destroyed? (Sētu. 33)
O brave one, why must you also perform a deed like that of Māruti— a feat whose fame remains unextinguished— by the leader of the monkeys, those with Hanumān as their chief?
(Setubandha 34) How could it be entrusted even to him, by whom the fruit was already secured and who had not yet spread far?

Just as a creeper clings to another tree when one has fallen, so does the command [of Rāma] cling [to you]. (Sētubandha 35) Seeking to kill him, yet unable to kill him, what do you wish to do against the swift Daśagrīva, who is dear to the Lord of the Jāmbavats, though he is an enemy to the Lord of the Raghus? (Sētubandha 36)
Having restrained Sugrīva and his ministers, the son of the Grandfather turned back like a mass of apocalyptic smoke facing the sun after having ground down the peaks of Mount Meru;
His face, bearing modesty and pride, is like a cluster of white filaments emerging from its own source.

(Setu 38) It is a matter of wonder that while his sovereignty extends over half the world, the three worlds are protected, the earth is supported even during the distress of the ocean at the time of universal dissolution, and he remains indifferent toward the sea itself. (Setu 39)

For you, whose glance is fixed for a mere moment upon the target in the sport of archery and who flash like a vivid lightning bolt, does not even the beginning of an action lead inevitably to its conclusion? (Sētu.
40) Even the fire from the mouth of the powerful [Rāvaṇa], which was capable of withstanding the burden of the world's destruction, is extinguished.
"Tell me, who will the ocean do for you now that it has been given? Right there, take heart!
[Sētu 41, a yugma] Then, with her physical frailty revealed and the pleasure of touching her lover’s chest forgotten...
Again and again rubbing with the palm of his left hand that deer, dark as the *tāla* tree,

Rāma— steadfast in his own glory, yet surpassed by the glory of the ocean— makes the earth heavy with his weight and fills the air with a roar that drowns out the thundering of the sea. (Sētubandha 42–43)

O Lord of Monkeys, when the world was like an ocean difficult to cross, when I was bewildered and despondent, it was you alone who sustained this burden of duty, which could not otherwise have been abandoned. (Sētubandha 44)
The speech of the lords of bears, heavy with essence, unassailable, and possessing the radiance of eternal fame, has surged forth like jewels from a mine of gems— Sētu 45—
in which those such as you, steadfast in support, find their ultimate value.
There, the burden of the task, though vast, rests upon the earth as if released by Mahīdhara (the Mountain).
(Sētu 46) Now, with only a small portion of the work remaining—a task whose essence was merely its commencement—it is he alone who bears the chest of the monkeys;
he alone drinks their fame. (Sētu 47)

Therefore, let us all together request the ocean— the abode of Makara, whose shores are frequented by gods and asuras, and which surpassed even the joyful leaps of Hanumān— to grant us passage across it.
(Setu 48) Even though I have approached him without cause, he will not release me from my firm resolve.
Behold, the monkey host has crossed even the ocean by means of the land!
(Sētubandha 49) Where I have fallen, how could another’s anger find a place there?
For where a venomous gaze falls, a second [gaze] does not see it again. (Sētubandha 50)

Then, the radiance of the night-stalkers appeared, dark like a mass of clouds struck by a sudden wind-born tempest, resembling the glow of a ripening mango fruit, and spreading forth as if woven from the luster of full-blown blossoms.
Then, the waters were scattered by the sky, which was filled with the dust raised by the wind of their rapid movement.
The night-stalkers beheld the monkeys’ army, which was like a mass of broad lightning whirling within the intervals between the suns, as it descended from the sky;

then, as if the night-stalkers were falling stones from the sky, they hastily seized the monkey host that had moved toward the uplifted peaks of the mountain, as if it were the very circle of the earth. (Sētubandha 52–53)
The sky appears as if falling— its waters agitated by clouds, its mountains standing unevenly and swaying with the force of the wind,
its revolving constellations scattered and loosened from their places.
(Setu 54) And then Vibhīṣaṇa, who had been seen and recognized by Laṅkā, [was addressed] by Māruti...
Having restrained the power of the monkeys, he was presented to Rāghava like the account of a previous birth;
by that Lord of the Raghus, with his hand lowered as if out of respect for one who stood bowed at his feet. (Setubandha 55)

Indeed, his head was raised far above the hosts of Rākṣasas. (Sētu 56) Having communicated his resolve, he was embraced by Sugrīva, who felt joy at having obtained a companion in Māruti, and whose forest garland upon his chest was being nipped by bees. (Sētu 57)
Then the son of Raghu spoke, radiating an ivory-white luster from his teeth in all ten directions, like a natural outflow of pure joy from his heart.

"Behold! Having attained her desire, Lakṣmī does not wish to leave the forest of Rākṣasas. (Sētubandha 59) "It is known, O Vibhīṣaṇa, that your wisdom—though nurtured by a gentle nature—is unassailable even by the night-stalkers, just as nectar is unassailable by those with poisoned eyes. (Sētubandha 60)

By you, who are pure by nature and clearly radiating a multitude of abundant virtues, the lineage of the night-stalkers (the Rākṣasas), though turbid with its own pride, has been brought to prosperity—just as the moon, with its rays of abundant qualities, brings prosperity to the Lunar dynasty, even though it is darkened by its own spot. Noble men become the vessels for the glory of kings, providing the support for their family’s honor. (Sētubandha 62) By the Lord of the Night-dwellers, who had long been captivated by her beauty, Sītā was brought to the abode of the Rākṣasas like a healing herb that neutralizes the poison of a glance. (Sētubandha 63)
The agitation of the gods having subsided, and the ocean having been bound by the bridge,
she who knows the end of the world-child seized by the Ten-faced one reached her final transformation.
Then, with ears filled with joy, [she heard] the sound of victory magnified by the monkeys.
He bestowed anointment upon his head and affection within his heart.
(Sētubandha 65) Thus ends the fourth canto in the great poem *Daśamukhavadha*, composed by Śrī Pravarasena.
[The Fifth Consolation] Now,
when the ocean has become even more impassioned by the sight of the moon, it expands...
To Rāma, distressed by separation, even the night began to grow longer. (Sētubandha 1) The sky, with its moon revealed; the shore of the ocean, where Rāvaṇa remains hidden;
and the waters of the great sea, embracing the moon—all these attain a further increase. (Sētubandha 2)

Those [days], which were once bold enough to cast their hearts upon him who was easily won through dalliance, now, as they arise one after another, wear away my grasp of fortitude by scattering my despondency.
(Sētubandha 3) The ocean will do what is dear [to me]; the moon will rise; the night will pass.
"Perhaps my beloved might hold onto life, yet she will not abandon her own life"—thus despondent, he censures the moonbeams, blames the flower-weaponed god of love, and loathes the night;
though already wasted away, he grows even thinner as he asks the wind, "Will she live? (Sētubandha 4–5).
"Because he dwells here, surely she despises the direction [of the east];
because the moon is seated here, she despises the earth; and because it is her own, she holds even the sky in high esteem.
(Setubandha 6) Thus, along with the firm instruction imparted by Night, the advice was not disregarded.
Along with her resolve, her arms and her words alike fail her.
(Sētu 7) Thinking, "She is steadfast," he steadies her; thinking, "She is fainting, for she is delicate with love," he holds her;
thinking, "She is my beloved," he maintains his grip; thinking, "She is emaciated by separation," he embraces her limbs. (Sētu 8)
With rays emerging from the tender sprouts of the creeper that is the prominent deer-mark,
and with the splendor of the sun’s glow, his moon alone became pleasant to behold.
(Sētubandha 9)
As the night draws to a close, the orb of the moon— its reflection falling upon the trembling waves— is swallowed by the ocean as if by a heart bewildered by what it must do.
(Sētubandha 10) And only then [does it emerge] with a clear resonance issuing forth, filling the mouth of the Malaya cave and overflowing from it.
The ocean water was struck by the wind as if it were the sounding of a drum for Rāghava’s departure.

(Sētubandha 11) Resounding with the cries of flocks of swans, spreading its reach through the ten directions as they opened up, and having cast off the waters of darkness, the face of day became manifest like a sandbank. (Sētubandha 12)
Then, when the ocean—deep and firmly established—had passed through the period of night, his anger, like a tempest, mounted the orb of the moon, which was the face of Rāghava;
[it was] dark as a *tamāla* tree, with a rounded forehead and droplets of perspiring water. (Setu 13)
His brow, with its firm and wide frown, was like a poisonous creeper clinging to the Vindhya mountain.
Then his face became marked by the knitting of brows, with a pair of eyes turned toward his bow, trembling with indignation, and the binding of his mass of matted hair loosened. (Setubandha 14–15)

Though gentle by nature, the son of Rahu became difficult to behold—like the orb of the sun at the time of universal destruction—as the essence of his fury increased through the repeated frustration of his pride and the recurring pangs of his grief.
Then, he [prepared] for the execution of a daring feat, which served as a secret repository for the splendor visible only to his friend. (Setu 16)
He takes up the bow, which has the pride of his arms as its target, for those whose anger was previously suppressed.

(Sētu 17) When even a small portion of water had not yet ascended the bow, the mass of water spilled from the surface of the earth, which had been pressed down by the weight of the drawn bow, entered into a state of uncertainty. (Sētu 18)
The sky-realm resounds with his bow, which smokes, is turbid with smoke, emits rising flames that bind living beings, fills the quarters with its echoes, and roars from its vibrating tips.
"Let the earth split asunder"—as if this were the clear intent, he made the terrible vow, "There is no ocean. (Sētubandha 19)
Thinking for a moment, "May he lose his life," he bent his bow;
then, with the impact of the soft string pressed against his arms, which were emaciated by long separation—
Now his left arm, occupied solely with the drawing of the bow, becomes something entirely different.

Then the three worlds, filled with apprehension, remember the resonance of the striking of that left arm, which spreads through the ten directions and exerts a pressure exceeding the dissolution of the world at the end of an aeon.

And he took the arrow, capable of withstanding the overturning of the ocean, which had fallen into his outstretched hand as he turned away from the city—like a single shaft of the sun’s rays [falling] upon the western mountain. Then, as he fixed the arrow, his brow was furrowed by the knitting of his brows, which were wrinkled by the exertion of drawing the bowstring. For a long time... [Sētubandha 23]
Having sighed, his face distressed by compassion for the Pulindas, the Ocean [was calmed].
Then Rāghava drew his bow—its string firmly pressed by his bent arms, its arrow aimed with a steady and unblinking gaze. (Sētubandha 24–25)

The spokes of the sun’s chariot rattle deeply with the sound of the bowstring being drawn, their shadows flashing from the tips of the bow as it is stretched wide over the uneven openings of the mountain caves;
they seem to threaten the fire-flames blazing from the mouths of the arrows, which are resonant with the clear twang of the bowstrings. (Setubandha 26)

The bow, drawn by the one who has checked the current of the ocean and pulled it back, seems to expand. (Sētubandha 27) With its surface bristling with hair from the agitation of the waters, and with a multitude of fireflies darting out as they flee, the arrow of Rāma is recognized as having fallen into the sea even while it is being drawn back. (Sētubandha 28)

The faces of the quarters, their eyes the clouds, burst open, ignited by the fire emitted from the mouths of the smoke-colored, lightning-tawny-eyed serpents; thick masses of smoke burst forth from the bowstring drawn with the force of the arms.
(Setubandha 29) Then... [the mass of thick smoke] produced by the bow being drawn with the speed of the arms...
He drank the arrow whose tip was drenched by the rays of the sun, which were being extinguished by the flames of fire issuing from his mouth.

Having burned in the sky, he fell into the ocean like the day—its face darkened by the submarine fire that had been quenched by the water of the celestial expanse, and its length diminished by the setting sun. (Sētubandha 30–31)
In the sky, it is like a flash of lightning; on the surface of the ocean, it is like the fire of cosmic destruction;
and in the netherworld, it is like the submarine fire—such is the arrow of Rāma, which remains fixed as it falls and has already fallen.
(Setubandha 32)
Then, as he was not yet engaged in the path of battle, his arrows fell like the smokeless flames of a fire, or like the rays of the sun when it has half-settled into the ocean.
Furthermore, there arose a mass of filaments scattered from the faces of female elephants pierced by his arrows.
The ocean surged upward, roaring like a lion that had awakened from a state of trustful sleep.

(Sētubandha 34) When the ocean rose up with great speed at the moment of its breach along the edge of the sky, it was as if the heavens were being milked by the thick showers of spray scattered back and forth from afar.
(Sētubandha 35)
When the middle of Rāvaṇa’s city was severed by the impact of the arrow, the mass of the Malaya forest fell down like a mountain slope split open and flowing with water from a broken spring;
its slopes were uneven with the oozing mountain minerals and shattered peaks. (Sētubandha 36)
The regions of the ocean, deep with their agitated waters and rows of sea-monsters, are being churned up. (Sētu.

37) The swarm of conchs, their pale bellies opened wide and their mouths filled with spray, whirls about, casting off the veil of the white lotus buds that were slightly opened by the rays of the sun-like mango trees. (Sētu. 38)

The masses of water flow on, white with the fangs of sea-monsters mangled by the blows of schools of fleeing fish; the hoods of venomous serpents, bent low by the weight of their jewels, are tossing about. From the agitation caused by the bursting coral groves, rays of light from gems emerge and spread forth. (Sētubandha 39)

The ocean water churns the shore, with pearls leaping forth like foam. (Sētu 40) The whirlpools of the sea, their breadth revealed for a moment when the spray is cast up by the water, become turbid at their mouths as they subside once more. (Sētu 41)
The ocean, turning back and rolling as it was long ago compressed by the mountain, began to settle down with its second foothold on the nether world (Pātāla), as if loosening its grip.
[The verse continues:
...which was half-supported by the sea as it was obstructed by Mount Suvela, which had been pushed aside by the force of the arrows.
[The sky], having cast off the southern quarter, appears as if its single side has been torn away.
[It is] neither seen even by the Primordial Boar, nor touched even by Mount Mandara. (Setubandha 43)
Even those regions of the ocean, deep with the roar of the terrifying waves, become like the depths of the sea itself.

(Sētubandha 44) In each interval between the falling blows of his arrows, the ocean—trembling as if terrified by the fire at the end of the aeon—falls into the supportless sky and sinks, as it were, into the subterranean realm. (Sētubandha 45)

Timid fish are seen, stunned by the firm blows from the arrows of the nectar of the *āsādita* [tree], their backs resting against the overturned peaks of Mount Mandara; they are tossed about by the great whirlpools and rendered pale with the red hue of crushed coral. (Sētu 46)
At the water-stalls, the sighs of great serpents are seen as they coil around [the trees].

(Sētubandha 47) A pair of serpents, bound by love, their bodies pressed together in a tight embrace that brings them joy, cling to one another, each protecting the other with its own life. (Sētubandha 48)

The arrows of Rāma, which have shattered the coral branches, rush into the water like flashes of lightning; with their broad pearl-like tips clinging to their mouths as they emerge from the midst of oyster shells, they appear like the spreading smoke-clouds of a forest fire consuming a thicket of poison-trees. (Sētubandha 49)
It darkens like the blood of the great ocean, encircled by coral reefs. (Sētubandha 50) The mountains fall, their broad flanks pierced by arrows launched from the agitated ocean;
their peaks, bent down by the uneven weight, hang over the edge of the sky in a curved line. (Sētubandha 51)
With their lives sustained by the throats of snakes whose mouths have been cut open and torn asunder, and filled with rage,
serpents release their lives after having struck them down with showers of arrows that are their very glances.
(Sētubandha 52) It causes distress, [as it is] filled with the abundance of the mouths of hissing snakes with upraised hoods.
The fire, having shattered the openings and hollows of the mountain sites where the tips of its branches were rubbed against the rocks,
struck the mountain ridges with great waves provided by the mouths of the rivers that had been split open and swept away.
(Sētubandha 53)
The rows of coral trees are shattered by the tusks of sea-monsters that have been struck down and pierced;

[Sītā’s] eyes, reddened like ripe mangoes by the smoke of the forest fires, avoid the schools of fish that turn away from the light of the nets and stumble as they dart through the waves of the water. (Setubandha 54–55)

The serpents, their masses of twin tongues scorched by the suppression of the white fumes of the upward-turning smoke, glide along as they emerge, their wide intervals filled with rising, small waves;
they appear like trickling streams of liquid fat heated by the fire of the sacrificial flame. (Sētubandha 5.6)
The elephants and deer, their heads struck by the unevenly raised iron goads and hooks, [flee].

(Sētu 57) The multitude of conchs, eager to move onto the sandbanks of the shore where the water is receding and becoming shallow, rolls about upon the surfaces of the jewel-stones situated unevenly as the tide turns back. (Sētu 58)

By the scattering of wings from the flanks of the ocean tossed by the wind, the great mountains, rising up in agitation, support the mass of earth situated upon their single, successive peaks. (Setu 59) Deepened by the emergence of the heads of great asuras severed by the coils of snakes that have turned helplessly upward.
The masses of water from the netherworld, their foundations uprooted by the jewels [of Rāvaṇa’s chariot], are crying out in distress (Sētu 60b).

The waves of water, lightened by being scattered by the wind, rise into the sky with foam produced by the flames of the fire extinguished by the downpour of Bāṇa’s arrows, and they roar even in the firmament (Sētu 61).

The serpents, their strength of movement failing as they are dragged by the force of the flood that has carried away the splendor of their venomous hoods, coil themselves with their lower bodies twisted unevenly, snagged by high waves;
their coils are broken and scattered by the multitude of whirlpools in the rivers and lakes, which tremble as they are torn apart. (Setubandha 62)

Like hands, the waves fell with a loud cry released as they were submerged and then cast up by the ocean; their broad chests were gripped by the water-filled caves of the mountain ridges, which were themselves filled with the fire.
(Sētubandha 63)
The great mountains rise into the sky with the slow and smooth ascent of long-settled dust (Sētu 64).

The ocean water blazes, shimmering with the mass of flaming aquatic creatures; it swirls with the network of revolving jewel-creeper corals; it roars with its whirling eddies; and it breaks apart as the mountains shatter within it (Sētu 65).

Just as the ocean appears with its movement obstructed by the surfaces of jewel-stones whose dust whirls within the churning cavities, and which is uneven with rolling waves, so too does the fire appear; having leaped up from the Malaya forest ignited by passion, it spreads across the expanse of that very forest. (Setubandha 6.66)
Even as it is being extinguished, the ocean flares up once again.

(Sētubandha 67) With its mass of flames unrestrained by the fat and marrow of the elephants of the quarters whose tusks are pinned up, the fire spreads vast, having stripped away the mountain peaks from the mountains with its torrential force.
(Sētubandha 68)

With their roots uprooted by the fire and tossed upward by the force of the water, they fall back down, whirling in vast eddies as they descend against the current of the surging flood. (Sētubandha 69) It smokes, it burns, its foundation crumbles, it slackens and collapses the mountain peaks.
Even so, the first surge of the ocean does not break the resolve of the steadfast man.

(Sētubandha 70) The radiance of the eyes of the lord of serpents, of the whales bursting asunder in the midst of the sea, and of the clouds of the dissolution-age consumed by the fire at the end of the aeon, pours forth.
(Sētubandha 71)

The river currents, resembling the shafts of flaming torches cast into the sky, fall down like darkened flames of smoke rising from a mass of fire piled upon a mountain peak; their banks, whose sandy slopes have been repeatedly abandoned as the surging masses of water rise and fall, are now being overwhelmed. (Setubandha 72)
The ocean appears to retreat step by step from its course, as if it were a bridge.

(Sētu 73) In the mass of fire where the water is ablaze with flames, and in the sky where the mass of water has arisen, the mass of water stands still, obstructing the ten directions and the sun in the vault of heaven. (Sētu 74)
As the ocean was agitated by the submarine fire and its waters were tossed about,
the whirlpools of the sea became as dark as the wheels of the sun’s chariot when slowed down by the summer heat. (Sētubandha 75)
In that vast expanse, the fire whirls as if covered in dust, its crest mingled with the upward-rising luster of emeralds from the mass of billowing smoke;
the submarine fire burns, and the mountain, struck by Rāma’s arrows, seems to shatter apart. (Setubandha 76)

Like a fire agitated by the ocean, it licks [the world]; like the wind, it leaps across the expanse of the sky. (Sētu 77) When the water subsides, it subsides; when it turns back, it retreats; when it is broken apart, it falls asunder;
when it increases, it grows; and when the water diminishes, the fire alone is extinguished. (Sētu 78)

Those very same circles of islands, their shores divided by the ocean drying up as it was consumed by the fire of Rāma’s arrows, are seen again with their former extent and height, forming a continuous chain. (Setubandha 79) [Ākula 8]
Rāma destroys the ocean— which reveals the flames of the subterranean fire with its surging masses of water, crushes the great mountains, and dries up the multitudes of serpents—
while it emits a wailing cry from the shells of oyster-banks whirling as they are overturned by the flood of water. (Setu 80)
Where the wandering venomous serpents are partially scorched by the flames of the bursting submarine fire;

where the peaks of the jewel-mountains are discernible by the rays reflected from the diminishing waters; and where the branches of clouds, shattered and fallen, resemble forest creepers along the quarters darkened by thick waves. (Sētu 81–82)

It has heaps of lion-maned tigers torn apart by the sharp claws of elephants; it possesses the white tusks of lordly elephants encircled by terrified, venomous serpents nearby; it has clusters of coral vines broken by falling jeweled slabs from the peaks of washed-away mountains. (Setu 83)
The multitude of lordly elephants, distressed as they were submerged in the mire of poison vomited by snakes scorched by the forest fire;
the mountain peaks shattered one against another as they fell upon the shore surging at the Runda whirlpool;
and the quarters of the sky made uneven by smoke-streaks trembling as they clung to the edge of the heavens—[all these are seen] at the Setu. (Sētu 84–85)
[The bridge],

which has filled the quarters with the multitude of arrows discharged by those standing to protect its flanks, and whose gaping fissures are made prominent by the intense radiance of clear jewels emerging from within the broken waters— Sētu 86.
The great crocodiles [of the ocean] were agitated by the heat of their own eyes, which were closed as they were scorched by the fire of the wind-born [Hanumān];
the multitude of conchs was brought forth by the strikes of arrows from an ever-increasing passion. (Sētubandha 87) Thus, the fifth chapter is completed.
— [The Sixth Chapter of Consolation]— [p. 35]

[Ākula 5] Then he departed, leaving behind the Pātāla forest filled with smoke— the mass of trees where great serpents were scorched by the blazing interior— just as the ocean recedes from the quarters of the horizon. (Setubandha 1)
Carrying upon his shoulders— arms as long as his body and deep like the forest’s interior— the uneven slopes of Mount Rishyamuka,
which were once firmly polished by Mount Mandara, scarred by the tusk of the Primeval Boar as he emerged from the dissolution,
and pained by the strike of Rama’s arrows; (Sētubandha 2).
Carrying the river of the Malaya mountain, which seems as if tossed up by the smoke from the incense of fresh sandalwood;

and bearing the moon—the brother of the nectar of immortality—which, though shaken by the frantic churning of Mount Mandara that reduced the Kauthubha jewel to insignificance, has not lost its single-starry-pearl necklace. (Sētubandha 3–4)
He leaned against Rāghava,
his left arm— bearing the weight [of the earth], its hair bristling red with blood, its touch forbidden by the forest creepers, and supported by the Gaṅgā as it flowed—
resting upon the jewel-studded rock of Mount Malaya, which was smeared with the luster of his own body. (Setubandha 5)
Like a creeper separated from the tree that grants the fruit of its cherished joys, the earth was left bereft by Jānakī.

(Sētu 6) With the blood from the wounds of the arrows as its flowers and entwined with the vines of the overflowing jewels and gems [from the ornaments], he fell at Rāma’s feet like a tree whose roots have been violently uprooted by the wind of the ocean. (Sētu 7)

Afterwards, with a heart full of distress, she departed; with her hands and face disheveled, she fell there even while walking upon the lotus-like feet of Hari, which were marked with the signs of the trident.
(Setu 8) Then, though soft, [the speech] was capable of bearing weight; though brief, it was overflowing with the essence of meaning.
The ocean, though heavy with its vastness, remains unswollen even when filled by the tribute of the rivers, which is both weighty with the dignity of the steadfast and bound together by praise.

(Sētu 9) By you alone has it been established in its state, its difficulty of crossing made heavy by the firm grasp of the steadfast; yet, while you remain indifferent, some slight displeasure toward you was somehow caused by me. (Sētu 10)
In autumn, the honeybee, intoxicated by the nectar of the blossoms that darken the king of trees, hovers over the trees; yet it neither gives nor takes back its own flower. (Sētu. 11)

Have I forgotten myself— myself who fell upon the threefold path arising from your feet, who was consumed by the fire at the time of the dissolution, and who was tossed about during the upheaval of the earth?
(Sētu 12) [This occurred] when you raised up the earth with your feet, obstructing its face with the blows of your tusks.
By you, with your arrow that possesses the brilliance of lightning, the Ten-faced one was struck down today.
(Sētubandha 13) O steadfast one, even though she is in her own natural state, this grief has been endured by you;
for, O wise one, even though he is naturally gentle, he has caused a discrepancy in the radiance of your face. (Sētubandha 14)

Therefore, protect this mass of water, preserved since the dissolution of the world, which is capable of providing rest from the exhaustion of thousands of such divine tasks for you, and which is fit for the subduing of the enemy.
(Setu 15) Now, with its base firmly established, it proceeds there, shattering the surface of the earth.
"Indeed, even when I have consumed [the ocean] until it is emptied of its waters, the netherworld (pātāla) will not be difficult to traverse.

(Setu 16) Having heard that speech of Rāvaṇa—which was uttered with some difficulty as his ten throats were torn open by Time, which was joined to the bridge of mountains, and which had long been drawn out—[Rāma spoke]. (Setu 17)

[The battle] ended when the Ocean-like Rāvaṇa, enraged by the unbearable harassment caused by the victory, was calmed by Rāghava— just as the ocean is restrained by an arrow— in the very presence of the Lord of the Monkeys. (Sētubandha 18)
The command of the Lord of Monkeys, having reached the forest-dwellers,
was like the earth— heavy with the essence of the three worlds cast upon the hoods of the serpent Śeṣa— descending upon the monkeys.
Then, moved by the first surge of joy, their eyelashes quivered and trembled.
The forest trees on the mountain ridges shook off their masses of filaments;

the ocean, emitting a clamor from its peaks as they fell—shaken by the monkeys and washed over the surface of the earth—surged upward like a bridge being constructed by mountains rushing together from all sides. (Sētubandha 20–21)
The mountain range of Mahendra trembles from the agitation of the ocean's waves, and the earth's crust splits apart;
yet, though soaked by the constant rain of foul weather, the pollen of the flowers in the Malaya forest does not rise up. (Sētubandha 22)
Then the army of monkeys, having lifted the mountain as if it were balanced on the tip of a scale, flew into the sky with the earth clinging to the tips of their tails, shaking equally as they moved;
the ocean, its waters flowing upstream against the mouths of the rivers and the surface of the earth rising and falling, followed after them. (Sētubandha 23)
The mountain performs the service of supporting the monkeys, who have become weary from the exhaustion of crossing the mass of waters.
(Sētubandha 24) Wherever the region of the sky is seen filled with monkeys leaping without interval, tawny as flickering flames, there it is perceived as a mass of smoke. (Sētubandha 25)
The monkey army is seen plunging into the ocean with its splendor sinking face-downward;

it appears like the netherworld (pātāla) descending, longing to lift up the mountain that supports the earth, as the multitude of directions vanishes and the world is obstructed by the host of monkeys. (Setubandha 26)
Even at the end of the day when the face of the sky is darkened by scattered clouds, the sky appears as if it were the close of day;

and the monkeys have descended upon the mountains, their backs resting on the slopes with impetuosity, while the rays of the sun stream forth from them, filling the depths of the caves with the echoes of their cries. (Sētubandha 27–28)

And they began to weigh the mountain peak—which had been uprooted by the gods, whose joints with the earth had been shattered, which was released from its bonds, and which remained somehow supported and held by serpents—as if it were a balance-beam; their broad cheeks, like mountain slopes, were pressed against their chests as they exerted themselves. (Setubandha 29)

The forest-dwellers fled from the agitation caused by the flight of the monkeys who had leaped over the mountain peaks; the mountains were left behind on the crags, and the great trees, heavy with their own weight, fell upon the other trees.
(Sētubandha 30) From the slopes, the mountain peaks were uprooted by the calves [of the monkeys], and the mountain ridges were overturned by the falling calves;
thus, the mountains became like mountains upon the mountains, and the great trees became like trees upon the trees. (Sētubandha 31)

The edges of the earth became uneven, rising up as they were pushed back by the mountains tossed upward by the arms of the wind, while the oceans repeatedly filled them as they turned over. (Sētubandha 32)

The mountain-bearers are capable of enduring the blows of thunderbolts, for they are like pillars against the winds of cosmic destruction; they are powerful enough to withstand the rising floods of the deluge, having disregarded the friction of the boar’s tusk.
They have been struck by the waters of the ocean and released, falling again into the riverbeds of the autumnal torrents. (Setu 33)
The mountains, their foundations loosened by being uprooted with a single stroke, crumble; Sētu 34.
