Shaken, they tremble; pressed down by the monkeys, they bend; bent, they incline; and when lifted up, they toss the surface of the earth aloft; Sētu 35.

The great mountains of the earth, their foundations loosened by the pressure of the Dalita-mahī-veḍha formation, sink into the netherworld even as they are being pulled by the hosts of elephants and shaken.
Fanned by cool breezes from the water beneath them, which is as green as fresh sprouts... [Sētubandha 36]
The Malaya trees, bewildered by being uprooted and tossed by the hands of Indra at that very moment, shed their blossoms.

(Sētubandha 37) The female swan, seated upon a thousand lotuses, seems as if she were resting on the news of her husband’s welfare; for she is surrounded by clouds driven by the wind from the peaks of the trembling mountains. (Sētubandha 38)
The currents of the rivers, having been drawn out by the wind and forced into the interior of the mountains, swirl and stumble unevenly;
they roar deeply as their exit is blocked by the broad expanse of the chest-like slopes.
(Setubandha 39) [The mountain] is half-raised, with its loosened slope-path half-dragged by serpents and half-stopped.

They uproot the mountains that were submerged in the mud of the netherworld at the mouths of the rivers—[Sētubandha 40]. As the great mountains are lifted up, the surface of the sky seems to surge upward; as they are lowered again, it seems to sink back down—[Sētubandha 41].

The mountain peaks, firmly grasped by the monkeys with their arms as steady as mountain summits, have their uneven, gaping fissures filled by the earth being lifted up from beneath; they are supported by the tight coils of serpents that were dragged out and released by the arms of Hari. (Setubandha 42)

Even when breaking, the branches of the sandalwood tree do not fall, for they are held up by the earth; the deep roar of the clouds filling the sky, which was long bound to the heavens, now subsides. (Sētubandha 43)
The roar of the mountain being shattered by the arms of Hari, which proclaims his prowess, resounds through the sky.
(Sētu 44) The rivers, cast by the arms of the monkeys toward the great mountain, turn back;
their currents swirl toward the mountain, heated by the dust being stirred up. (Sētu 45)

Mountains appear like whirlpools formed by rivers turning back within the great ocean, as they are caught in the eddies of the currents swirling from their own momentum; [they are] cast out by forest creepers swaying under the heavy weight of the nectar [of the blossoms]. (Sētubandha 46)
The pair of bees does not abandon the cluster of blossoms, even though its honey-nectar has been tasted.

(Sētubandha 47) The lotus groves, delighted by the fragrant pollen and nectar rising upward, and graced by swarms of bees hovering and resting upon them, have blossomed at the touch of the sun and appear as if washed in the waters of the lakes. (Sētubandha 48)
The mountains, their roots firmly gripped by the arms of monkeys who have clung to their peaks, are tossed about by the upraised hoods of venomous serpents enraged by the noise;
the rivers are overwhelmed by the currents of great streams flowing together from all sides. (Setubandha 49)
For a moment, they were carried along by the mountain ridges submerged in the mud stirred up by the elephants;

then the lords of the serpents, their white and black lusters twisting unevenly on all sides, were dragged out as they clung to the roots of the mountains and rolled back and forth against the red arsenic. (Sētubandha 50–51)

The creepers of the forest deities, who were fleeing in terror from the mountain being uprooted by Rāma, shed even their fresh blossoms and cast off their young shoots that had not yet been bound together.
(Sētubandha 52)
In an instant, the earth is known to be entirely uprooted from all directions; the sky is made whole by the great mountains;

the quarters of space are filled with the peaks of the waters; and the creeper-like horizons are expanded by the mountain-tops. (Setubandha 53) And each one, lifting a mountain held by the pair of his lotus-like hands, has performed [this feat].
The sky is half-filled with [the bodies of] elephants, and the surface of the earth has its netherworld half-exposed;

the mountain slopes, where the riverbeds are revealed by the sparse tracks left by their feet, reach the very edge of the earth’s surface as they are supported by the hoods of the lords of serpents. (Sētubandha 54–55)
The earth-shaker has set forth with his moving caves; the herd of elephants is bursting through the unobstructed ravines;
the mountain peaks, curved with fresh harītakī trees, bend unevenly under the weight of the monkey troops.
Having emerged from the treetops, he is enveloped by a spreading mass of dust raised by the wind purified by the Malaya forest. (Setu 56)
The pollen of flowers, crushed by the rays of the sun, settles upon the sky like the twilight glow.

(Sētu 57) The great mountains grow as if they were composed of mud from the waters uplifted from the netherworld by their incessant roots being pulled out; thus it is known that they do not leave the surface of the earth. (Sētu 58)
The sky was filled by the peaks of Mount Malaya, which had been obtained by Mahendra;
and the earth was filled by the elephants of the Vindhya ridges, who were named after their pride and whose full names were known for their strength.
The measurement of the mountain peaks was surpassed by the heads of the arms [of Rāvaṇa], and the measure of the caves was exceeded by his chests.
The mountains, with their forest-clefts, were equalled by the monkeys' fore-paws as they reached into the caves;
their faces turned toward their ears and their arms stretched out and lowered. (Sētubandha 60)
"Does the herd of elephants sleep, their eyes closed in slumber, or does it rest, exhausted from wandering? (Setu 61) "The trees are crushed, appearing like mountains overturned;
the clouds are shattered, sounding like the crashing of Mount Mahendra; and the forest creepers are whirling, as if the earth itself were being slightly uprooted. (Setu 62)
Even as they were being crushed with a roar by the mountain peaks tossed down by the arms of the monkey, the serpents—
whose hoods were pinned down by the weight of the mountain that served as their food— could not be seen.
(Sētubandha 63) The mountain, having slightly revealed the netherworld and causing the serpents to emerge from their holes, toss them up in distress and let them fall back down.
The earth’s circumference, with its mountains barely able to support it, appears as if it were being carried away by the poets;
even the schools of fish lose their lives, yet the rivers do not abandon them.

As the mountains are swept away in the agitation, the eyes of the buffalo herds—long as rivers—are not left behind, like the jeweled stone creepers of the forest sandalwood trees. Even a remnant does not remain of the rising darkness, just as there is none left of the sandalwood trees when they are destroyed by fire. (Setu 64–65)

In some places, mountains fall with their peaks shattered; in others, they are split by the arms of the mountain-dwellers, leaving them hemmed between stone slabs that have burst apart; and in yet others, they fall with their summits broken in half. (Sētubandha 66) That mountain whose peak is shattered falls, while that one which remains whole is held up.
He himself is being sent away even while the burden [of grief] remains unfulfilled.

(Sētubandha 67) With their ears separated by the movement of their eyes, weeping, they let fall tears from their ear-tips; and in this separation from the young elephant, they consider hope to be poison, as the leader of the herd speaks with a dejected face. (Sētubandha 68)

As the earth is agitated by the lord of serpents, who has lowered his hoods out of resentment toward the king intent on removing the mountain, so too does it become capable of supporting the weight of the monkeys' bodies. (Sētubandha 69)

The mountains have collapsed upon their mid-slopes and at the bases of their ridges; their stone enclosures, loosened by the violent displacement of their once-still arms [the peaks], have fallen from the half-summits and the foothills.
The sky seems to have been lifted up high, and the horizons appear as if drawn back. (Sētubandha 70)
The surface of the earth appears like a mountain being uprooted by monkeys;

from the deep chasms where the mountains collapsed under the weight of the hosts of monkeys, there issues forth the spreading radiance of the jewels on the hoods of the serpent Śeṣa, who has emerged as a refuge for the clouds of the cataclysmic dissolution. (Sētubandha 71–72)

Even the arm-strength of the lord of the night-rangers, which had once been as solid as Mount Kailāsa, was rendered insignificant by the monkeys who, lifting one mountain after another, hurled them down;
[a strength] where the masses of darkness were met by the radiance of the sun falling through the gaps between the uprooted mountains. (Sētubandha 73)
The netherworld has become pale with smoke, its darkness thinned.

(Sētu 74) And by you, who performed the lifting of the mountain-dweller without regard for yourselves, though your mouths were intent solely on the task of your master, you have made yourselves vessels of glory. (Sētu 75)

The masses of mountains, though heavy, became light; their broad bases were fixed upon the peaks of the monkeys' arms, and their waterfalls were cast far away by the winds forcefully exhaled in haste.
(Setubandha 76) Then, with great effort, he drew up the entire multitude of monkeys and the mass of mountains.
Even with their wings, they easily flew into the sky, having abandoned all clamor.
(Sētubandha 77) The poets, though unsteady, leaped lightly as if to fly;
yet, heavy with their expansive bodies, they crossed the sky in a single bound like mountains with their wings. (Sētubandha 78)

The earth-girdle, which flows forth from the eastern direction, released and scattered toward the sky, then turning back as it strikes the mountains joined together at the mouths of the rivers; (this is the Setu). 79.
The forests enchant [the beholder] as they are gazed upon by those who, though their minds are fixed on the great mountains within them, have turned back from their flight out of fear;
they look about with faces bewildered and agitated by the sudden shifting of the terrain.
(Sētu 80) The uprooted trees, having fallen and being tossed upward, descend straight down...
The river currents have set out along the path of the Nīrāja mountains as they are being carried away.

(Sētu 81) The sky—where the essence of the clouds has been crushed, where the mountain ranges are split apart within the openings of the caves, and where the sun is obscured by revolving peaks—is struck by the upward-facing antelopes. (Sētu 82)
The monkeys turn back, their right hands raised as they lift mountain peaks placed upon their shoulders, while their upturned left palms support the expanse of their hips;
for even at the start of their journey, there was no limit to those who rushed forth out of mere curiosity. (Sētu 83)
That very [bridge] became their protection; for poets and mountains alike, the sky is their own domain.

(Sētu 84) The mountain ranges—whose base edges met as they were lifted up by the monkey host of equal strength, and whose river mouths were rubbed away by the friction of their peaks rising one after another—are now bearing [the weight]. (Sētu 85)

Having observed for a long time, the rivers pass by the sites of the first great mountains, which resemble the ocean and appear weary under the burden of the earth; these sites were established by the mountain-rivers being tossed upward by the wind from the masses of clouds joined in an instant. (Setu 86)
Like the currents of great rivers, they carry along the clouds that increase in volume within the vault of the sky.

(Sētu 87) On the mountain peaks that touch the surface of the sky as high as the mountains themselves, the forest-rivers, with their boulders joined together like tusks, do not emerge even when the monkeys have scattered them, though they have been dispersed by the monkeys. (Sētu 88)
The faces of the directions, whose trembling breasts were revealed by the mountain caves and whose slender waists were glimpsed within the mountain clefts,
closed their eyes as if from the inhalation of the fragrant pollen of flowers. (Sētu 89) The monkeys,
holding with their palms the trembling serpents that had burst forth from the mouths of the sky, [restrained them].

The great mountains, their peaks shattered by the force of the earth and their slopes split open, are being steadied by the hands of the monkeys who have rushed forth at the impact against the surface of the sky;
yet they stumble upon the mountain peaks that are being carried away by those same monkeys. (Setu 90)

The mountain torrents, which for a moment become the currents of great rivers, [subside]. (Sētubandha 91) When the clouds emerge from being crushed against the slopes by the mass of trees uprooted by the wind, the mountains—where herds of elephants sit within the cave-mouths of the cliffs, cooled by the ancient waterfalls—carry the rainwater away. (Sētubandha 92)
The mountain peak of Malaya, with its interior being carried away by monkeys who have rushed forth in haste, runs as if it were a severed arm, following the path of its own shadow.
Though looked for, they were not seen; though searched for, they were not found by those who had descended together.
By those poets who did not cast even the uprooted great mountains into the ocean—
[by them] the mountain range, filled with broken trees and fragments, strewn with uplifted, shattered, and fallen peaks,
appears to the monkeys like a second bridge as it reaches the sea. (Sētubandha 94–95)
The monkey army, having seized the mountains with their trunks, turned back after reaching the edge of the shore;
facing toward Rāma, their eyes blossomed with passion. (Setubandha 96) Thus ends the sixth canto in the epic poem *Daśamukhavadha* composed by the illustrious Pravarasena.
[The Seventh Consolation] [p.
45] [The Seventh Consolation]

Then they began to construct the causeway, which was marked by the fame of Rāma—who had exhaled his breath after his heroic efforts—and which surpassed the heat of the sun with its peaks that leaped over the ocean.
Just then, the great mountains, released from the surface of the earth, were cast into the sea by the monkeys. (Setubandha 1)
The surface of the earth was split open by the powerful trampling of the boar’s snout.

When the mass of mountains fell, it was not seen from afar; when they shook, they were momentarily struck down; when they were shattered, they were cast away; and as they subsided, the ocean swelled. (Sētubandha 2–3)

The water of the great ocean, which had first surged forth, became dark with the shadows of the trees dragged along by the sea-monsters tossing up their tails, as it whirled around the hollows; meanwhile, the great mountains were submerged in the water, yet the masses of those mountains remained unseen as they merged back together. (Setubandha 4)
Thus, even though its peaks were joined together, the expanse of the intermediate space between heaven and the ocean appeared [as if divided].
(Setubandha 5) The mountains, which had caused fear in the enemy, were shaken by the monkeys;
the ocean was not merely agitated, for even the great efforts of those with powerful hearts are indeed heavy. (Setubandha 6)

The earth is known by its mountains, the ocean is known because it is bound by this [bridge], and the lands are known by the water in the midst of the sea; where have they gone? [Yet] the path of the sun’s chariot is obstructed by the thousands of vast peaks that encircle the entire earth. (Setu 7)
Yet even that lofty great mountain vanished like a blade of grass within the mouth of the Timingila fish.
(Setu 8) Whatever water, raised up by the mountain peaks, rushed toward the vault of the sky, that appeared together with the jewels as if it were a circle of falling stars. (Setu 9)
Even though they are obstructed by the broad, rolling torrents of their own waterfalls diverted by monkeys,
these mountains whirl about as if they have not yet reached the ocean, within the circles of its eddies. (Sētubandha 10)

The mass of mountains, having first met in the sky, falls into the ocean; meanwhile, the host of monkeys, who had been cast away and thrown into the gaps between the peaks, now emerges from within them. Long and wide gashes, filled with wind, turn toward the sea. (Setu 11)
The mountain torrents, having pierced deep into the heart of the Pāriyātra mountains, become the paths for the elephants of the quarters.
(Sētubandha 12) Lifted up and then released into the sky, each mountain shattered upon its descent falls into the ocean of jewels like those struck by lightning out of fear. (Sētubandha 13)

Dusted with the pollen of flowers fallen from trees shaken by the peaks of split rock-crags, the mountain torrents fall first; afterwards, the great river currents, driven by the wind, follow. (Setu 14) Their uneven course of movement is visible as it is divided within the midst of the pure waters.
The great mountains, observed by the monkeys stationed upon them, do not sink down for a long time.

(Sētubandha 15) The jewels, emerging from the depths of the ocean with their rays trembling as they pass through the flower-like foam, indicate that the great sea has been agitated at its very root. (Sētubandha 16)
Like Time, he shakes the earth; like the Equal One (Yama), he splits the multitude of mountain peaks;
like Fear, he seizes the sky; and like his own nature, the ocean releases the underworld.
As the branches of trees return through the gaps between the revolving mountain ridges, they grow intertwined.

The mountain peaks, from which waterfalls tumble as the ocean mouths are bent down by their roots, appear like mountains whose slopes are darkened by the dense clouds of water falling from the great peaks; yet, when the mountains themselves have subsided, it is only the echo from the agitated ocean that proclaims the presence of those mountains as they fall. (Sētubandha 18–19)
With their faces smeared with mountain dust, which is sticky from contact with the pollen of the saffron flowers shaken by their tails,
the monkeys retreat, their shoulders heaving as they drag along great mountains.
(Sētubandha 20)

The great mountains, their upper slopes shaken by the light winds from the cascading torrents, fall into the ocean with their peaks cast upward by the clouds; they are like heaps of flowers gathered by the waters retreating after breaking through the paths of the submerged mountains. (Sētubandha 21)
There are groves of Kadamba trees, fragrant with the pollen of yellowish-green blossoms, [swaying] in the wind.
(Sētu 22) The wild buffaloes of the forest, their eyes bloodshot and rolling like coppery [leaves], fall upon the mountain peaks that have been shaken by the force of the angry waters;
they twist their bodies in single spirals as they struggle. (Sētu 23)
Though they had been separated and then reunited, the herd of deer was once again made happy by the sight of one another;
as they were carried along by the waves raised by the mountain-like elephants, their forms were drawn out like streaks of ink.
(Sētubandha 24) The tusks of the rutting elephants, whose temples were split open, were being pulled out by the steady trunks [of other elephants].
The lions roar from the cave-like mouths filled with pearls, embryos, and blood.
(Sētubandha 25) The female elephants, having overturned the male elephants and fallen, fall down with fierce rage at the shock of the collapsing mountain;
their bodies are disheveled as they are bitten by the male elephants who have descended and lost their senses. (Sētubandha 26)
The forest creepers have entwined themselves around the trees as if struggling, their faces—the mountain peaks—turned away in fear as they tremble at the sprouting young shoots;
meanwhile, the earth resounds with the roar of masses of mountains being simultaneously uplifted and cast down. (Setu 27)
The underworld of the ocean is incessantly opened up by the earth.

(Sētubandha 28) Surrounded by rows of waterfalls that gush forth and swirl from their mouths, and embraced by creepers that cling to the masses of dense clouds, the great mountains fall down. (Sētubandha 29)
The hosts of monkeys pass by, their mountain peaks shattered by the thrusts of their respective arms;
they are followed by surges of water leaping up from the sky as their thick manes are washed clean.
Again and again, the ocean appears filled with the mass of water tossed up by the impact against the mountains.
The netherworld, with its vast interior like the expanse of the sky or the hollow of the heavens,
has its lotus-forests withered by the water that flowed from the surface of the earth when it was shattered by the agitation [of the ocean]. (Setubandha 31)
The great mountains fall, their peaks shattered and crumbling as they are seized by the helpless lord of elephants.

(Sētu 32) The ocean roars as its shores are split by the impact of the mountain; it leaps, it turns back, stumbling over uneven ground, and reaches a state of churning; yet, even now, it does not yield the nectar of immortality. (Sētu 33)
With the rocks uprooted and polished, the ocean’s roar intensified as it was struck;
even the means for reaching the city of the Rākṣasas involved a terrible undertaking.
(Sētubandha 34) There, the golden rock-enclosures were tossed about by the wind, rising into the sky and spinning.
The mountain range, its valleys fragrant with flowers, is cast down by the wind stirred up by the monkeys (Sētu 35).
The ocean, its mouth turned back as it hears the clamor of the monkeys, swells;
the mountains, their trees blown away by the wind, fall with their waterfalls standing upright (Sētu 36).
The great river fish, dragged from afar, turned back, crushed, and ground upon the sandbanks, are gasping piteously as they are violently tossed into the ocean by the force of the current.
With their uneven flanks shattered, they lie there, clutching the jewels of venomous serpents.
The mountain ranges, with their green caves above the thickets of trees, were shrouded by the rays of the sun.

(Sētu 38) Having turned back, the Lord of Serpents somehow supported the circumference of the earth—which was uneven at its extremities—upon the ocean whose waters had been drained from the mountain slopes by the wind-swept cavities. (Sētu 39)
The earth, along with its fear of fault, forgot at once the pressure from the hooves of the Boar who lifted it; and the ocean remembered its agitation during the churning.
[Setubandha 40] Remembering, as it were, the sorrow of the churning that had been cast down in the Malaya sandalwood groves, he remembered.

The mountain peaks, their waters having receded due to the fault of the lord of rivers (the ocean), are being licked by the elephants of the quarters; as the mountains rise up from the water that has subsided, they appear like crushed coral and lotuses. (Setubandha 41)
The mass of spray from the mountain peaks, like a cloud of mineral dust stirred up by the pounding of the waves, mingles with the ocean water as it rolls over the mountains;

the seawater resounds as it flows over the peaks, its surface stained by the mineral juices squeezed out by the crushing of the mountain summits, and it overflows with the essence of crushed sandalwood and medicinal herbs. (Sētubandha 42–43)

Trees with their leafy branches meeting the roots of the water as it falls from the mountains and flows upward, though not drawn up by the sky due to their lightness, become attached to it; so too do trees with their leafy branches meeting the roots of the water as it falls from the mountains and flows upward, though not drawn up by the sky due to their lightness, become attached to it. (Sētubandha 44) By the forces of the monkeys, who were filled with royal pride and terrified the celestial nymphs by rending the clouds that obscured the sky—by the forces of the monkeys, who were filled with royal pride and terrified the celestial nymphs by rending the clouds that obscured the sky—

The waters of the ocean are split apart by the mountains whose peaks are pushed aside by their firmly fixed, white, protruding tusks. (Sētubandha 45) The Mahendra mountain peak falls, its caves filled with wind, its masses of rocks shattered by the force of the wind, and pregnant with the rainbows of Indra rising from the mountain torrents. (Sētubandha 46)
In the sky, the mountain peaks themselves— whose water-filled caves have been silenced by the impact of the rocks and whose interiors are filled with the roar [of the waters]—
have surely fallen, for the vine-groves are now devoid of their abundance and the sandalwood trees are stripped of their leaves.
(Sētubandha 47) The mountains are visible in the ocean, their forms carved out by the fierce winds whirled up by the collision with the peaks.
Even though they are joined by the foam of blood flowing from their wounds, the herd-leaders do not abandon the forest thickets out of fear;
the Siddhas, however, abandon the leaf-huts that have become drenched with sweat born from the intensity of their amorous play. (Sētubandha 48)
The sighs vanish into the mouths of the mountain rivers; the waters of the great ocean whirl through the quarters of the sky.
(Sētu 49) A herd of elephants has arrived, their trunks raised high, warding off the pure crocodiles with their tusks;
they circle about, their faces turned toward the vast, turbulent whirlpools. (Sētu 50)

Rāghava somehow casts his gaze upon the rivers, whose banks are entwined by creepers from the broad mountain peaks falling down in masses, and which are tossed by the force of winds swirling through their channels;
yet he does not perceive them within his heart, for they are merely known [as objects of sight].
(Setubandha 51) The forests of coral are slightly scorched, and the conch shells are blackened by the smoke of forest fires.
The masses of water, their reeds withered by Rāma’s arrows drawn back against the netherworld, [seem to] wail;
the netherworld itself is seen with its waters divided, its mountains overturned as they collapse under their own weight in fear, and its serpents awakened and writhing. (Sētubandha 52–53)

The lordly elephants fall, having been intercepted by other lordly elephants who were intent upon them; they had stumbled as they fled from the great mountain situated on the shore facing the agitated ocean, yet they were caught by those other elephant-kings.
(Sētubandha 54) Even so, the monkeys—though heavy with their broad hips tossed upward—did not [reach] the root of the underworld...
Just as the great mountains come surging forward, carrying with them a mass of water tossed up and scattered;

and as the waves of the ocean, having struck the trees and mountain ranges, turned back by the blows of the peaks, become dazed and turn upward when dashed against the coastal rocks— *Setubandha* 55–56.
From the caves of the mountain, whose peaks are shattered as it is being scaled by a herd of elephants reeling from the poison of the half-eaten *aṣṭamī* moon,
a pair of deities emerges like its very life suddenly departing into the sky.
(Sētu 57)
The mountain peaks are held up by the arms, the trees by the trees, and the masses of clouds by the clouds;
it is not even known whether they are binding or lifting the vault of the sky.

(Setu 58) One by one, dispatched in haste, the earth-supporting mountains fall into the ocean as they turn and shake off their rocks. They crush the netherworld (rasātala), which has its clefts opened by the great serpents who have slithered out from their hoods, broken by the pressure of those earth-bearing mountains. (Setu 59)

That water of the ocean which perishes—turbid with falling mountain fragments from the crushed mountains of Maṇōśilā—is indeed the terrible fruit of [Rāvaṇa] being gazed upon by Jānaki, who was overwhelmed with tears as she watched the lords of the night-stalkers (the Rākṣasas) being torn apart.
(Sētubandha 59) The mountain rocks are pulverized within the depths of the sea; the expanses of the leaders of the jewel-mines are ground to dust.
The sky is filled with the rows of swans that are the clouds of the ocean, and with the forest ranges that serve as its girdles. (Sētubandha 60)

The netherworld licks [the earth], the earth splits open, masses of water spout forth, and the peaks of mountains fall into the courtyard of the sky. Struck by the mountain, the ocean itself rolls for a long time upon the dry land.

The rows of trees, fallen into the sea with their branches still clinging to them and adorned with fresh sprouts like floral ornaments, become decorated with thick, white pearls emerging from the midst of split oyster shells. The forests on the mountains that have set [into the sea] are trampled by the jealous forest-dwelling elephants. *Sētubandha 61* [The forests on the mountains that have set into the sea are trampled by the jealous forest-dwelling elephants.]
The dust of flowers, like a banner, covers the forests whose splendor is enhanced by the unremitting fragrance of flowing honey;
the host of monkeys advances, the vault of the sky blossoms, and the ocean receives them. (Sētubandha 62)
They even give the earth, and even the netherworld with its vast, gaping caverns.

(Sētu 63) Thus do the monkeys agitate the ocean—the abode of sea-monsters—whose buffaloes are refreshed by mountain mud adorned with the foam of the waves, and whose waters are joined by aquatic creatures on forest shores where trees have become entwined with coral. (Sētu 64)
The forest, where lions roar in opposition, enraged by the scent of the forest-elephants;
where the herds of elephants turn back in fear as mountain peaks fall before them, creating a swirling vortex;
and which is strewn with yellow leaves fallen from the trees on the forest floor, withered by the transformation of the setting sun—[Sētu 65].
With fish rolling about, exhausted by the bitter taste of the sap flowing from the broken trees of passion;

with masses of creepers whose tender sprouts and leaves are bent down by the weight of the mountain; and with poisonous-colored flowers withering from being struck by the wind of poisonous hue—Sētu 66–67.
The sky is filled with the spray from mountain peaks whirling in eddies;
the poison of the serpents, rising up from the underworld, is overwhelmed by the fragrance of medicinal herbs.
[The ocean] is being surpassed by the splendor of the mountain ridges as they turn within the circles of its whirlpools. (Setu 68)

The course of the bridge, appearing as if fashioned from the sky, is seen falling into the ocean; it is composed of mountains joined together without interval, having been cast down in an unbroken succession, while being illuminated by the luster of the jewels on the wide-spreading hoods of the serpents of the netherworld. (Sētubandha 69–70)
Then the monkeys, with great exertion, began to seize one after another those bridge-rafters capable of joining Lanka together,
as if they were [seizing] their own passion (*anurāga*) which is capable of uniting the ends of Laṅkā.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, the *Āśvāsa*.
— [The Eighth Chapter of Consolation]—
[The Eighth Chapter of Consolation]—

When the great mountains, whose peaks were washed by the torrents falling from their summits, drenched the masses of the celestial chariots of the gods, and whose vastness filled the expanse of the sky,
The poets established those great mountains at the edge of the shore, their slopes having been scraped away by the palms of the hands of the Nisuddhas, Śeṣas, Āvevas, and Uvvattas;
they were marked with the weight of the digging tools, yet remained exhausted from the upheaval of the mountains, having failed to achieve even the first stage of their journey. (Setubandha 2)

The masses of ocean water, as if moved by the gentle swaying of the mountain, [rush forth]; then the sea recedes, its whirlpools broken and their boundaries blurred, with great mountains tumbling within the shifting eddies, and its waters scattered and withdrawn from the agitation caused by the mountain’s fall. (Sētu 3–4)
The state of calmness of the ocean is seen, momentarily difficult to perceive, as its tumultuous roar ceases and its swirling eddies, which were previously directed toward their accustomed places,
subside. (Setubandha 5) [It appears] like a pearl-clustered flower, filled with circular ripples of emerald-green waves.
The water, white as a conch shell and possessing young shoots touched by coral, brings tranquility.

(Sētu 6) As it recedes, the reflection of the setting sun appears like a mass of mineral mud upon the surface of the ocean of reddish tawny clouds, with flowers scattered as they rise up, washed clean in an instant. (Sētu 7)
The male elephants, having lost their scent from the forest, turn back again;
distressed by the oncoming wind, they repeatedly shake their faces with their trunks.
Their waters are turbid from breaking trees and white with foam broken by the taste of bitter *kaṣāya*. (Sētubandha 8)
The faces of the rivers become grey with the dust raised by their surging and swirling currents.
(Sētu 9) The peaks of Mount Mahendra, cast up from the agitated ocean, have been joined to the slopes of the Malaya mountains as if to sever the mountain walls;
meanwhile, the herds of elephants are crushed upon the ridges of the Malaya range, and the summits of Mount Mahendra are likewise joined. (Sētu 10)

The sandbanks appear like rows of pearls, white with foam, with their surfaces covered by circular ripples of water receding after the rain has ceased, and with pearls clinging closely together from the incessant dripping of the clouds. (Sētubandha 11)

The masses of water, which had been tossed up by the mountain strike, were long gazed upon by the sky-dwellers as they returned from their flight; now, having struck the mouths of the caves, they roar with a hollow sound.
Then, his eyes fixed on Nala, he speaks while seated upon a crumbling jeweled stone throne.
The lord of monkeys, bearing the weight of Tārā—who was seated upon his left thigh as he turned around—crossed over the earth-girdle where mountains stood far apart;
yet the path of the bridge did not appear, for the heavy bow of Rāma would surely have bent again. (Sētubandha 13–14)
Is it because the ocean, having spoken, did not give the moon its nectar, nor Lakṣmī with her Kaustubha jewel,
nor the wish-fulfilling tree its jewels,
that it remains even today emitting smoke from its depths, clinging to the body of the underworld? (Setu 15)
The arrows of Rāma extinguished the fire with the sound of the splashing water;
O steadfast one, build that bridge today while you are still far from its end, until the vast expanse of the ocean is divided into two parts between Mount Malaya and Mount Suvela. (Setubandha 16–17)

Then Nala, his splendor clearly emerging from the assembly of monkeys who were shaken by the power of the wind-gods, spoke with eyes wide with fear and agitation at the sudden onset of the monkey-lord:
"O Lord of Monkeys, it is said before the presence of the Lord of the Wind-gods that you are fearless. (Setu 18)
In this matter produced by the construction of your bridge, your promise shall not prove false.
(Sētubandha 19) The mass of mountains has been exhausted as if the underworld were being crushed;
the ocean has been shaken as if its very life were being surrendered; today your promise has been fulfilled. (Sētubandha 20)

Behold that bridge, a vast expanse upon the surface of the earth, constructed like a great ocean within the circle of the world, joined with the mountains being piled up, and possessing the mountain range of Suvela as its central peak. (Sētu 21)
What need is there for the monkey host to cross the ocean by means of a bridge constructed from mountains joined together incessantly,
when the circle of the earth has already been lifted up by the wind? Behold,
Malaya itself, as if seeking its own reflection, has gone toward Suvela.

May he shake the ocean, which is obstructed and agitated by the great beings, like a pot with his mouth. (Setu 23) I shall construct a bridge-path capable of supporting the movement of monkeys who have rushed forward swiftly through the sky, with mountain peaks joined together in successive rows. (Setu 24)
O mountains of the netherworld, having cast yourselves motionless upon the surface within the interior of the ocean, with your flanks touching the clouds, bring about the destruction of Laṅkā!
O you who have not yet set out on my path, release the great mountains according to your respective duties. (Setubandha 25)
The army of monkeys set forth, its faults visible even from afar, a bond of happiness for those who were weary, a causeway [to the other shore].

(Sētu 26) Thus, at the sound of Nala’s words, the monkey host—its fatigue vanished and its weariness cast off by joy, letting out a tumultuous roar, and filling the ten directions with the weight of its bodies as it moved like shifting mountains—set out.
(Sētu 27)
Then, having bathed slowly in the water that was fragrant with the touch of his beloved, he first paid homage to the feet of Rāma and afterwards to the son of the Sun (Yama). (Setubandha 28)
Then, with its caves filled by the trees of the *ambōsa* creeper whose sprouts were like molten gold,
Mount Maināka was first cast into the ocean by Nala like an auspicious vessel for the journey; likewise,
that mountain was first positioned by Nala upon the edge of the shore.
Just as the commencement of the bridge-building for the sake of Laṅkā’s destruction was seen, so too did the ocean in the sky whirl, its waters checked by the blows of the mountain;
and just as the faces of the quarters were simultaneously washed, they became stained with the dust of the mountains. (Sētubandha 30–31)
Even the great mountains, though struck by the agitated ocean and their paths of formation rendered invisible by the drenching spray of water, do not abandon one another. (Sētubandha 32)

Those very same paths which were the routes for entry when the mountain masses fell upon the riverbanks at the time of the floodwaters flowing downstream, became the very same routes for exit as well.
Even though they fall headlong into the fire, the mountain peaks released from the mountain slopes descend [into the ocean]. (Setubandha 33)
Having wandered about, the mountains—heavy at their bases due to their own weight—were uprooted right there.

(Sētu 34) The lions, shaking the faces of elephants and tigers as they themselves are shaken, have fixed their claws firmly in their mouths; their manes swirl around as they strike with the frontal globes of elephants that provide sufficient and firm sustenance for their mouths. (Sētu 35)

The forest elephants, their temples drenched with rutting juice that flowed from the wounds of the elephant-kings who had extended their trunks to seize the scent, recognized [the bridge] only by its forest-like face, as it were, when it was stained by the waters of the Kuvilāla forest.
(Sētu 36) Having leaped up from the bridge constructed by the monkeys, the monkeys flew into the ocean.
The mountain-bearers draw [the bridge] while their chests are pressed together by their joined palms.
Nala also binds the path of the bridge, his mass of quivering manes bristling at that moment, as he is lifted by the hand of Hari, who has turned back and extended his arm. (Setubandha 37–38)

The mountain-dweller [Rāma], standing alone with his chest broad and firm, holds back that fissure in the earth which was produced by many mountains and made manifest by the cast-off feet of the ocean.
As for each mountain that the hosts of monkeys bring, having found its place in the sea, [he holds it back]. *Sētubandha* 39.1.39.1–2.
The path of the bridge was constructed by Nala, who first took his position there and there, having placed his foot forward.

When the path of the bridge was abandoned by the mountain, Nala, receiving the mountain as it fell simultaneously into the void, pushed it aside and arranged it in an asymmetrical manner. (Sētu 40–41)
Leaning upon the mountain peaks that were bent by the weight of Nala’s labor, the ocean, with its surging waters, constructs the bridge; and before him, it increases in volume.
(Setubandha 42)
Whatever mountain with peaks polished by the wheels of the chariot of the Sun’s daughter Hanumān brings,

Nala playfully casts it into the ocean, its summit struck by the palm of his left hand. (Setubandha 43) [Upon the island of broad lotuses, where the bridge-crossing shines as it is gradually constructed.]
The earth, its foundations resting upon the cool peaks of the ocean, supports those cool peaks.

(Sētu 44) Connected to the coastal ridges, the forest line—shaken by the spray of water receding from the shore and trembling as it is tossed by the rays [of the sun]—sways like the luster of emeralds. (Sētu 45)
The black circles of the snakes, cast up by the collisions of elephants and horses whose trunks were caught and twisted in their tusks,
fall into the sea like the reflections of dark lotus-pools.
It is as if the very light of the ocean, intensified by the falling of the mountain, is first returning [to it].
He alone crossed the path of the Nala-fire, which was difficult to traverse as it turned toward the shore of the waters.

(Setu 47) The Mātaṅgas, whose streams of rut-fluid remained unbroken, stumbled as they were halted by the ocean agitated [by him]; they appeared like serpents being dragged along by their tails, clinging to his feet. (Setu 48)

The waves, filled with the juice of the *arā* fruit which has the luster of lapis lazuli and is slightly split open like a mass of emeralds, are tossed about, white with foam from the multitude of conchs crushed by them; and as they strike together, the ocean appears to be filled with rocks. (Setubandha 49)

It surges up just as much as it was, filling the roots of the mountain that had been dug out [by the bridge]. (Sētubandha 50) The upheavals of the earth seem to rock the sky, as the great mountains slip loose from their positions at the mouths of the rivers where they were tossed upward, causing the oceans to sway. (Sētubandha 51)
The ocean water— its flow of the bridge half-completed, momentarily bestowing happiness upon the heart of Hari,
with the mountain half-descended and the netherworld half-ejected—
is recognized as "constructed" once the sea has been driven far back. (Setubandha 52)
As it recedes, that very ocean appears as if it has begun to dry up;
yet it still fills the underworld, for it is not diminished by the trampling of the elephants of the quarters who are enraged. (Setu 53)

The footprints of the Great Boar, which fill the hopes granted by the ocean, [are seen]. (Sētu 54) The ocean water has become like wine arising from the mountain: its juice is fresh from the crushing of the mountain’s rocky ridges, it possesses the redness of sprouts, it is fragrant with the resin from the breaking of trees, and it is becoming intoxicating. (Sētu 55)
Just as the ocean stirs up the range of mountains situated far apart, so too the bridge-construction proceeds,
made stable by filling the gaps with its glittering peaks.
(Setubandha 56) Does it fall from the vault of the sky, or is it being drawn out from the Malaya mountains, having been fashioned long ago?
Does the ocean pour its water into the sky, or does the submarine fire flow out from the netherworld?
(Sētubandha 57) In the sky, the waters of the ocean are seen;
in the netherworld, the expanse of the sky is seen; and in all three—the sky, the waters, and the netherworld—the multitude of mountains appears equally. (Sētubandha 58)
Having encircled with his coils the pillar of the bridge situated in the ocean,
even though it rests upon the underworld, the serpent Vāsuki shakes it as he twists, like a wild elephant.
(Sētubandha 59) As the waters are agitated by the monkeys, they are driven back ever more firmly, drenched by the spray.
Striking one against the other, the great mountains thus pass by one another.
(Sētubandha 60) Seized by the arms that are the monkeys, the mountain-kings with their scattered jewels fall;
the ocean, agitated, roars loudly as if sinking under the weight of the intense fear of the rivers. (Sētubandha 61)

The ocean seems to be carried away when driven far; it seems to be shaken by the mud falling from the collapsing mountains; it seems to be obstructed when turned back; and it seems to be joined together by the radiance of the jewels. (Setubandha 62) On the path of the bridge, the elephants and deer, who had lost confidence because the ocean was agitated, regained their confidence when they saw the masses of fallen mountains. (Setubandha 63)
[59] The herds of forest elephants, enraged by the scent of musth, charge headlong against the mountain peaks that are likewise enraged by the scent of musth.
(Setubandha 63) Having leaped over the masses of trees and long sniffed the hollows along the banks of the Setu river...
The waves, having gone far beyond the reach of the iron shackles, surge upward. (Sētubandha 64) The ocean is seen by the herds of elephants with eyes raised in fear of the falling mountain;
the water of the rivers, which had been blocked, now flows forth as the expanse of its current is opened by the roar of the monkeys. (Sētubandha 65)
This is the mountain range of Kula, its great undertaking fashioned by a multitude of mountains that exhaust all the earth's wealth;
it darkens the surface of the ocean's waters with the play of its own shadow. (Setu 66)
The stone embankment where the rear portions of fish were cast up by the forceful impact of rocks displaced by uneven currents;

where the coils of serpents were torn apart as they were crushed between stones split in their midsections; where lions rushed along paths trodden by elephants who, in their agitation at the uprooting of crags, had seized and trampled them; [Rāmasetu 67].

The water of the rivers, noisy as they flow down from the mountain peaks where the clouds rest, is split in two by the great mountain torrents obstructed by forest elephants that have fallen into the shallows; and the fragments of the Malaya peaks are recognized by the sandalwood forests situated between the mountains. (Sētubandha 68–69)
With the rows of trees hanging down, tossed about by the force of the wind, and with the ocean agitated as it enters between the jagged peaks, they construct the path for Nala;
the bridge-building expands, and the ocean is split apart by the mountains. (Setubandha 70)
The monkey army, having seen the slopes of Mount Suvela, is tasting the echoes resounding through the quarters.

(Sētubandha 71) In the midst of the ocean with its waters divided, the monkeys are seen—exhausted by the labor of building the bridge, dragged along in their agitation, and with the wings of mountains shattered by the falling dust of the rocks. (Sētubandha 72)
The monkeys are again connecting the bridge of Nala, whose base shines with water tested by the impact of mountain peaks, which has been repeatedly pulled back and then drawn forward. (Setubandha 73)
Just as he draws closer to the ocean after winning the wager for the construction of the bridge, so too does the water, struck by the earth, splash far away due to its thinness.
As for those [waves] of the bridge that fall stumbling, their flight interrupted by the blows of the mountains... (Setu 74)
Those very same surges of water become the great river currents, winding and uneven.
(Sētubandha 75) The bridge-path bestows a complete splendor upon the surface of the ocean, which is filled with whales fleeing in terror;
it is flanked by the slopes of Mount Suvela, which has drawn near to its center. (Sētubandha 76)
When Nala shook the great mountain fixed upon the bridge, which was situated in a precarious position, then the ocean—
its waters having long since exhausted the entire earth— finally retreated.
Rolling as it was struck by the rocks hurled by the hosts of monkeys, who were delighted by their swift execution of the mission.
Like a river current between the Setu and Mount Suvela, he was carried along for a moment by the ocean.

(Sētu 78) Just as the mountain peaks were constructed as a bridge-pathway by the leaders of the monkeys, so too was the heart of the Ten-faced One torn asunder along with the waters of the sea. (Sētu 79)
Mount Suvela, though standing firm, fell headlong into the ocean— the flow of which had been uninterrupted from its source meeting the netherworld— due to the pressure of the mountain being moved.
(Sētubandha 80) [Thus it was said] by the Lord of Monkeys, who had gone to the lap of Mount Malaya while remaining near the side of the Lord of the Rākṣasas.
The ocean channel was filled by the monkeys with the roar of their clamor, reaching as far as the western mountain.
(Sētubandha 81) When the construction of the bridge began, it appeared difficult and uneven;
when Nala’s path was established, it became even on both sides; yet once completed, the ocean remains the same again and again. (Sētubandha 82)

The heavy bridge-boat, its burden of monkeys leaping about and clinging to the edge of the railing, was held back as if by one tree against another as it struck the Tiuḍa mountain; thus the eastern and western quarters of the world appear doubled by the great expanse of the bridge. (Sētubandha 83)

[The mountain] stands reflected in the ocean water, which resembles the sky, appearing as if it were bending down with its uneven slopes cast between the upturned arms of Mount Malaya and Mount Suvela. (Setu 84)
The path of the bridge appears like the track of the sun’s chariot when it has risen from the eastern mountain;
the bridge-path is seen like a great mountain whose massive peaks are reflected in the ocean stirred by the wind, appearing as if its broad wings were being spread out. (Sētubandha 85–86)
Discontent, heavy sighs, loss of sleep, pallor, and weakness— these [symptoms] resulting from the grief over Rāma being transferred to Rāvaṇa as he was being bound by the bridge (Setu 87)—
then [resulted in] the destruction of the ten-faced one along with his kinsmen, whose broad, lofty, and expansive chest [was crushed].
The bridge-fleet spread out like an arm reaching toward the ocean, which had been made into a mere puddle by the *dohā* songs.

(Sētu 88) By the bridge, though situated at a distance, the heart of Daśānana was pierced—just as if by a spear—as difficult [to cross] as the earth itself, heavy with mountains, and burdened by the audacity of battle. (Sētu 89)

The trees on the mountain ridges appear with bees clinging to clusters of flowers tossed up by the waters of the agitated ocean, and with young shoots curling upward as they emerge from the slopes of the mountains;
in some places, they are seen fallen into the interior of the mountains, their shadows resembling the still ocean. (Setu 90)
The hope for the construction of the bridge is as if severed in the midst of being joined by crystals, stones, and coral.

(Sētu 91) Even though they have been joined together by the falling of snow, the peaks of Mount Malaya are clearly recognized in the passage of the fire by their fragrance, like crushed sandalwood. (Sētu 92)

Even when the ocean was completely filled with crocodiles, the paths of its shores remained clearly visible, shimmering as the water receded; yet they were now overwhelmed by the heavy mass of filaments stirred up by the waters falling from the mountain that served as a bridge. (Setu 93)
Lions are seen standing on the thresholds, doorways,
and porches of their dens.
(Setubandha 94) Having gone to drink from the eastern and western oceans, those born of the eastern and western oceans [are seen].
The mountain-dwellers do not see the openings of their caves again, which were previously blocked by the bridge. (Sēu.
95) The lofty peaks of the mountains, standing upon the surface of the ocean and appearing like banners with white waterfalls scattered by the winds from Mount Ambā, are visible. (Sēu. 96)
Then the monkey army set forth, its mountain-loaders stationed upon ground far exceeding the breadth of the constructed bridge;
it moved with the joy of battle being instilled into the heart of the wandering Rāghava, while its width was diminished by the gaps left by the monkeys leaping across.
(Setubandha 97) And they beheld it as its extent was reduced by the intervals between those who were crossing.
The ocean, its waters severed by a single side left remaining after being struck by the tip of Balarāma’s plow;
resembling a mass of conch shells, white lotuses, emerald-green leaves, and water-weeds. (Setubandha 98, a *yugmaka*)
The monkey host traverses the Nala-bridge, which has become a narrow path along its banks due to the coral and budding sprouts;
the bridge-river bends like a great mountain, while the ocean, having submerged its very foundations in the netherworld, bears it with all its might. (Sētubandha 99–100)
The ocean, as if a forest elephant bound to a pillar upon the bridge of the causeway, shifts its hips and bears the mass of its wave-hands upon its back.
And the monkeys have crossed over, their sweat turned to frost by the exertion of carrying the weight of the rocks. (Setu 101)
Shaking off the mountain torrents clinging to their hands as they were soiled by the minerals,
they reached the region of the grove of trees belonging to the son of Daśamukha’s sister (Rāvaṇa),
where the forest creepers were bent down by the weight of clouds resting heavily upon them, and which lay upon the lap of Mount Suvela. (Sētubandha 102–103)

Having seen the monkey army having crossed the ocean with its prowess unimpeded, the world of the Rākṣasas became timid toward the command of the Lord of the Rākṣasas. (Setu 104) While the monkey army was occupied with seizing dwellings on the ridges of the great ocean...
At that moment, the beloved Rāma placed the touch of his left hand upon the head of Rāvaṇa— a touch unique to the space between this world and the next. (Setu 105)
When the army was split in two by the expanding and retreating frontiers, the beauty of the ocean-like Mahiya became equal to that of Lakṣmī;
for Rāma had descended [from the sky] like the moon marked with a deer, bringing joy to the wives of the gods. (Sētu 106–107)
Thus ends the eighth chapter of the *Daśamukhavadha* composed by Śrī Pravarasena.

[The Ninth Chapter of Consolation] Then the monkeys beheld Mount Suvēla, whose great peaks had been increased by the exertions of all the monkeys, and which seemed to have carried away the faces of all the other directions, leaving only the southern quarter behind. (Sētu. 1)
Like Viṣṇu for the world; like Śeṣa for Viṣṇu, who was exhausted by the burden of the world; like the ocean for Śeṣa;
[he was] like a river for its lord, capable of bearing a burden that would otherwise be difficult to traverse.
(Setubandha 2) He was capable of supporting the earth as if it were to be carried away, and the powerful flow of rivers as if they were to be borne by the ocean.
Its slopes are capable of withstanding the wind of universal destruction like the wind at the end of an eon;
it has driven the quarters far away and bent down the entire surface of the underworld; it has cast the sky far aloft, while its nearby trees bear fruits and flowers. (Setu 3–4)

The surrounding rim of the earth, its surface of the netherworld-ocean released from its subterranean confines, appears like the crust of the world rising up and remaining firm at the moment it was overturned by the Primeval Boar;
its base filled with the netherworld, rendered motionless by the upward thrust of the jaws of the Thunderbolt-Mouthed One. (Setu 5)
The pillar of his tethering post, its rope smoothed by the rubbing against the shoulders of the elephant of the gods;

[the mountain] whose roots were not seen to be severed by the Lord of the Poison-Eaters (Śeṣa) who had cleansed the netherworld, and whose lofty peaks were not reached even by Hari, who grew in size while lifting the three worlds—[this is the mountain]. (Sētubandha 6–7)

With its waters cast aside by the coils of the serpent king, it was embraced by the mountain Mandara—just as a deer is seized by a lion standing nearby—as the serpent’s head was encircled by the rays of the sun; and the darkness of the netherworld was dispelled by the light from the jewels at the base of the gems upon his remaining heads. (Setubandha 8)
The sky is darkened by the solar disc lost in the narrowness of the peaks of the lofty mountains;
there, beautiful streaks of light spread across the black stone walls that have been polished by contact with the orb of the moon. (Setubandha 9)
The path of the sun’s chariot was revealed by the moonlight, which was shimmering and hot from being splashed by the water;

with its peaks lined by the crescent moon and fragments of clouds holding water scattered upon them, the mountain appeared at night like a celestial elephant whose lotus stalks had fallen and whose heart was filled with uneven mud. (Setubandha 10–11)
Its mountain peaks, whose distant and rugged slopes were indicated by the rows of green forests, had river paths [winding] along them;
its young shoots were tossed upward and withered by the wind, only to sprout back again against the surface of the moon;
its lofty peaks rose so high that they appeared like massive, visible reflections in the waters of the ocean. (Setubandha 12)
Standing like a single severed rope struck upward by a thunderbolt,
its base repeatedly obstructed by the hoods of Śeṣa, who was exhausted by the weight of the mountain;
with the remaining great mountains shattered as they fell from their lofty peaks, driven down by the winds of the cosmic dissolution— (Sētubandha 13–14).
The great buffalo stands silent and exhausted, driven by clouds that have drawn up water;
the mountain slope is covered with clusters of pearls formed from the blood of slain elephants as it dries upon the stone surfaces.
The red hue of the fresh sprouts of trees is being washed away by the spray of the salt waters. (Setu 15)
With one ear pricked up and one foot turned back as they fled, terrified by the lion’s roar;

[the mountain] appears like the quarters of the sky, filled with caves revealed by the trampling of the army of Rāvaṇa, which have been pushed aside by their anklets and stand now with one side pressed against the other. (Sētu 16–17)
At night, its peaks were illuminated by jewels rising high; its summits were frequented by herds of deer resting in the comfort of its rays;
it was pierced by the firm arrows of the enraged Rāma which struck the ocean; and it was bathed by the moon’s orb as it emerged, clinging to its peaks.
(Setu 18)

The world, whose base is carried far away and whose peaks have passed beyond the circle of the sun, has its light extinguished halfway; as it is in the waters of the ocean, so too it is in the expanse of the sky. (Setubandha 19) A mass of fragrant smoke rises from the friction of sandalwood trees tossed by the wind.
Its peaks were embraced by the ocean, which was rendered pale-white by the remnants of the waters made heavy by the weight of the mountain;
its lion-like roar was intensified by the spray of the ocean’s waves dashed against its base;
and it seemed to swallow the circle of the moon situated upon its peak, as if drawn in by the garland of planets. (Setu 20–21)
In front of the moon, within the caves spread out before it, where the waters flow unceasingly and without agitation;
where the young elephants, sleeping comfortably upon jeweled slabs, rest peacefully;
and where the tigers, having seized the frontal globes of elephants, turn away and spring back with a roar. (Setu 22)
[The mountain] has the luster of gems emerging from the spray of water droplets falling upon serpents sleeping within its caves;

its jeweled ridges are pressed down by the peaks of the ocean that have come to rest there; and lions emerge from the mouths of elephants perched upon the pearl-like fruits clinging to the sky. (Sētubandha 23–24)
The forests, with their tender shoots emerging, appear like wish-granting creepers— cleansed by rain, released from clouds, and possessing white rays of light stirred by the wind.
(Sētubandha 25) [They are] mountains where trees lean precariously on uneven slopes, half-submerged in the waters of the ocean.
Carrying river currents filled with flowers and flowing along the slopes of the crystal-like mountain ridges,

[the mountain] shakes the mouths of the sun’s chariot horses— mouths whose reins are loosened and which are filled with the foam of saliva blown forth by the winds from the mountain peaks’ cascades. (Setu 26–27)
In the nights, he bears the moon— its long horns touching the summit, its peaks ablaze with the brilliance of medicinal herbs,
and its dark spot made manifest like a mass of soot. (Sētubandha 28)

The lake of Māyāpurī, which had been dried up by the heat of the sun and the moon, is now being filled by the streams of rivers that have plunged deep into the hollows of the hearts of the great boars who have uprooted the broad earth;
meanwhile, my mind has turned back, terrified by the echoes from ahead in the direction from which I did not expect to come. *Sētubandha 29*
In the forest regions where the cries of great monkeys resound, filling the caves and reaching the ears;

where the sweet warbling of birds is heard amidst the waters reddened by the pollen of lotuses; where the female lions have seized their prey; and where the forest is tossed by the waves of the sea-wind—Rāmasetu 30–31.

In the sky, which has the ocean as its boundary and the moon as its central jewel, where the ten directions have been pervaded and the sun has set and risen again, he is traveling through a cave that is like a wandering through the world itself—
[a cave] filled with the waters of the surging ocean, whose depths have been drained as the water recedes. (Setubandha 32)
Flowing with sweet waters in the east and salty waters at the peaks,

it possesses the luster of jewels, is stirred by the wide hoods of the coiling Śeṣa, increases the lotuses in its lakes, and bears the stains of the sun’s chariot and moon caught in its forest groves. (Sētubandha 33–34)
On the mountain ridges, which are as blue as the sky, where the heat of the sun is checked by the cover of the path of the wandering buffalo,
and where the rays spread across the slopes like lakes surrounded by thirst,
the forest of tamāla trees is crushed by elephants, while the peaks are shattered by the great claws of lions’ paws. (Setubandha 35)
[The bridge] which provoked the anger of the forest-dwellers by releasing them from their places in accordance with the black stone of the Mahisha-slaying [Vishnu];
[the bridge] which possessed pearls and jewels from the frontal globes of elephants broken by the soles of the feet of lions fulfilling their vows;
[the bridge] which served as a crossing over the confluence of rivers trampled by herds of elephants fleeing in fear of forest fires—Sētubandha 36–37.

With its prominent stars reflecting the rows of forest trees on the surface of the sun’s chariot as it turns at the end of the day, it appears to be the second world resting upon the lap of him who is seated in repose.
(Sētu. 38)

In that place where the entire mass of moonbeams was as if eclipsed by the half-severed rays of the sun, and where the mountain peaks were sought out by Garuḍa as he swooped down and turned back upon his severed wings;
there, the ocean—which is the very essence of the nectar of the hearts of the wives of the gods—was fashioned as if from the quintessence of jewels. (Setubandha 39)

The air is sweet with the fragrance of lotus stalks and buds, and filled with the flow of honey-nectar dripping from the groves of *vaula* trees. (Sētu 40) The deer have forgotten their hunger for green grass due to the intense heat of the summer sun;
meanwhile, the rocks are being licked by buffaloes who are greedy for the salty spray from the ocean’s waves. (Sētu 41)

With its peaks rising high like the horns of a bull, it possesses the brilliance of pearls formed from the blood of elephants slain by lions; it bears the marks of the destruction of many couples through its heavy and steadfast currents, and it displays the beauty of conch shells reflected in the waters of the ocean. (Setu 42) It is as dark as a blue lotus made of jewels. (Maṇipahamma-sāmōaaṃ) Maṇipahamma-sāmōaaṃ.

One who causes sleep in the forest of the lake, one whose speech is a refuge for those seeking sleep; one who has destroyed the demon Rākṣasāmōya, one who is like a protector (Sāmōya) who does not harm the innocent; one who causes the destruction of the enemy's wealth, one who destroys the poison-like splendor of the foe. (Setu 43–44)

The sandalwood trees, whose trunks were abandoned by serpents encircled by withered, parched medicinal herbs, have their shadows marred by the light from the jewels on the hoods of gliding venomous snakes;
the mass of their rays whitens the earth as if it were being sprinkled by the lovely faces of celestial nymphs. (Setu 45)

Even by the waters equal to the ocean at the time of dissolution, it cannot be entirely washed away; it possesses a luster like that of the new moon emerging from a rift, and it has the beautiful radiance of the king of the lovely islands. (Setu 46)
The perfection of the conjunction of the planets at the time of grasping the zenith of heaven;
the lion who slew the boar that had escaped while crossing the mud and was turning back;
and the cluster of golden sprouts satisfied by its own weight as it fell into the lake of water. (Sētubandha 47–48)

The glory of the sky, possessing the loveliness of all dark clouds, appearing as if girt with a girdle by the constellations, veiling the quarters with its peaks as if with arms, and concealing the directions like a jealous lover;
it is the common support for the non-gods and the destroyer of the pride of the gods. (Setu 49)

The hero who dispels darkness, the protector who holds the sun like a crest-jewel— when the oceans were being filled with water at the time of Hari’s lifting of the earth, he remained standing after filling the world with his own body, which could not be contained by them even as they overflowed. (Setu 50–51)
The sun, its orb vanished as it has passed through the forest fire near the mountain peaks, appears like smoke rising through the lattice-work of clouds, with upward-reaching rays of light;
meanwhile, the heavy waves, shattered by the heat of the submarine fire, strike against the shore. (Sētubandha 52)
By the power of the ocean, which never fails to carry away the family treasures [of the enemies], it bears [the light] at night;
it displays the reflection of the young moon’s splendor cast upon the surface of a single *kāntamaṇi* stone, as if it were the hoof-print of the horses of the Sun remaining there. (Setubandha 53–54)

It is encircled by golden plateaus that rest upon unevenly situated peaks and are covered with trees growing in a disordered fashion, appearing like severed circles of clouds; [peaks] where snakes remain on the summits out of fear of the sun before it has reached them. (Setubandha 55)
The forests, with their shade increased by growth toward the top, seem to be carried upward by the trunks;
their mouth-like openings are fashioned by the width and expansion sufficient for their great height.
On the slopes of the mountain, marked by the pairs of tusks like ploughshares of the celestial elephants as they pass by;

on the mountain, where the red hue of the sprouts is scorched by the heat of their trunks, and where the branches of the Pārijāta trees—long carried and then released during the tossing of their trunks—are now tawny with dust. (Sētubandha 57–58)

The palace, bearing a moonlight-white radiance from the luster of its jeweled bracelets, appears like the moon with its orb turned upward by the impact of the great waterfalls cascading down its slopes;
its upper stories are visible through the flowers slightly moistened by the spray of the waters. (Setubandha 59)
The dark line of forest, appearing even darker as it flowed along the banks of the Māraharā river;

the paths of the celestial elephants, where bees returned from the sky after following their far-reaching tracks, and where the exits were obscured by those descending to enter and those ascending to depart. (Setubandha 60–61)

Carrying away the darkness that has been somewhat dispelled, with rays of light only slightly emerged, their interiors filled with smoke from the fires of the setting sun, they reveal the places where the sprouts of jewels have just emerged from the water; while the trees, their trunks bent and their branches swaying, break apart the masses of clouds that had gathered. (Setubandha 62)
It bears the fragrance arising from the battle of the forest elephants, where the splendor of their tusks has been shattered by blows;
it still carries the nectar-like water of the ocean that surged up from the strike of Mount Mandara and was deposited upon the vast expanse of its jeweled floor. (Sētubandha 63–64)
Carried along by the agitation of the waters, with its multitude of boats shattered and wrecked,
that mass of Rāvaṇa’s arrows stood there like a flock of birds whose wings were clipped by the beaks of thunderbolts;
The mountain stream flows with its creeper-flowers shaken by bees that turn back upon perceiving the cry of the peacocks;
it flows cool as frost, while the wind carries the chill of the month of Māgha, and the moonstone streams water from its core, broken forth by the intense heat of the day. (Sētubandha 66–67)

Bearing upon it the essence of the Pāraja tree, sanctified by its shade over the emerald stone slabs, where the waters swirl around the circles of lotuses whose fragrance is diffused unevenly— Sētu 68.
At the break of day, it seems to ascend with its orb rising high and moving swiftly;
at the end of the day, Rati seems to descend as it traverses the level circle.
There, at nightfall, the wind-girdled trees seem to embrace one another, turning about to avoid the uneven ground. (Sētubandha 69)
In the caves, the forest-dwellers call out with eyes as bright as stars;

and there, the orb of the moon—meeting the mountain peaks and struck by the upturned hands of the Cīra women, whose palms are wet with tears shed for their separated lovers—scatters handfuls of flower-like droplets. (Sētubandha 70–71)
Like the surface of the sky purified by the planets, with its palaces obstructing the force of the wind from the peaks of the sky;
darkened by the clouds of rays emerging from its jeweled summits, with lions darting through the caves like thick clouds;
in which the quarters appear as if completed, the earth as if exhausted, and the sky as if it has reached its end. (Setubandha 72)
Like the eighth ocean, like the netherworld submerged, or like the world come to rest—[so it appears] on whose peaks the celestial horses of Rati descend repeatedly;
their necks bend as they turn, and their chowries sway as their muzzes are turned back, reddened with fear. (Sētubandha 73–74)
Where forests appear as if carrying heaps of flowers along the paths of the stars, with their first shoots grasped and their stars severed by the dawn;
where, in those nights, people find sleep whose waters are as delicate as breaths agitated by sighing. (Setubandha 75)
Where the forest buffaloes are drenched by streams of water from moonstones manifested by the rays of the full moon,
and where they lean against the rugged slopes of rock walls fallen from the mountain peaks. (Sētubandha 76)
The orb of the moon, its mass of radiance vanished upon being eclipsed by the jewel on the head of the lord of serpents;

the ocean, having swallowed the remainder of the earth’s surface, agitates the netherworld as it is shaken by the trembling of the submarine fire that has emerged from the mouth of the serpent-king. (Sētubandha 77–78)

Where lions roam, their manes slightly singed by the sparks from the lightning-bolts falling upon their mouths as they drag down clouds with their snouts near the peaks of Mount Nahuṃkuśa; where, moreover, those who have been refreshed by bathing in the mountain torrents yet again grow weary under the heat of the day. (Setubandha 79)
The elephants rest beneath the *hari-candana* trees, which are resonant with the trumpeting of the herds settled there.

(Sētubandha 80) And where the white chowrie tufts of the female elephants, clinging to the creepers that are embraced by swarms of wandering bees, appear like the dust raised by the flowers shaken by the moon, as they follow the swift stallions of Rati. (Sētubandha 81)

Where the tears falling from the eyes of the celestial captive women—dripping down their cheeks which are grey with the constant application of collyrium—soil the fibers of the *kalpa* trees. And where, on a single peak, the multitude of trees, withered and crushed, come to an end. (Sētubandha 82)
The path of Rāvaṇa, agitated by his coming and going through the sky from south to north, was blocked by him.

By him, as he grew, the three worlds—as if they were expanding—were increased: the earth was split by his weight, the netherworld was filled, the sky was reached, and all directions were cast asunder. (Sētubandha 83–84)
Where the gods dwell together with their followers, amidst bees clinging to the fragrance, the months stand like celestial elephants on a single pillar, moving in opposite directions. (Sētu.
There the sun is seen retreating, terrified by the presence of the nearby Rāvaṇa, with his orb of rays clinging to the intervals between the mountain peaks.
And there, the eyes of the deer are closed in bliss, delighted by the enchanting songs of the kinnaras.
The chewing of the cud by those who had been startled was only restored after a long time.

(Setu 87) In the lakes where the cries of swans were resonant on the banks, and where the trumpeting of agitated elephants had ceased, there the petals of the lily groves—touching the vault of the sky—did not close even at the sight of the sun’s orb. (Setu 88)

While the Moon was setting, Ananta lowered his vast mass of hoods, which were deeply burdened by the weight [of the earth] and appeared as if illuminated by the radiance of jewels emerging from their crevices;
and upon him, clinging to his chest, the moon is seen with its brilliant, intoxicating luster resembling the opening of a cave. (Setubandha 89)
Like the moon whose orb is split by the spray from the cascades of Mount Aṣṭāvakra;
where the three worlds stand together, closely packed and formidable in their middle, like the three thick bangles on the arm of Hari. (Sētubandha 90–91)
Where the moonbeams, cool and pleasant like a forest row of pleasure-ships for the night-blooming lotuses,
thin out as they pass through the gaps between the trees, the paths of the stars are no longer discernible. [Sētu 92] There,
the pollen from the garlands of the Gandharva brides clinging to their hair is ground away by the surface of the rocks.
Where the wind blows the fragrant young shoots of the *tamāla* tree, which are drying in the breeze;
and where the ocean waves, their water-sprays momentarily drunk by their mouths as they travel upstream against the current, again cling to the caves exhausted by the wind. (Sētubandha 93–94)
[The battlefield] where lions, having fainted from the impact against the banks as they fell, were driven away by the onset of unseen elephants.
Where pairs of *kiṃnara*s fall one after another, bewildered by the roar of the tiger;

where, at the edge of the dark jewel-like rock-face of Mount Īja, facing the mouths of the high mountain cascades, the passion of the wives of the gods does not grow slack as they wait upon him. (Sētubandha 95–96)
Thus ends the ninth canto, titled "The Description of Suvēla," in the great poem *Daśamukhavadha* composed by Śrī Pavarasēṇa.

Now, even though the Ten-faced one was slain, the monkey host remained settled and confident, as if on their own mountain peaks, upon the Vasuvela summits. (Setubandha 1)
The slopes of Mount Suvela were not crushed by the King [Rāvaṇa], nor were they shaken by Māruta (the Wind-god), nor were they avoided by the gods, yet they were trampled by the monkeys;
thus, Janaka’s daughter dwells here with anger because it is the city of her enemy, and with joy because she lives here. (Setu 2)
The lord cast his gaze toward Laṅkā, which was shaken by the roar of the ocean;
then, as its peak was struck by the news of Rāma’s arrival, Suvela—his fortitude melted away by rage and filled with indignation—made the Ten-faced One tremble. (Sētubandha 3–4)

Meanwhile, the day— its light drawn away like a lotus by the king who resembles the elephant of the gods— lost its splendor as the ten-faced Rāvaṇa’s gaze fell upon it, which had been turbid with the roar of the monkey host standing nearby and whose attendants had scattered in fear. (Sētu 5)
The mass of rays, tawny with yellow orpiment and reddened by the pollen of lotuses, is held aloft like a flood of water.
(Sētubandha 6) The thinness of the shadows of the trees is being perceived as they are being moistened by the touch of the breezes, which have lost their radiance as it fades away.
(Sētubandha 7)

The orb of the moon is seen, possessing the luster of the frontal globes of an elephant reddened by coral and saffron, and appearing like the circle of the sky stained by the mineral dust of Mount Mandara; the shadows of the quarters of the world fade away, leaving the expanse of the earth dark-blue in hue. (Setubandha 8)

The mountains, their slender bodies clinging to the peaks as the day draws to a close, stand like the dwellings of gods when the sun has faded from the slopes of the western mountain.
