The orb of the sun is seen spreading out, like a mountain peak whose minerals have crumbled away.
(Sētu 10) At the departure of day, the petals of the lotuses—exhausted by their waning luster—close up;
they are sprinkled with honey-juice by the fluttering wings of bees intoxicated by nectar. (Sētu 11)
Both are seen alike: the earth, its dust trampled by the feet of monkeys;
and Rāvaṇa, his splendor extinguished by the destruction brought near by Rati, remaining like the sun half-set, its light diminished as it stays in the high vault of the sky. (Sētu 12)
In the sky, the day withers away, its surface parched by the heat spreading from the earth released [by the sun].
(Sētubandha 13) Like a forest-dweller who has turned his back on the day, the mass of the sun’s rays appears like a thick, formidable root-system of a tree being uprooted. (Sētubandha 14)
And only at twilight, when the orb of the sun had set, did the great mass of Rāvaṇa’s blood sink into the mud of his own gore like the circle of the severed head of the first victim;
it was heavy with the weight of bees and thickened by the red juice oozing from the decaying filaments. (Setu 15)

The leaves of the lotuses, meeting with the separation from the sun, become terrifying. (Sētu 16) The mass of rays, spreading through the western quarter and rendered uneven by their long-reaching beams, appears as if filled with dust—the path for dragging out the day cast from the mouth of Time. (Sētu 17)
When the sun had passed far away, as if plunging the earth with its upward-turned orb, the golden twilight—its waters surging forth—was cast into the sky like a mass of evening mud;
it was seen upon the western peak of Meru, where the mountain’s slopes were drenched in molten gold. (Sētubandha 18)
The twilight glow, like a mass of dust raised by the chariot of the sun as it turns and hastens,
blossoms with the hue of a lion’s mane smeared with the blood of a white elephant. (Sētu 19)
The grove of night-lotuses, its filaments reddened by the twilight and trembling in the sway of the wind;
[Sētu 20] The hue of day’s end, with its uneven twilight glow being gradually severed by the unmanifest long shadows, has turned the ten directions into a mass of swirling darkness. [Sētu 21]
The sky has assumed the form of a whirlpool lake: its fire-altars have been extinguished by the twilight offerings made with palms joined;

the splendor of the sun has receded far away; and it possesses the dark hue produced by the dense darkness that has grown thick through its absorption of the twilight’s royal radiance. (Sētubandha 22)
As the splendor of day fades away, the lights of lamps emerge.

(Sētu 23) The pair of cakravāka birds, whose pleasure was the sight of each other as they stood on the banks of the river whose flow was broken by the loosening of the bond of night, have now been separated;
their lives are drawn out only by their cries of lamentation. (Sētu 24)
Then, having pushed aside the thick twilight glow like a golden belt as dark as the *tāla* tree,
the darkness stood still like the hoof-print of a celestial elephant in the mud.
(Setu 25) It is sparse when near, thick at a moderate distance, and dense when far away.

Even though it stands level everywhere, darkness is seen spreading forth as if on a downward slope. (Sētubandha 26) The trees are recognized only by the fragrance of flowers resting upon their sprouts—sprouts whose tender tips are darkened, smeared with both darkness and light situated within their dense foliage. (Sētubandha 27)

The darkness, which has vanished from the sight of the eyes even though it was close to all directions, which makes the surface of the earth seem as if it were to be inferred [rather than seen], and which is worthy of the great power of the sun, now advances with a dense mass to be uprooted and a firm onset to be shattered. (Setu 28)

The mass of darkness, fit to be supported by the moon and capable of being pierced, flows as if filling the surface of the earth, washes away as if from behind, and holds fast as if in front. (Setubandha 29)
The mass of darkness, situated above, appears like a dark-green forest on the bank of a river;
it looks white with the spray of water broken by dark stones and mingled with gloom, its slender form revealed by the moonbeams as they emerge through the quarters of the sky. (Sētubandha 30–31)

In the hour of twilight, the eastern quarter appears like the ocean being consumed by a fire of rising smoke, its darkness dispelled by the rays of the moon that has ascended the slope of the Vindhya mountains; and now,
it is further filled with a mass of thick moonlight falling from the mountain of Acchaloāua.
The eastern quarter has become white like the face of the full moon, its darkness having vanished.
(Sētu 33) The orb of the moon does not yet entirely dispel the darkness that clings close by, though it spreads rays as soft as the filaments of a cluster of fresh lotuses. (Sētu 34)

Then the lunar orb appeared, touching the peak of the eastern mountain, its white radiance dispelling the darkness, its circumference marked by the tooth-prints of the celestial elephant standing before it;
and thereafter, the multitude of stars became turbid as they were overwhelmed by the darkness fleeing from the moon's rays. (Setu 35)
The expanse of the sky has become like a stone floor strewn with many fallen blossoms.

(Sētu 36) The trees possess circles of shadow formed by their slender branches, which are only slightly visible, while the darkness is being shaken away by the rays of the moon that have just begun to emerge. (Sētu 37)

The orb of the night-maker (the moon), its darkness diminished by rays whose strength was born from leaping across the sky, has lost its youthful nature and appears withered and white; likewise, the mountain stands as it was, the quarters are vast, and the flow of the river remains direct. (Setu 38)
Having once again scraped away the mass of darkness from the surface of the earth with his sharp rays,
as if with a chisel, he revealed their true forms even amidst the thick density of the gloom. (Sētubandha 39)
The bees pursue the moonbeams; they cannot bear to leave the shade of the trees.
Only the bees, however, tear open the night-lotus—its mass of petals withered from being nibbled by the face of the moon, its interior a place of mutual longing. (Setubandha 40–41)

Has the mass of darkness been crushed without remainder by the sun at midday? Or has it been pushed aside by his thick rays? Or has it been scattered? Or has it been drunk up entirely by the full moon? (Sētubandha 42) Having ground down the quarters of the sky, it is as if graspable by hands smeared with thick mud.
The surface of the sky, as if having endured a mass of darkness, appears as though it has been polished by the moonlight.

(Sētubandha 43) Even the forests, whose gloomy days of darkness have been dispelled and through whose branches the rays of the moon fall sparsely, now manifest a slight, pleasant light, appearing like tender young shoots. (Sētubandha 44)

The bees swarm over the beds of night-lotuses, where the forests of day-lotuses have withered; they are drenched in the ichor flowing from the temples of the elephants of the quarters, who are intoxicated by the fragrance of the blossoms of the trees.
It is as if the moon, having fallen upon the broad chest of the quarter-elephant, has become free of its dark spots.

The mass of his trunk, seizing the water of the lake as if it were a dark jeweled pavement, [is visible]. (Sētubandha 46) In the masses of darkness pierced by the white moonbeams—the food of the herds of elephants—there appear the long shadows of the feet of those who have emerged from the mud, like the clusters of smoke from the houses. (Sētubandha 47)
The moon clings to those mountain peaks, its rays streaming forth from the lattice of its orb through the hollows;
it breaks through the darkness of the caves and spreads its light, while the shadows are obscured by clouds distinguished by the scattering of falling snow.
(Sētubandha 48) The shadow is rendered distinct by the clouds infused with the mass of scattered powder.
The moonlight, meeting with the light of lamps reflected in the windows of the palace, grows dim;
it is filled with thick moonlight that must be turned back, as it is already turned away by the bitterness of its transformation.
(Sētubandha 49)
The night-lotus trembles, its petals spread wide as if to bear the weight of the buds that have closed at dawn.

(Sētubandha 50) With their branches bending back from the peaks shaken by the wind, their shadows scattered, the trees—encircled by moonbeams and drenched in the touch of moonlight—seem to be dancing. (Sētubandha 51)

The mass of moonlight appears like a pool of water pierced by the radiance of the house-jewels, thick with the scent of sandalwood paste, and uneven with gaps where the darkness has been scattered about; it makes the moon itself seem to have its natural luster lost, as it is overwhelmed by the overflowing moonlight. (Sētu 52)
The expanse of the sky appears like a mass of scattered rays of light, its soft stars indistinguishable.
(Sētu 53) The mountain ranges, with their towering peaks clearly manifest and white, are seen as they emerge from the surface of the earth;
their shadows are severed by the moon situated in the midst of the heavens. (Sētu 54)
Avoiding the darkness that has entered the circle of dense tree-shadows, he fearlessly descends into the cave, which is like a plateau filled with a mass of moonlight. (Sētubandha 55) [Couplet]

In the evening, when the cakravāka birds—awakened by the god of love, languishing on their banks, and emerging from their shells—had become like bees distressed by the closing of the blue lotuses; and when the women were overcome by passion and their longing for Rāma’s arrival had increased. (Sētubandha 56)
The hearts of wanton women abandon their aversion to love-making; they become as fluid as molten lac.

(Sētu 57) The kiss of the lover, which possesses a bliss overflowing with passion that is divided by the pain of the trickling saliva once obtained, and whose aesthetic flavor is broken and then reconstituted, is not to be despised for young women. (Sētu 58)
He trembles, sighs, and languishes upon his bed; exhausted, he casts down his limbs.
It is not known whether this host of wanton women is terrified or overcome by love, as their breasts are marked by the tusks of the forest elephants that roam the quarters of the sky.
(Sētubandha 59) Upon the breasts of their beloveds, which are scratched by the tusks of the wild elephants roaming the directions.

Having long beheld the jasmine blossoms— resembling the faces of young women whose eyes are half-closed in the bliss of love and who are slightly distressed by bees— the lover, having experienced the intensity of battle for a long time, now enters [the embrace]. (Sētu 60)

Her pair of eyes, with pupils rolling upward as she braced herself for the onset of battle, overcomes the assault of the enemy. (Setu 61 [Couplet]) Then, in the joy of the beloved’s arrival, which increased through the nectar born of the moon...
In the evening, where the pleasure of love has been lost due to the uprooting of pride, the company of wanton women turns back;
their shame is crushed by their own dejection and anger, they sigh as their bodies weary, and their hearts are revealed through the pleasure of being kissed. (Setu 62–63)
The heavy sighs of young women, whose anger has been dispelled by the kisses of their lovers upon their cheeks flushed with rage,
steal away the words they had spoken in defiance when turned away.
(Sētubandha 64) She does not accept his advances, she does not steady her disheveled hair, nor does she question the messenger.
The host of wanton women, their hearts deluded, are led away by the outcaste;

the arrival of the rainy season shines forth, accompanied by the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, while disregarding the talk of Rāma and resuming the activities of the young women as they had been before. (Sētu 65–66)

How can the multitude of lovers turn back that which the female messenger, turning away from her beloved with affectionate glances, says even though it is false, as she repeatedly restrains him who is departing? (Sētubandha 6.7) By those [women] who,
while their lovers are seated on the beds after a quarrel born of love, are being entreated by them...
It could not be turned back, yet it did not cease; rather, the flood of tears overflowed from their eyes.

(Setubandha 68) In the hearts of proud women, which are distressed and exhausted by remembering their resentment even after having found a moment of happiness through a lover’s conciliation, anger—weighed down by their subsequent submission—is finally pacified after a long time. (Setubandha 69)

The group of wanton women, distressed by the gaze of their friends, is enough to cause confusion: they touch [their faces], they hurriedly rearrange their girdles, they assume a feigned indifference, and they speak to their companions with affected composure.
(Sētu 70)
The departure to bed of the playful women— eager to rise,
radiant with the embrace of their lovers, yet with their ornaments still unfinished— is most beautiful at that very moment.
(Setubandha 71) [Those women] whose fatigue was relieved by the application of soothing medicinal herbs, who had stilled their tears with steady gazes and silent restraint...
A group of playful women, though feigning anger toward their lovers, is recognized by their hearts being truly agitated.
(Sētubandha 72) Love itself first casts off its long-held modesty and prevents a friend who has grown up with her from approaching when there is an obstacle to summoning her beloved. (Sētubandha 73)
Having observed the particular marks drawn on their faces by the hands of their female friends, the young women turn back and address the female messengers with agitation;
meanwhile, the messengers speak one thing in the presence of the friends, while saying something quite different to the messengers themselves. (Sētubandha 74)
At the sight of their beloveds, the young women utter cries of "Victory! and abandon all other composure.

(Sētu 75) In the assembly of newlywed brides, who somehow turn their faces toward their laps and somehow turn back their faces while being kissed, even though they falter in their speech, they maintain their composure despite their hearts being pierced by passion.
(Sētu 76)
The assembly of playful women, their hearts turned away even as they sat facing their beloveds, sighed with a dense and rising thrill of horripilation;
though their faces were offered, they did not drink from them, nor did they lower their lips, nor did they release them by force. (Setubandha 7.77)
In some places, young women turn their faces away from the king, averse to a first encounter. (Sētu 78) "Let him be patient;
he will not come here even when the evening has passed"—thus is the company of wanton women weighed by their messengers, who have already brought back the news of their lovers. (Sētu 79)
She is gracious toward the playful women, manifesting her true nature in both joy and sorrow;
like a friend who disregards shame, she speaks with confidence and is well-disposed. (Sētu. 80)
Is the moon increased in its expansion by the wine of the spring?
Or is the god of love increased by both of them—the moon and the spring-wine? Or have both of them been driven to excess by their own respective natures?
By the moon, she is made to suffer at night; and simultaneously, by the god of love, who is intoxicated with honeyed wine. (Sētubandha 81)
Love for beloveds is far-reaching, ascends to great heights, and possesses manifold flavors, even for young women— thus ends the eighty-second verse of the *Setubandha*.
Herein concludes the tenth chapter.

The Consolation] [The Couple]
When the evening had passed— its onset marked by the cessation of the moon’s rising and its descent behind the mountain peaks,
and uneven with the intervals between the sighs of love-stricken women—
Having simultaneously gazed with all ten mouths upon the ten directions and found them empty, the Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa) sighed;

he ponders, sighs, frets, drenches his arms [with tears], shakes his mass of heads, and laughs a laugh devoid of joy, for the god of love has ceased to flow forth from him due to the cold. (Sētubandha 2–3)
He prizes the cowherd’s flute, which is embraced by the tender grass of Janaka’s daughter, yet he despises the multitude of words that have not yet reached the nectar-draught of his beloved’s mouth.
(Sētubandha 4) Even as he restrains himself, [the flute] is broken, having been set aside after being turned back from its fortune.
With her trembling caused by the uneven pulling [of the garment], she stumbles even when moving slowly, yet remains composed.

(Sētubandha 5) Then, her face—resting upon the tips of her fingers which were unevenly turned upward and thinly spread—is slipped over her shoulder, while her arms are pressed together as they slip down from her outstretched neck. (Sētubandha 6)

He hears the sound of victory from his beloveds—stuttered as their teeth wound by the sweet, bitter pain of being bitten—and it pierces his heart as it falls upon him; he yawns, longs for sleep, seeks the end of the night, and loathes the day. (Sētubandha 7)
She goes out and returns again, her heart intent on searching for a way to win him back.

(Sētubandha 8) Even as he conceals himself, a conversation proceeds in front of his beloveds, who are unaware that he is standing right there in their midst; though he remains hidden, he is frequently present in their hearts. (Sētubandha 9)
When he is glanced at, she calls out his name; and even when he thinks of something else entirely, she alone remains in his heart. (Sētu 10)
The offering of a cluster of flowers gathered unevenly at the edge of a forest grove, with sprouts from the trees of heaven withered by the sighs of those who have arrived, allays his torment.
(Sētu 11) On her body, broad as a mountain slope, he plays with the weight [of the flowers], which crushes the edges of her sides as they are pressed upward by its burden.
In the middle of the inner apartments, upon the uneven ground-couches, with his hands tossing about—
his heart given over to longing for Janaka’s daughter, granted only through courtesy— he tosses about momentarily embarrassed before the faces of the women in the inner court. (Sētubandha 12–13)
When that playful woman approaches another with a laugh,
her face— once so difficult to endure in its heat— becomes dejected with grief for him. (Sētu 14) [It is] a contradiction consisting of the attainment of a secret, interwoven with clever laughter.
Hearing [the conversation] yet not perceiving it clearly, Daśamukha’s heart was fixed elsewhere upon his beloveds; Sētu 15.
Increasing his pride, envy, and arrogance, he somehow passes the moment during the conversation with the women by means of embarrassed smiles; Sētu 16.
Because his remaining arms were obstructed by his chest, and his shoulders, throat, and uneven steps were constrained, it was suspected that he was faltering in his name;
yet, with their minds distracted, his beloveds clearly could not discern the slip of his name.
Somehow Daśamukha steadied himself, uttering words given out of delusion even before they were spoken. (Setubandha 17)
He beholds himself gazed upon by his wives, who are rendered speechless by the flow of tears and their suppressed anger;

and though he has no heart for it, the Ten-faced One welcomes the defiant *huṃkāra* of his beloveds, which is uttered with wide-open mouths and accompanied by the quivering of their lips as they roll their eyes in indignation. (Sētubandha 18–19)
Even while being led away by her beloveds with ill-conceived plans,
she laughs for a moment at herself as she turns back from the seats they have left behind in their heartless haste, during that time of confusion and disorder.
Thus he reached an extreme state such that even his beloveds did not recognize him as he was being carried off.
[86] Neither by knowing nor by not knowing, neither by laughing nor by having laughed, was he consoled; nor did he cross over.
Having placed his hand upon the temples of his nearby face, he restrains the army of monkeys who have come to his lap, fearing an obstacle to the evening dalliance;
yet it is my own heart, deprived of union, that clings to him for the sake of its sorrow. (Sētubandha 22–23)

Why should I destroy the monkey host— fruitless, fickle, and clamorous— which has been driven forth, seized, dragged out, and slain by the agitation spreading through the clefts of the earth, and which stands nearby in vain?
(Sētubandha 24) Oh, [the ocean] whose waves of tears are tossed about as its eyes are upturned toward the moonbeams!
I hope that the daughter of Janaka, her face rendered speechless by the firm grasp of her hope, [remains so].
(Sētubandha 25) How will she, whose heart is turned away from separation, be when her husband has arrived?
She does not even wish for the moon; how much less so when the sun is seen? (Sētubandha 26)
She does not accept consolation; she is not led away even by the splendor of the three worlds; she feels no greed for it;
nor does she account for the destruction of her body. How can she be thought of as one who possesses affection?
(Sētu 27) She is established in her husband’s majesty, having disregarded the valor of all other virtuous men.
If only Janaka’s daughter had been there to witness the sight of Vāsālua and Rāhava’s heads!
When the bond of hope for protection from a shameful defeat has vanished, a person—powerless, friendless, and weighed down by fear—recklessly commits the act of suicide. (Sētu. 28–29)

But then, as her mass of faces—with their wrinkles raised and yawning from the lassitude of intoxication—was simultaneously commanded by the knitting of her brows, her attendants gathered at her sides.
Then, with ten mouths, she spoke to herself at once, as if her heart were multiplied into ten. (Setubandha 30)
The speech, heavy with syllables pregnant with the long-awaited attainment of the Ten-faced One, could not be uttered;
by one it was begun, by another it was seized and dropped in joy. (Sētubandha 31)
By one [mouth] half-spoken, by another mouth it was somehow completed for him.
Then, with sorrow gripped by that speaking [Rāvaṇa], whose mouth emitted smoke, his single heart tormented, and faltering due to the ten throats, he sighed heavily. (Sētubandha 32–33)
And she laughs at the night-stalkers, who give their responses simultaneously with her command,
while her body is bent by the weight of the triple-curved bow resting upon the slope of her palm as it touches the earth.
(Setubandha 34) At him, created by magic, whose eyes are fixed motionless and turned askance at the sight of the enemy—
"Indeed, here is Rāma’s head, severed from the neck and pale from the separation from Sītā.

(Sētu 35) Then, with their brows knit together in indignation and their foreheads furrowed by the knitting, they created that very head of Rāma right there on the spot, as if it were a thing cut off and brought back. (Sētu 36)
Having set out, the Rākṣasas— stumbling as they rose from falling at his feet in agitation,
somehow having completed the forest of joy, and busily engaged in carrying out the command of Daśagrīva—
reached the lotus buds formed by the water gushing from the fissures in the jeweled slopes. (Sētu 37)

And they behold the pleasure grove, where young sprouts have emerged from the breaking of trees by the wind, and where the palms of their hands rest upon breasts that have become disordered due to sleep. (Setubandha 38)
[She was] Janaka’s daughter, whose eyes were agitated by the sound of footsteps suspected to be the arrival of the Ten-faced one;

her braid, loosened because it had been untied by the hand of her beloved, remained so; and she was languid, her breasts drenched by the falling streams of tears white as washed silver. (Sētubandha 39–40)

Her face was covered by the flowing tears from her eyes, which resembled the thick filaments of a lotus; her waist was bereft of its girdle; and her beauty was wasted away as she cast off her ornaments. (Sētubandha 41)
With eyes motionless and empty because her beloved’s heart was fixed upon the horse Thōa-maüa, her joy surged like waves of tears upon hearing the roar of the monkey host;
at that moment, the places where drops of tears fell—rough with the Vasūka flowers and slightly reddened by the pollen of the *pāṭala*—marked her face. (Setubandha 42)
Bearing a face whose lower lip rests in its own natural state, free from the stain of rouge,
he resembles the moon when its orb is still incomplete— its dark fortnight not yet ended, with its digits insufficient and its fullness yet to be attained at the end of the day. (Sētubandha 43–44)
Bearing a complexion whose luster is like that of a fresh wound, with its surface visible through the openings where the fastenings of her ornaments have slipped off,
and revealing its thinness along the lines where those ornaments were bound;
she who has eyes restless to see [her beloved] and arms quivering in longing for his embrace— Sētubandha 45.
[She] languishes as if on a single bed with the beloved standing nearby;

her limbs are collapsed, exhausted by the unbearable longing doubled by the sight of the moon; and her heart is motionless, as if rubbed away by the hands of the Night-River (Yamunā), fearing that her life has departed. (Sētubandha 46–47)
She bears a face whose single side is revealed by the luster of the gems from the rings on her beloved’s fingers, while her veil hangs down far, held aloft by her hand which is weighted by her arm—
[like the bridge] whose single side is made manifest by the radiance of the jewels on the rings of the fingers of his beloved, as she carries it with her hand hanging down far, weighted by her arm.
[Sētu 48] He who had been despondent at the imminent battle is now relieved of his distress by the embrace of Rāma’s arms.
Her heart was distracted by the thought, "What will become of the Ten-faced one? as she turned away;

her heart was eager to see her beloved, yet distressed by his repeated glances that forced her eyes to close, and she was tormented by the face of her husband which emerged from the opening of her garment as it slipped away. (Setu 49–50)
And having seen him, the Rākṣasas— whose hearts were pained and who were agitated by the duties they had to perform— approached,
acting as the messengers of Māyāmaya and Rāvaṇa.
(Sētu 51)
Then, by them, the bow was placed before him with the string wound around the middle and the left hand resting upon it, having been positioned according to Rāghava’s instructions;
and upon seeing it being presented as if to cause despondency, she began to tremble. (Setubandha 52)
Upon hearing from the night-stalkers that it was Rāma’s head, Sītā fell into a swoon.
(Sētu 53) And Janaka’s daughter collapsed, her cheeks pale and heaving as she relaxed her grip with her hands;
her right breast rose unevenly, pushed forward by her left side. (Sētu 54)
At the death of her kinsmen, what can even a relative do for a person?
Thus, when her mouth was swallowed by great sorrow, the daughter of the Earth fell down unconscious;
she did not shed tears, nor could she even look upon the head of Rāma. (Sētu 55)
Having just succumbed to delusion, her life-breath exhausted, she sat upon the ground.

(Sētu 56) Her face—where breath was momentarily still, where the darkness of delusion cast a pale luster, where the orbs of her eyes were barely closed, and where the pupils were being drawn away by fainting—[remained thus]. (Sētu 57)
Having lost the hope for Rāma’s death at the very moment the suffering of separation was forgotten, Janaka’s daughter found only the bliss of fainting with eyes closed.
Not even a slight space was seen in her heart, which was filled by the circumference of her breasts. (Setubandha 58)
Even though she has sighed deeply, it is betrayed only by her trembling lips.
(Sētu 59) With indistinct sighs, she has fallen exhausted even upon the cessation of her fainting;
her eyes are upturned, bearing the sorrow made heavy by incessant tears. (Sētu 60)

[Family 4] He beholds the battlefield, uneven with the blows from the edges of discuses whirled with impetuosity, and curved with the dark marks of arrow-fletchings struck by arrows drawn and released from bows held at full stretch. (Setubandha 61)
[Its] opening is forced wide by the flesh of the neck, white with the blood that has flowed out;
it is covered in the spray from the streams of blood clinging slightly to the neck where the weapon, falling while striking, has severed it. (Sētubandha 62)

With the roots of his lower lip bitten by sleep and his fangs slightly visible, he fills the dark cavity of his throat with a mass of sloughed-off skin and blood; his brow is furrowed with a knitting of the eyebrows, seized by the grasp of night-stalkers. (Setubandha 63)
The head of Rāma, lightened by the flow of blood from his severed neck, its pupils rolling upward, [fell].

(Sētu 64) Even as her gaze remained fixed [on him], she, distressed with cheeks abandoned by sight, her hand [clinging] to her breast, went to the surface of the earth with the weight of her bosom—the supreme abode of motionlessness since the departure of life. (Sētu 65)
As she fainted, her face—its eyes rolling aimlessly in the air and in all directions, equally vacant and wandering, uttering delirious lamentations—became one with the sky.
Having observed this, he stood facing her, sinking down as he sat. (Sētu 66)
While she was still in doubt, neither did she receive a reply nor did death somehow come upon her.

But then, with her limbs outstretched, having resolved to cross the path filled with the dust of her feet, Janaka’s daughter fell, her breasts rolling upon the surface of the earth which was pressed against her chest. (Sētubandha 67–68)
Though seated with her entire body, the middle part of her— rendered bare by the complete disappearance of all folds and yet made formidable by her breasts and hips— could not reach the ground.
(Sētubandha 69) Upon seeing her husband’s face, radiant with sudden joy, she was unable to look at him without feeling bashful.
Having fallen into a long swoon, her heart returned [to life] through the touch of his arm.
Then, having somehow regained consciousness, she sought to restrain him as he bit the surface of her cheek with his arm; yet, rendered helpless, her hand could not reach him. (Sētubandha 70–71)
Thrown up by the force of the current and tossed about by the gusts of wind, his pair of hands fell upon her lap before they could even reach her breasts. (Sētubandha 72)
With her heart bewildered, unable to look directly at it, she somehow caught sight of that head of Rāma with a sidelong glance;
her face was bent by the flow of her sighs and her creeper-like arms were drooping in exhaustion. (Sētubandha 73) Having begun to lament, she cast aside the grief for Rāghava from her own body.
With her high breasts discolored by the blood from the wounds on her hands and feet, Janaka’s daughter [is thus].
(Sētu 74) The terrifying onset of calamity itself is not as painful to endure as this final end, which was witnessed by the timid eyes of women and yet endured by me. (Sētu 75)
"‘I shall release the heat from your arms and chest’—this was established in my heart;
now that you have emerged upon the earth, tell me, in whom shall this suffering be appeased? During our separation, I somehow maintained my life only by thinking, ‘I shall see you. (Sētubandha 7.6)
"Even though I have seen him, my desires are not yet fulfilled. (Setu 77) "The royal glory of the earth is fickle, being shared among many distinguished men;
how then can this extraordinary burden of sovereignty be borne by me alone? (Setu 78)
"What is this? she cried, and with eyes wide open in alarm, she beheld it;
then, her modesty vanished, she wept aloud, saying clearly, "O Lord, it is your face!
O friend, your separation has been endured together with the female cranes as if with your own companions.
"Even now, though my life is fading away, the thought that I might see you still persists.

(Sētu 80) "When the time has come for me to depart for the next world—a state where only the mere hope of seeing you brings joy—my heart still burns with longing, as it has not yet witnessed the slaying of the Ten-faced one. (Sētu 81)
My arm does not support me, nor does the bond of hope restrain my heart; yet, even as it is being thought upon, by whom has life been obstructed? (Sētubandha 82)
"O Lord, having passed beyond the midst of the ocean of worldly existence, death itself was accepted by me for your sake;
yet even now, my heart maintains its ungratefulness toward you.
(Setu 83) "O Rāma, having grasped you and reckoned your virtues, people consider you a mere mortal... (Setu 84)
How will she turn back from me, forgetting her own nature as a noble woman?

(Sētubandha 84) My desires, which had turned toward the opening of the cave of my brother-in-law’s heart—thinking, “I shall gaze upon the face of the Ten-Necked One, whose eyes are struck down by your arrows”—have been cast aside. (Sētubandha 85)

"That which people suspect of even a slight separation due to the bonds of love— that very thing has now become my sole fruit as I behold this [state]. (Setubandha 86) Then, with her pair of eyes vacant and her heart trembling, motionless, and weeping...
Consoling him with sweet words, her face bowed down, Tiaḍā says to him: "His sorrow has overflowed;
the innocent girl is broken. The fool does not perceive love; though accompanied by young women, he fears even the darkness as if it were the sun. (Sētu 87–88)
Knowing that you have taken up the burden of battle, which was abandoned and then borne by the fierce Mahinda—the sustainer of the three worlds—why do you tremble, following the example of other men?
(Sētubandha 89) The great mountains, standing in the sky above the waters of the ocean that had been churned, were not curved [in submission]. (Sētubandha 90)
How is it that the earth bears your head, which has fallen severed from Rāma?

(Sētu 90) How can the garden of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa’s lower lip become devoid of luster at the sight of Rāma, its lotuses closed by the rays of the moon-like mark on his forehead and the branches of its trees broken by the wind? (Sētu 91)

Do not weep; wipe away your tears by repeatedly turning your face from shoulder to shoulder, remembering the sorrow of separation; O lady, you must weep again upon the lap of your husband. (Sētubandha 92)
O Airāvata, you shall behold the son of Daśaratha, his complexion pale and withered by separation from you, his joy in anger now vanished, finding peace through the casting aside of his bow—
yet filled with indignation, even by Hara he would find his throat-severing undesirable. (Setubandha 93)

Even if Rāma’s head were still touching [the bowstring] and held fast by his hand when it was severed— why do you despair, seeing the Pampa forest, which shattered the pride of the Ten-faced one, where trees were uprooted by the monkeys dispatched on Rāma’s command? (Sētu 94–95)
How could he, whose world is supported by his arms, not destroy in an instant that world of the gods which was being overwhelmed by the sleep of the night-demon who had seized it?
(Sētubandha 96) Thus you have fallen into such a state of delusion, your limbs exhausted and despondent, having collapsed from a swoon.
"Clearly knowing that she is the mother of a Rākṣasa, I too am despondent. (Sētu.

97) "Even now, why is there no acceptance of you by Rāghava, whose path was fashioned through the interior of the Malaya mountains at the very moment the city of the Night-Stalker was reached, and who cast down the peaks of Trikuṭa? (Sētu. 98)
Having wandered upon the slopes of Mount Malaya as if they were the surface of the earth, and having dwelt upon the peak of Mount Suvela in the waters of the great ocean—
even now, O Rāghava, why is there no capture of you? (Setu 99) Then,
her instruction unheeded, she whose life was ebbing away and who was being revived—
Tārā sat upon her lap, in a manner consistent with the natural affection of a mother for her child;
and Tārā’s son sat upon her shoulder, clinging there through the movement of her eyes.
Then Janaka’s daughter spoke again, her voice choked with tears as she was tormented by the pressure of the heavy stone being pushed;
her sighs were loud as she gasped for breath, and the dust of the earth was raised by her hair tossing against her chest and breasts. (Sētubandha 101–102)
O friend, as soon as I first saw him seated upon the ground, I fell into a swoon;
yet when I regained my sight, I beheld him once more and held fast to my life. O Lord, such was the end you witnessed in the abode of the Rākṣasa.
Even today, my heart does not burn, though it is as if scorched by the smoke of reproach.
(Sētubandha 104) This deed of yours is like that of a man; yet, O Lord of the Niśācaras, why has this act been committed like that of a Rākṣasa?
How is it that death—which is easy to contemplate—does not come to me like that of a woman? (Sētubandha 105)
O Rāghava, as you approach here with a speed swiftened by the wind’s song, my life—though lightened by separation—is sustained;
for me, living, your heart lives on. (Sētubandha 10.6) With face veiled by tears, her braid of hair loosened from the neck as she turns toward you...
Distressed by the words spoken by her husband, whose heart was overcome by delusion, she sat down once more.

Then, with her hair disheveled and unevenly scattered as the knot of her braid unraveled and broke, she fell upon the surface of the earth, her heart despairing of the bed that was Rāma’s chest. (Sētubandha 107–108)
She was unable to wipe her face with her hand, which was trembling and distressed by fresh sprouts;
somehow, she managed to apply the *ālaka* (forehead mark) so that it met only upon one cheek.
Though the *jāhērūa* (a type of cosmetic paste) was brought before her, her vision, distressed by tears, could not take it up. (Sētu 109)
Then, somehow or other, her face—with eyes reddened by the smoke of the fire—was made to look upon [the ocean].

Then she, with tears flowing from her eyelashes due to the uneven vow of the wandering wind, beheld the face of Rāghava, which was as vast as the surface of the earth submerged in the ocean. (Sētubandha 110–111)
With her eyes fixed motionlessly, wide open and overflowing with visible tears, and directed toward Rāma’s head, her gaze cannot be restrained by her arm. (Sētubandha 112)

Seeing him, with eyes fixed on the ground and a piteous smile, she said with a wretched laugh, "Farewell to me," her voice choked with tears and her every fiber tasting only the sorrow of imminent death.
(Setubandha 113) When the unbearable agony of separation from Rāma was endured, it was received by her heart as a cruel torment.
"Better for me this shameless death than a light life devoid of affection"—saying this, she wept.
"This is the way of all women; moreover, this end is fitting for one so full of pride," she said, and striking her firm, heavy breasts, she fell down. (Sētubandha 114–115)
Thus, though she was trembling with shame for her life and exhausted by despair, Sītā did not abandon her resolve to call out "O son of Daśaratha!
Even when reproached, she did not wish to be consoled, nor did she allow a blow upon her body as if it were that of another. (Setubandha 116)

He releases his arm and does not restrain it; his heart has gained conviction that he must die. Then she began to speak to him, whose heart was turning away from the cause of death. *Setubandha* 117 [a yugalaka].
[She] whose limbs are unevenly applied as they fall and are caught by the tips of her trembling hands...
[Sētu 118] O night-stalker, do not despise my words spoken out of affection:
"In the garden, today she gathers that fragrant flower from the creepers. [Sētu 119]
"O friend, why even speak of you being alive, if the death of Rāghava were not a falsehood?
Otherwise, my heart, distressed by grief, suffers for the sake of the Lord of the Raghus.
(Setubandha 12.0) "If this were actually so, as you imagine it, it would not be possible even to think of it."
Now that the people have been informed, what consolation of mine would be appropriate?
[Sētu.
121] The entire city of the Nisācaras has let out a cry of weeping as resonant as a procession of houses.
By this one poet, what will become of the lineage of Raghu, which was once free of Rākṣasas?
(Sētubandha 122) Rāma will be slain; the three worlds will become free of Rākṣasas.
I speak this clearly: who would believe that even the destruction of their own family is dear to someone? (Sētubandha 123)
Rise up, abandon your grief; wipe this breast-surface soiled by tears.
Listen, O bird: when the husband stands facing the battle, the shedding of tears is not appropriate.
Or by whom else was Rāvaṇa rendered lusterless, his power obstructed by the ramparts?

(Sētubandha 125) And soon, O King, the son of Raghu will loosen that braid which has its dark fringe touched by the tips of the trembling hands of the captive women, and which is held unevenly aloft by fingers quivering with fear. (Sētubandha 126)

I am not so pained by you acting with such lack of shame and lightness toward the Lord of the Raghus, as I am by the transformation of the nature of the Ten-faced one— who, having witnessed Vālin’s prowess, crushed the ocean and provided a path across the land. (Sētubandha 12.7) [vāli-vadha-dṛṣṭa-sārambha-ānala-galasthika-samudra-datta-sthala-patham]
"Behold quickly the strength of Rāghava’s arms, which has carried away the ramparts of Laṅkā!

(Sētu 128) "You have been seen by me in a dream, your face soiled by the smearing of the rays of the moon and sun, with the white cloth on your shoulder half-torn by the tossing of the ears of the celestial elephant. (Sētu 129)

I have seen the path by which the row of the ten mouths of the Ten-Faced One was dragged wide open, and the mass of his mouths, which were partially joined and opened as they were pulled apart by the firm noose of Time. (Setu 130) Therefore, take heart; let this inauspiciousness perish now.

[97] Let the illusion, whose purpose has been understood and which is now rendered fruitless and contemptible, cease! Even if Rāma’s head were in such a state, it would still be gasping for breath. *Sētubandha* 131.
"Having tasted the nectar of your touch like ambrosia," [she says].

(Setu 132) Thus, her heart tormented by the unbearable thunderbolt-strike of the praise of Rāma’s love, she remembered him and wept aloud with a choked voice; though death was certain, she wept. (Setu 133)
Even with those tender words, she could not be consoled until she heard the roar of the mountain, deep with the resonance of the battle-preparations—the auspicious drum for Rāghava’s heroic exploit.
Then, her bond of hope for life was being drawn back by various kinds of consolations... [Sētubandha 13.4]... ah, the binding of the hope for life being restored through manifold reassurances.
Sighing toward her breasts, which were raised high by the weight of her heavy hips, she sighed.
(Setu 135) Then, although her beloved had been reassured by her and had become confident through repeated oaths, the fear of separation vanished;
yet once again, the pain of separation reassembles in her heart. (Setu 136)
When the sound of the monkeys’ preparations for battle has faded into illusion and delusion,
the fruit of the affectionate words spoken out of love for the daughter of the Earth (Sītā) has been seen. Thus ends the eleventh chapter,
the "Consolation."
The Twelfth Chapter: Consolation [p.
Then the dawn arrived, with its flocks of swans soiled by the pollen falling from lotuses slightly opened,
and its beds of night-lotuses slightly closed and turning yellow.
(Sētubandha 1) With the moonlight as its root, it was turbid with fresh water reddened by the glow of the dawn.
The western quarter of the night recedes like a bank eroded by the flow of a river.

On the surface of the earth, where the moonlight has descended upon the tips of the dawn-red [crests], the forms of the tree-shadows are being observed as they turn grey and begin to move anew. (Sētubandha 2–3)
The cluster of night-lotuses closes; the orb of the moon, its light half-faded and vanished, sinks away.
The eastern quarter, its face stained by the dawn-red glow of the departing night’s shadow, reveals its young stars.
And the sky appears, its surface reddened by the fresh dawn-sun, like a tree with sprouts of dark-blue darkness.
The sky is like a mountain slope where the slabs of dark stone have been unevenly split apart, revealing the harsh surface of the underlying gems.

(Setubandha 5) Meanwhile, the moon has arrived with its western slopes reddened; turbid with the hue of the hooves of elephants entering the waters of the new flood, it appears as if it were descending from the sky, having tilted its face toward the east. (Setubandha 6)
The forests possess trees whose fruits have fallen by the wind, where birds clearly utter sweet cries, where bees hum, and where the young shoots are light with honey and resin.
(Sētu 7) [The moon] is touched by the dawn, its own body is revealed, and it is filled with thick moonlight following its own form.
Having descended from the mountain peaks, the orb of the moon, with its rays acting as a supporting hand, rises up as if to welcome the cakravāka bird,
who follows it at dawn after somehow passing the night’s sorrow of separation from her beloved,
calling out in response. (Setubandha 8–9)
[The mountain] has been born with its slopes made formidable by the tips of medicinal herbs that rival the crescent moon,
possessing peaks of wealth, and emitting a flow of moonstones from the nectar flowing from the deer-marked moon. (Setubandha 10)
With the moonlight dimmed by the rays of the dawn that has eclipsed the stars in the deep interior of the sky,
the vault of heaven seems to set along with the moon, or rather, it rises again from the mountains of the ocean.
Through the reunion with her husband, the night has become fruitful both as the evening and as the pleasure of love.
The dawn, its passion for separation from night now exhausted, yet its love unabated, is fading away.

The beauty of the dawn, which surpassed the rainy season by its skillful artifice—its lingering passion having been interrupted by the king of night as his own desire increased through trust—is now vanished. (Sētubandha 12–13)

The fragrance does not leave the *cassia* flower, which has been placed upon a lotus resting in wine from a cup whose handle was carried away; it remains clinging to the body of the *vaula* [mango] tree, having been released by a passionate woman.
(Sētu 14) With her mass of hair loosened and her hips obstructed by a displaced girdle...
The company of wanton women, their bodies released by their lovers who were satiated by the fragrance clinging to their garments, [proceeds on].

(Sētu 15) With their left feet planted firmly, their heavy thighs swaying as they lift them unevenly, the young women establish themselves with difficulty, having turned back toward their beloveds even as they were heading away. (Sētu 16)
Having wandered through the night as if fallen from its place, the day has returned with its face soiled by the dust of the evening clouds, which are like lotus ponds churned up in anger.
To the rising sun, who has just emerged from the dawn, it appears as if he has arrived. (Sētubandha 17)
The lotuses, fallen apart by day, support the foot of the Goddess of Day as she departs; Sētu 18.

In the waters of the ocean, the multitude of conchs—each one separated and scattered at ease during the night—gathers together like the mother embracing the reflection of the moon that has wandered about; Sētu 19.
In the lotus ponds where the stalks have long since ceased to grow,
the fragrance remains thick and full, though it is broken by the breeze sweet with honey that stirs from them.
(Sētubandha 20)
That very same [sight] which was a pillar of support for the arms of the Rākṣasa warriors as they cried out to their throngs of beloved women,
has now become the joy of the final embrace for those who have perished.
(Setu 21) Now, this day has arrived to release the enmity that had been bound by the mouths of the heroes who were delighted by the intervening battle.
Having obtained the opportunity for his death, Rāvaṇa, who had not even found sleep, was struck down.

(Sētubandha 22) For the Lord of the Raghus, who was enduring the sorrow of separation from Sītā, a long time passed—only four watches [of the night]—yet that single night seemed like an entire aeon. (Sētubandha 23)
Their eyes, with pupils remaining moist from tears, roll and falter;
their gaze, heavy and sinking under the burden of grief, is fixed upon the bow seen in the battle.
They faint, their breaths choked by the scent of withered flowers and the dust of the battlefield. (Setubandha 24)
The stone couch, betraying the pain of her uneven tossing in sleep; [a yugma].
Then, heavy with the essence of the mountain, it betrays the approaching union with her beloved.
Having greeted him for a long time with his throbbing, exceptionally thick left arm,

he binds his mass of matted hair— which had been momentarily honored and then set aside as it was drawn back from the path of the bow of Dharma— and which is fragrant with crushed *tamāla* leaves used as a pillow. (Sētubandha 26–27)
Having given the signal, with tears trickling down, his chest heaving from long-restrained anger,
he cast his gaze toward Laṅkā— a look difficult to behold because the pupils were fully dilated. (Setubandha 28)
She takes up the bow—its strength already seized—which was placed on the path of her bed empty of Śītā;
a bow whose millions of parts were fashioned from the tears shed by her face as she repeatedly turned it toward him in the longing of separation.
Then, that [bow], resting upon the surface of the earth, was grasped firmly with the encircling grip of her left hand.
Having made his opponent bend down under the weight of his body as it was being shifted by his right hand,
and having struck him with a heavy head-thrust that was slow due to a sigh,
the Lord of the Raghus— whose only weapon was his bow bent like a moving mountain— advanced against his adversary. (Sētu 30–31)
And the monkey army moved forth, with its single great mountain formed by the peaks of the weighed-and-lifted mountains meeting together,
and with the trees recognizable by their branches resting upon corresponding arms. (Sētubandha 32)
The wicked are consumed by the burden of their own evil armor; what can even the capable do?

For those who wear their own strength as armor, their own irresistible arms are the weapon. (Sētubandha 33) [Awakened to the way of battle, which is the essence of the Nāga-Nisācaras and free from the impurity of deceit.]
Having arranged the vanguard of the army of Vibhīṣaṇa with skillful routes through Laṅkā, [Rāma] set out.
(Sētubandha 34) "How can he be abandoned while he is rushing toward battle?"—thus was Sugrīva grieved;
and when Rāma had taken up his weapons, Vibhīṣaṇa consoled him regarding the race of the night-stalkers. (Sētubandha 35)
When the bow was strung by the Lord of the Raghus, who had churned the ocean with its mountains uprooted, Laṅkā trembled as if from the uneven collapsing of its houses, walls, and gate-towers;
Hearing the roar of the bow, like Rāvaṇa’s first words after being reassured, the clamor of the monkeys— like a thunderbolt strike upon the mountain-like hearts of the Rakshasa lords,
causing young women to faint— delights the city folk as it reaches the ears of the Śītā. (Sētubandha 37–38)

The mountain, having crossed the ocean whose waters were agitated by the force of the wind’s violent friction, now causes its echoing roar to subside as it fills the caves with its mass of water; it is a mountain that has conquered all other mountains, its thundering sound like the first twang of a bowstring drawn to its full extent. (Setubandha 39)
Having heard the words of the Ten-faced one, whose face was filled with agitation and wonder, [Rāvaṇa’s] anger finally subsided after a long time.
(Sētubandha 40) Meanwhile, the Lord of the Rākṣasas, disregarding the monkey army that had crossed over the ramparts and was exulting in battle, woke up from his sleep-induced stupor. (Sētubandha 41)
Daśagrīva carries away Pārvatī,
who has fallen asleep amidst the auspicious sounds of uneven musical instruments— a sleep interrupted by the shifting of her limbs as she tosses and turns in her restless slumber. (Sētubandha 42)

Then, as the sound of the bowstring awakened him, the sleep of the Ten-faced One— who was melting with honey-like intoxication and whose eyes were heavy with blood— vanished, shattered by his wrath. (Sētubandha 43) The high jeweled archways, made formidable by fingers that had leaped over them one by one...
Having turned back his two upraised arms, he placed them upon the lap of his own seat.

Then, portending the commencement of battle, the drum of the Ten-faced One began to strike—a sound that caused a great agitation among the gods as it shattered the pillars of Rāvaṇa’s palace, which had already been trembling with fear. (Sētubandha 44–45)
The night-stalkers, having received the signal for battle and seized their respective weapons,

emerged with the young women clinging to their necks in a tight embrace. [Sētubandha 46] When the matter was understood from the one who had received the summons, the single signal for battle fell upon them.

The lower lips of the young women, their grip loosened, slip from the mouths of their beloveds. (Sētubandha 47) When the sound of the battle preparations is heard, the young women’s arms—clinging to the necks of their lovers—are slightly slackened;
yet, due to the intensity of their passion, they do not fall, but merely dangle. (Sētubandha 48)

Hastening at the sound of their own cries, they take up their weapons with hands agitated and trembling; the night-stalkers writhe, their breasts heaving as they press against the embrace of their beloveds, even as their lovers restrain them from breaking their modesty through excessive passion. (Setubandha 49)
In the hearts of gamblers, which have long been held back by fear, pride finds no foothold.
(Sētubandha 50) The more the beloved restrains him, the more his martial ardor increases through a pride that is further inflamed by the imagined insult to his lordly status. (Sētubandha 51)
Held back by the hands of their lovers, checked by affection, restrained by love,
and suppressed by the joy of their husbands' reconciliation, the night-prowlers have departed. (Sētubandha 52)
In the burden of battle, where the gods, the wind-gods, and the Gandharvas were equally exhausted, the swords of the enemy felt ashamed to arm themselves and could not endure their own expansion.
In the forest glades and amidst the thickets of trees, they were formidable, resonant, and faltering as they struck. (Setu 53)
He fastens his great shark-hide armor, which fits perfectly against the uneven surface of his chest and back;
[this armor] is a moving fortress for the Lord of the Rākṣasas, whose prowess was witnessed in the battle with the gods, and it serves as a ready hand in the discharge of arrows.
Delighted, he gradually puts it on with skill. (Setu 54–55)

When Tisira raised his arm, his armor—terrible to behold with its gap between his neck and shoulder—slipped loosely down upon his chest, which was made thin by his hand being held up for a single moment.
As he moved the great earth, which had been placed upon his shoulders like a heavy burden, he [dragged] himself along. (Setubandha 56)
The armor of Indrajit falls away with a heavy weight from his chest, which resembles a heap of young calves.
From the chest of Indrajit, a breastplate is raised, its surface appearing smooth from the polish of Rāvaṇa’s tusks that were used as pestles. (Sētubandha 57–58)
Even for a single elephant, after a long time, the sky— freed from the radiance of its body with its long, hanging trunk resting upon its thighs—
appears as if its dark clouds have vanished.
(Sētubandha 5.9) One who is eager for battle sighs, his shoulders raised and revealed by the upward-turning of his chest.
Having fastened his armor, whose bonds had been severed by the mouth of Vajra, Dhūmrākṣa,

with eyes rolling in rage, let blood flow for a long time from the wounds on his body— which had long since healed and burst open— through the openings in the armor, like blood from a cloud of the rising sun. (Sētubandha 60–61)
The broad forehead of the dwarf, bent by the pain of indignation at being tossed up, expands with its copper-colored circlet split open by the clearly visible parting of his hair.
(Sētu. 62)
Though his shoulders were capable of enduring the blows of the gods' weapons, he fastened his well-examined armor;

yet, standing face-to-face, he did not perceive before him the unbearable arrows of Rāma, which were difficult to ward off—arrows recognizable by the embraces of the amorous women who had turned back in haste. (Setubandha 63)

Sāraṇa does not fasten his armor until he has first smelled the fragrance of [Rāvaṇa’s] breasts. (Setubandha 64) On the chariot of Kuṃbhakarṇa, there are lions whose manes are darkened by the smoke of burning temples, whose claws are stained with the blood of gods, and who are seized by serpents writhing in their disheveled manes. (Setubandha 65)
He harbors indignation, resists even the weighty good deeds of his master, and shakes off the pride of others; his hand is clenched into a fist upon the hilt of his sword.
All capable men are agitated, the clamor is endured [with difficulty], and the heart grows weary. (Setubandha 66)
The hosts of celestial damsels, descending from the archways of their vimānas, laid aside their ornaments.

(Sētubandha 67) While the delighted host of night-stalkers was thus preparing for the joy of battle, the army of monkeys was already seen gathered on all sides around the son of Raghu. (Sētubandha 68)
The city of the night-stalkers (Rāvaṇa), its splendor enhanced by monkeys leaping up as they emerge from the Bhaggarāma, Viōlaṇḍali,
and Ujjāṇa gardens and palaces,
is being held fast by the lord of monkeys, who has descended with steady steps upon the mountain peak. (Sētubandha 69)
It licks up the monkey host that has been left behind, fleeing in panic due to the sudden onset of poison and anger;

it beholds the city of the night-stalkers, where the gods have fled to the sky at the command of the arrogant monkey army as they rush away in haste, and which must now be seen as the bride of the gods. (Sētubandha 70–71)

The trees, having first been shattered by the monkeys as they slipped from the mountain peaks split open by the force of their thighs while rushing to the battle, fall along the path expected by them;
meanwhile, the monkeys [proceed] with their bodies shielded by the clouds that have risen up to the surface of the sky. (Sētubandha 72)
The night-rangers, stationed in formations like the trappings of elephants adorned with bells, are heard [roaring].
The wind, following the force of the monkeys' army, swirls as it is turned back and rebounds.
The sound of the breaking of trees, heavy with the earth being dragged out by the uneven terrain, and the dust raised by the shouting;

the state of the mountain ridges where the jewel-like peaks have been crushed, filling the nearby caves, and where the cascades have burst forth from the slopes as Mount Suvela was overturned, casting its spray toward the quarters of the sky—[all this is described]. (Sētubandha 74–75)
Those footprints of Mahendra, which had been firmly impressed long ago by his strides upon the mountain, were now shattered by monkeys eager to tear open the interior of the cave;
they became merely heaps of ashes remaining within the ramparts of the city of the Nisācaras. (Setubandha 76)
With the flames of the Lord of Rākṣasas extinguished by the monkeys who scrambled over the rocks in an instant,
the city of the Rākṣasas— surrounded by monkeys standing close together like massive mountains— became like a fortress with its iron gates buried in the middle of the ramparts. (Sētubandha 77–78)
Then that army of monkeys, with their broad faces turned back and their wives divided [among them], formed a circular formation joined to the ramparts of Laṅkā, which were packed without any gaps;
they were like a second mountain range bound together upon the whirlpool of the moat, as deep as the second ocean. (Setubandha 79)
The army set out to leap across Suvela as monkeys [leap] over the Laṅkā mountain; it was like crossing a ford.

(Sētubandha 80) But when the abode of the Ten-faced one was shaken by the monkeys, the host of night-rangers moved with a great clamor, like the waters of the ocean when the earth is split open by the fire at the end of an aeon. (Sētubandha 81)
Having mounted his chariot, he ascends it with arrows that bend upon leaping over the elephants nearby;
the battle is equalized by the lions that have broken their pairs and fled. (Setu 82) Somehow having fastened his armor, he [stands] with the entire host of monkeys gathered for the encounter.
The foot-soldier, his horse urged on by the lash of the bowstring, proceeded in his chariot;

the chariot of Indrajit, with its wide pole-fastenings scraping against the walls of the houses in the clusters of swaying banners, seemed as if it were the very city of the Rākṣasas spread out in a single location. (Sētubandha 83–84)
In a single moment, his elephants appear like flashes of lightning; in another moment, they become buffaloes;
for a mere instant, they bear clouds; and in a moment, they become horses and mountains. (Sētu 85)
The breaking of the command of the Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa), though it caused his face to become turbid with the agitation of his position as he emerged without hesitation,
was nevertheless pleasing to his own forces at that moment—
a battle in which the beauty of the warriors was being repeatedly intensified, and chariots were yoked and engaged with speed.
The army of the night-stalkers moves out, with its elephants moving as they are yoked, and its horses galloping as they are harnessed.
(Sētu 87) The army departs, with Rāma led by his elephant, the Lord of the Monkeys (Vibhīṣaṇa) informed by his chariot, Hanumān led by his horse, and the host of monkeys led by the earth.
(Sētu 88)
The army turns back, stumbling through the narrow openings of the cow-pens, their elephants' trunks piled up as they collide;
they are tossed about between the houses, emerging from single openings that cannot be closed.
With difficulty, the gates of the cow-pens are opened by the tips of the yokes turning within them. (Setubandha 89)
The earth, its surface covered by the dust raised by the chariots of the Rākṣasas,

endures the burden of the Rakṣasas— though heavy, it becomes light through their impetuosity— as they crush the elephants of the quarters, break the hoods of the serpents, and shatter the underworld. (Setubandha 90–91)
The army marches forth, its vanguard collapsing in the center, its mass blocked at the gateway,
its broad front gasping for breath, filling the courtyards of the mansions.
Thus the host of night-stalkers marches, with pillars made of children and its vast ranks divided.

The courtyards of the Rākṣasa dwellings, which for a moment possessed the beauty of riverbanks where rivers had been filled and then exhausted, now appeared like rivers flowing level across the ground, emerging from a single mouth and proceeding toward the sea; they were deserted by the warriors who had gone forth to face the battle with the monkeys. (Setu 93–94)
The host of Rākṣasas, emerging from the gates of Laṅkā—which had been opened with speed by the siege—rushed forth;
and the multitude of monkeys, like forest fire fanned by a fierce wind, was set in motion.
(Sētubandha 95)
The army of the night-stalkers increased its combat readiness, with its cavalry spreading out in the wings,
its elephants freed from their goads, and the reins of its chariots loosened. Then,
in a single charge, they struck one another, their feet finding no foothold on the ground beneath them.
Thus the monkey army advanced in a circle, with warriors who were not dependent on others.
(Sētu 97) Filled with rage, they set forth; those heroes of great price and prowess in battle are urged forward.
They slay or are slain, yet by their mutual affection alone, the warriors do not break ranks. (Sētu 98)
Thus ends the twelfth canto in the great poem *Daśamukhavadha*, composed by Śrī Pravarasena.

[The Thirteenth Consolation: Then, by the night-stalkers and the monkeys, who had emerged and met together, having joined and closed ranks, the heavy departure for battle was both signaled with a roar and endured. (Setubandha 1)

Thus, with their bodies turned away by those standing in front, they stepped forward one after another, eager for the embrace and longing for the strike, until they were drawn back. (Sētubandha 2) Just as it was resolved in hearts turbid with passion, so was it manifested by eyes clouded with love.
In the face of the enemy at the front of the battle, the Rākṣasas withdrew their weapons.
(Sētu 3) The warriors do not break; with swords held motionless in fists whose speed is increased by the weight of their feet, they have realized the mark and are intent on the first blow. (Sētu 4)

The female elephants, with their trunks raised like trees shaken by the force of the monkeys' hands, scatter vermilion powder from the swirling circles of their faces as they shake their branches; they are the ones who struck the temples of the elephants with their trunks. (Sētubandha 5) [This is] for the sake of the wrath of the descendant of Daśaratha, and for the sake of the unbearable pride of the Lord of the Rākṣasas.

The result for both sides was equally terrible and appropriate to their respective positions. (Sētubandha 6) The monkeys destroyed the elephants with elephants, the charioteers with horses, and the riders with chariots; meanwhile, the army of the Rākṣasas became both the adversary and the weapon for the monkeys. (Sētubandha 7)
The mass of the mountain’s thick trunk, emerging as it is enveloped, surges upward like a flood of water; it is a mountain ground by the chest of the nāga king, crushed by the fury of the monkeys.
(Setubandha 9) [p.
109] Of the mountain shattered against the surface of the nāga king’s chest and pulverized by the rage of the monkeys...
The mass of rocks rises upward and falls back down with faces turned toward the earth.

(Sētu 10) The paths through which the warriors are seen being slaughtered in dense, continuous succession in the midst of the enemy's forces are difficult for soldiers to traverse, even for those possessing extraordinary valor. (Sētu 11)
He breathes out with courage; his unimpeded and swift hand laughs;
the bond of enmity increases; and he is capable of reconciling himself with daring deeds.
(Setubandha 12) Even when his head falls, it does not fall; even when rent by the agony of a headache, his heart does not break.
Even when being incited, the fear of battle does not cling to those of perverse understanding (Sētu 13).

Amidst the blows and the occasions for displaying pride, the assembly of men endures; even during blameless withdrawals from the field by the warriors, the essence of their wrath does not recede (Sētu 14).
The monkeys close their eyes with indignation, shaking their thick masses of mane which are tossed about as they tear apart the riverbank;
having bitten down firmly on the roots of the teeth, they roar in resentment. (Setubandha 15) One should not show contempt, but rather remember the good deed of one’s master even in times of doubt.

Death is not taken into account; even when danger is seen, shame is remembered. (Sētu 16) Those very same *rākṣasa* demons who were long ago cast aside by the first-born [goddesses] even at the risk of their own lives, have now been pursued by the *asura* captives who have come face-to-face with them. (Sētu 17)
The monkeys, their limbs pale from the blood of the enemy warriors they have targeted, disregard the pain of wounds and the heat of the forest;
savoring the fresh blows, they leap about.
(Setubandha 18) They do not wait for an opportunity; they uproot the evil deed committed by another.
They proceed as described, entering with great acclaim.
(Setu 19 [Ākulaka 12]) Thus,
that [palace] of theirs was manifested as a secret chamber for the amorous dalliance of celestial maidens.
The battle, which shattered the bond of the world and its inhabitants, and which reached as far as the palaces of Mahendra,
was such that the tusks of elephants were splintered against the chests of monkeys who had embraced them. (Setubandha 20)
The path of the monkey-host was resonant with the tinkling of the moving bracelets of celestial damsels falling upon the ground where slain warriors lay;

the chariots were cleared away by the uprooting of trees, the leaders of the elephant herds were scattered by the upward heaving of the earth, the horses were seized and cast aside, and the ranks of the Rākṣasas were struck down by the pursuing monkeys. (Sētubandha 21–22)
[The army] where the blows from sandalwood trees—unbearable due to the bliss of the cool surface of the lake—are being endured;
where the sound of arrows passes through mouths opened wide with a roar as they exit;
where the foot soldiers are turned back and driven away by the breaking and mending of their pots. (Setu 23)
The horses were silenced by their neighing, which was choked with foam from the exhaustion of drawing the chariot through the blood-stained path;

[the battlefield] resounded with the shouts of "Well done! uttered in joy at the enemy's wounds, while heads fell amidst the groans of warriors who had collapsed, unconscious from the force of the blows, their cries muffled within their mouths. (Sētubandha 24–25)
The army of elephants, having been halted in their distress by rocks hurled at them, has turned back;
the chariots are being identified with difficulty as they flee, their banners shattered and their own warriors bewildered and lost;
the horses, exhausted from dragging the chariots pushed down by mountains, have dropped their heads and are groaning. (Setubandha 26)
The white blood was broken and mixed with the red juice of the mountain minerals crushed by the earth-shaking [monkey] as he rolled upon the ground;
the path of the fresh river was discernible through the mountains that had been hurled down and pulverized by the monkeys;
and the monkey host descended along the paths where the *vañciā* and *iñciā* trees had been uprooted. (Sētubandha 27–28)
[The battle] where masses of manes were scattered by the leaps of monkeys charging forward;
where warriors, struck by staff-weapons fallen from the hands of those in their midst, were cast upon the earth;
and where tusks were driven into the chests of night-stalkers whose heads had been seized by monkeys. (Sētubandha 29)
The dust was laid by the spray from mountain torrents held aloft by the clouds;
the chariots were drawn by horses whose mouths were turned back as they were guided by the palms of the charioteers’ hands. (Setubandha 30)
The streams of rivers of blood, formed by mountain torrents crushed by the impact of arrows, flow forth. (Sētu 31) The armies cry out, unable to endure;
their flanks are being torn apart, their faces are being cut off, and their opposing warriors are being shattered and driven back. (Sētu 32)
The night-stalkers, their sword-blows aimed at targets unobserved by monkeys who have shattered trees with their strikes,
continue to fall even as they are dragged away, their eyes closed in a swoon.
(Sētubandha 33) The battlefield, where the heavy, fallen warriors are crushed and the Rākṣasa heroes lie motionless and exhausted, throbs with life.
The monkey warrior fell, his armor shattered and his chest torn open. (Sētubandha 34) Through valor, one protects one's followers from calamities;
through prowess, one protects one's retinue; through life, one protects one's honor; and through the body, one protects one's fame. (Sētubandha 35)
The chest is shattered, but not the heart; the chariot is broken, but not the spirit.
The lofty peaks of their heads are severed, yet not the warriors' longing for battle.
(Sētubandha 36) With mountain torrents that stream with floods of blood red as the sky, along the paths of the downpour...
The expanse of the earth’s surface is not submerged by the waters of the rivers poured into the jars.

(Rāmasetu 37) Resembling the frontal globes of elephants that have endured the blows of swords, the mountain peaks, fractured unevenly by the forceful strikes of the monkeys’ arms, shatter apart. (Rāmasetu 38)

Even though thirsty for a long time, the bird drinks with a rasping sound from the iron vessel—its mouth appearing like a forest opening pregnant with the breaking of its armor—and even after drinking, he gazes about; though fallen, he trembles, yet he maintains his indignation in his pure heart. (Sētubandha 39)
Even his severed head runs along with its trunk, with a stream of blood flowing from its upraised throat;
the enemy of valor provides the flavor and bears the burden of his prowess. (Setubandha 40)
The onset increases the pride born of the intensity of battle;

it brings about fame as if it were an enemy, does not tolerate delay as if it were a foe, attains happiness as if it were life, and casts away its own life as a warrior hurls his weapon at the front. (Sētubandha 41–42)
The monkeys, their sapless arms exhausted by wounds from the blows of swords and drenched in blood, fainting and overcome by exhaustion, are supported by their own mountain peaks.
They display their pride like a flower, yet they do not believe their glory to be unblemished, even as it grows. (Sētubandha 43)

The army of warriors does not merely proceed with the gravity of the world; it advances with a specific strategic formation. (Sētu 44) Capable [warriors] enter the enemy's tumultuous mass—which has increased its weight through the burden of advancing troops—swiftly along their own path of flow, having observed the position of the enemy's soldiers. (Sētu 45)
They bear the burden of their fame, they do not tolerate the humiliation of their valor,

they manifest anger, increase their pride, and are capable of daring deeds. (Sētubandha 46) [The joy of the warriors' desires for battle has melted away due to fainting from the momentary loss of consciousness caused by the shock of being struck.]
The battle unfolds, its fame circulating through the world, acquired by the life-blood of those slain.
(Sētubandha 47) In moments of doubt one laughs; in daring one is delighted; in calamity one takes pleasure;
in fainting one rests; but in death alone is it reckoned as truly endured. (Sētubandha 48)

The sun has set, having been seized by the circle of night as if by a foot-path, its day broken by the force of its sudden descent; it is a mountain of earth, with its base deeply buried and its lightning-like rays spread wide in the mid-sky. (Setubandha 49)
The dust of the earth falls in all directions, spreading out like a mass of clouds due to its weight.
(Sētu 50) Does the dust die away, or does it fill the earth? Does it go forth from the quarters, or does it stand within the quarters?
Its path of departure unseen, it falls from the sky; does it cling to the heavens? (Sētu 51)
The army of the night-stalkers is seen, thick with monkey warriors, standing before the mountain of jewels like the shadow of a slain elephant at the foot of a mountain. (Sētubandha 52)
The mass of dust, rising from the horses' hooves as they gallop, obscures the sky;
with the foam from the mouths of the weary steeds and the dark clouds, the thick cloud of dust appears like a dark rain-cloud in the narrow expanse of the heavens.
(Sētubandha 53) The path of the mountain, having descended into the sky when hurled by the impetuosity of the monkeys, is now cleared of its tracks.
The radiance of the sun’s rays falls like a stream from a conduit, its brilliance obscured by turbidity.

(Sētu 54) Blood is bound together in streams of gathered gore, resembling thick honeycombs, filling the hollows of the broad shoulders of the mountain-like demons who were dragged away in anger. (Sētu 55)
Their eyes closed and weary from being struck by the rays of the sun, which were themselves distressed by the dust raised during the tumultuous movement of the battle, the elephants find relief;
their faces are choked with the dust mingled with the ichor flowing from their temples.
Spreading through the midst of the multitude of blood-channels gaping from the wounds at their bases... [Sētubandha 56]
One by one, the masses of earth, piled upon one another, are bound together.

(Sētubandha 57) Having extinguished them in the sky and dried them with the clouds, the wind now draws up the streaks of dust—grey from being cast into the path of the uneven shadows and thinned by the revolving mass of smoke. (Sētubandha 58)

In the theater of battle, the dust of the earth, tossed by the wind, appears like a veil for the faces of the horses charging headlong toward one another, obscuring their vision. (Setubandha 59) And then, [the dust] was scattered by the winds rushing along the paths through the forest-like chests of the warriors...
Like a river of blood that has uprooted the trees on its banks with the mud of the earth, he lies prostrate.

(Sētubandha 60) The remaining dust, lying thin upon the ground and scattered by the wind, whirls in fragments; it possesses the faint luster of lotus stalk-fibers gathered together by a mass of frost from a Palāśa flower. (Sētubandha 61)

The army turns back, following the path of the river channels winding between the mountains and hills, with its banners fluttering as it maneuvers through the gaps left by fallen herds of elephants. (Sētubandha 62)

The monkeys fall, having endured blows difficult to bear, having fulfilled their burden in battles where they could not be abandoned once engaged, and having performed difficult tasks on paths made impassable by being trampled. They bring about the satisfaction of the headless trunks that have sworn enmity toward the slaughter of their kinsmen. (Sētubandha 63)

The battle increases with the falling of many heroes, their arms severed by sword-strokes and rendered useless as they are deprived of the strength provided by the weapons held in their grasp. (Sētubandha 64) Śyāmā cannot bear to carry the arm of Niśicara, which is heavy from being severed at the root; though the bracelets remain bound around the wrist, the armor has been stripped away and gathered up. (Sētubandha 65)

The yak-tail fans, their foam clinging to the sides as they fall into the deep whirlpools of blood, sink down, heavy with eyelashes dripping with moisture; their front halves have been lifted by upward-directed cries, while their rear portions sag under the weight of that effort. (Sētubandha 66)
In the mountain-enclosure, the lordly elephants shake their trunks, which are raised upward and plunged into the rocks of the mountain praised by the monkeys (Sētu. 67).
Then, the Rākṣasa warriors, intent on breaking the gods who were struggling under the weight of the monkeys, became ready to strike;
