they turned toward the opposing army, which was difficult to withstand as it was first advanced by the Rākṣasas (Sētu. 68).
The army of the night-stalkers— its elephants bewildered by broken neck-chains, its chariots overturned by the shifting of positions,
its cavalry turned back on a single step, and its horses urged on in circular maneuvers—
having wandered about, exhausted by their efforts, now turns back as its fury subsides. (Setu 69)
The monkeys, having slightly turned aside, were cast off and then fearlessly huddled together; the night-stalkers [turned back].

(Sētubandha 70) The army turns back, crowded with chariots that are being broken by elephants following the ranks of foot-soldiers, with foot-soldiers whose horses have bolted because they were tethered to the chariots, and with the backs of the steeds slipping away from the chariots.
(Sētubandha 71)

The monkey army lay prostrate, its trees broken by the weight of its limbs as they trembled with violent and simple fear; its warriors had fallen away in exhaustion, and the night-stalkers were driven back in terror. (Sētubandha 72)

The Rākṣasas, who have not yet found an opportunity to shatter their first pride by the report of unbroken valor, continue to roam even though they are defeated; they do not succumb to fear. (Setubandha 73) [Antyakulaka 4]

Nevertheless, he whose heavy chariot with its wheels was being turned with difficulty by the horses as they veered aside, and who had acquired the glory of battle through his skill in restraining those who had fled in all directions;
he, the night-stalker, whose broad forehead was bent and half-broken by the monkeys turning their backs and bowing down. (Setu 74)
The army was filled with horses rearing up as they were struck by elephants retreating from the enemy's camp;

the chariots were being dragged away by horses that had been terrified by monkeys who had killed their warriors and slain their charioteers, while the horses stood motionless, held back by their tails which were being pulled by fleeing monkeys. (Sētubandha 75–76)
The army of the night-stalkers was broken; its path was made sparse by the cries of those whose strength was checked as they were struck down in the stream of the road;

their arms were rendered useless as their weapons fell away. Then, their hearts filled with anxiety for the protection of their own eyes, one after another, they were overcome by a lightness born of heart-rending envy.
The night-stalkers, their rows of ten faces fallen into despair, have abandoned the fear of battle;

their fame, once joined and now severed, has turned away; their courage, which had been displayed facing the enemy, has vanished; and their burden of war, which they had undertaken with difficulty under the power of the monkeys, has slackened. (Sētu 78–79)
Then, for the night-stalking monkeys who were ashamed by their defeat yet thrilled by the increasing momentum, a battle commenced against the enemy warriors, fierce and full of valor.
Sugrīva, whose face was like a blossoming tree, granted them the joy of combat. (Setubandha 80)
He was struck by the fragrant laughter of flowers scattered from the temples of rutting elephants;

he went, smelling the life-breath of the son of Aśaniprabha, who had closed his eyes in bliss as he inhaled the scent of fresh sandalwood fallen upon his chest in the battle for his daughter’s wedding. (Sētubandha 81–82)
Having struck Vajramuṣṭi with his fist, the Lord of Monkeys laughs, while Vajramuṣṭi’s pair of eyes—
reddened by the flames issuing from his wrathful gaze and burst open by the blow of that fist— stare in agony.
(Sētubandha 83)
Delighted by his long battle with Kuvera, Susena, having been struck by Nala’s blow,
was rendered motionless as his arm— its bracelets shattered and its nails protruding— was caught and lifted up by Nala’s pair of feet.
(Setu 84) [Nala] endured the blow, while the other’s neck was broken by the force of the palm-strike.
Having slain Jambumālī, the son of the Wind (Hanumān) immediately split him in two; he placed his head upon his body and half of his body upon the surface of the earth.
With the marrow of his head gushing forth, drenched by the intense impact against the entire ground, the ten directions were sprinkled. (Sētubandha 85–86)
Then he attains an extreme degree of martial valor in the battle between Indrajit and Vālin—a valor that, as each slew the other's attendants, was weighed upon a balance held in their own hands;
[Indrajit] excels his opponent, who has filled the quarters with arrows and is encompassed by a circle of bows. *Sētubandha* 87. b.1–2.
The monkeys [are like] mountains by the thousands, released and falling from the trees they have uprooted.
(Sētubandha 88) The masses of trees fall, their branches bending and closing together under the weight of abundant blossoms, carrying bees upon them;
their trunks are lightened by the scattered fruit, while their shoots break off from the middle as they sway. (Sētubandha 89)
The son of Vālin does not reach him; the multitude of arrows quivers in the sky;
the trees are being severed while still half-clinging [to him], yet they do not overtake the son of the Ten-faced One.
(Sētubandha 90) The scent of sandalwood is wafted upward by the wind, scattering the blossoms of the *loddhra* tree.
The sky becomes filled with the essence of crushed mandāra flowers and cloves.
(Sētu 91 [Ākula 7]) Thus,
that [battle] was characterized by equal skill and repeatedly received shouts of acclaim from both sides.
Even as the elephants, the supreme standard for the sons of Indrajit and Vālin, advance, the battle increases.
(Sētu 92) The bees clinging to the arrow-shafts emerging from the midst of tree blossoms are driven away;
the armies, terrified by the confusion of soldiers fleeing in disorder, look on in amazement. (Sētu 93)
The son of Vālin, who had ascended into the vault of the sky with arrows discharged by the son of the Ten-faced One;
and the son of the Ten-faced One, who was obstructed by the *śāla* trees, rocks, and mountains hurled in wrath by the son of Vālin.
(Sētubandha 94)

The horizon was reddened by the blood from the bodies of monkeys torn apart by the arrows of the night-stalkers; the surface of the earth was made muddy by the flow of blood from the Rākṣasas who were struck down by the blows of the monkeys; and the grief of the monkeys was offered [in mourning] for Vālin’s son, who was being dragged away, tormented by the enemy’s spear. (Sētubandha 95)
The army of the night-stalkers was shattered by fear for the son of the Ten-faced one, who had fainted from the blow of the rock;
there arose the clamor of the monkey host as the night-stalkers, led by the son of Tārā, exerted themselves;
and the world of the Rākṣasas was filled with the joy of the Vānaras, who were pained by the son of Mandodarī. (Sētubandha 96–97)
The monkey host laughs with ease at the shattering of the fruitless rocks fallen upon the earth;
the sky is whitened by the loud laughter released from the mountain caves, whose chest-slabs have been split asunder.
(Setubandha 98) Now, when Indrajit, the son of Vālin, had his enthusiasm broken in battle...
"The [monkey] is slain! they cry with laughter; "He stands [victorious]! the Rākṣasas rejoice.
(Sētubandha 99) Thus the thirteenth chapter is completed.
[The Fourteenth Act: Consolation] Now,
when the days have passed fruitlessly and the hope for the recovery of the Ten-faced one has been shattered by his capture—
The Lord of the Raghus, his face turned toward Laṅkā and his slain Rākṣasas falling away in exhaustion, is weary.

(Sētubandha 1) Thinking, "Daśānana will not go to battle while comfortably seated among these [mountains]," he desires to discharge a multitude of arrows at the enemy hosts who have received their breath [of life]. (Sētubandha 2)

When their enemy has fallen into their view, has come within reach, and is being crushed by their arrows in battle, the monkeys wander about, having rendered the trees unconscious with their exertion.
Having shattered the masses of rocks that were hurled swiftly and driven back in the opposite direction, [they advance]. (Sētubandha 3)
First, the arrows of Rāma, which shatter the mental aspirations of the enemy monkeys, succeed; [Sītā] is found.
The weapon of the monkeys is severed by the hand simultaneously with the tree being uprooted;
it is dragged away by the demons, yet the weapon of the monkey does not reach the sky nor the demon who released it so swiftly.
When the calf was pierced, an arrow—released in fury by monkeys whose prowess was joined with haste—fell upon the place where the head had been severed from the rock-mountain peak;
yet that very arrow was joined back together by Rāvaṇa, and the bow was likewise made whole once more. (Sētubandha 6)

The earth is strewn with the heads of Rākṣasas, crushed by the arrows of Śarabha. (Sētubandha 7) On the bodies of those Rākṣasas, one sees the reflections of the openings of the holes made by venomous serpents—whose fire-like poison was ignited by the unevenly struck shafts—but the arrows themselves are not seen. (Sētubandha 8)
As he leaps up, strikes his palms together, and roars in his heart,
only the arrows of Rāma— marked by the falling of his head as it was severed and bound— are visible in his mouth. (Sētubandha 9)
Wherever he was seen, wherever his roar vanished,
and wherever he moved as he willed, right there did Rāma’s arrows fall.
(Sētubandha 10) In that army of Rākṣasas, elephants, warriors, horses, and so forth, were seen [slain].
The arrows of Rāma, having shattered the formidable mass of the foremost ranks, have emerged [from the fray].

(Sētu 11) Only that which was already struck by the arrows of Rāma was seen to fall; indeed, the entire army of the night-stalkers fell simultaneously with the very commencement of their flight, overcome by fear. (Sētu 12)

In the highest sense, after a long time, the day has emerged, its fear of the Rākṣasa having vanished. (Sētubandha 14) Then, with his bow raised, Vālin’s son, who had crushed Rāvaṇa’s son, moved through the sky where the darkness was blended with the luster of the clouds. (Sētubandha 15)

Having brought the lord of the night-stalkers (the moon) to an end, those two, whose roots of intense enmity were consumed, were simultaneously perceived by the Creator as if they were two tender sprouts;
and [so too were] the tongues of fire issuing from the mouths of serpents, upon which Śambhu had bestowed his protection. (Sētu. 16)
With their arms hanging down in confidence, having slain all the Rākṣasas without exception, [the arrows] fell upon the bridge.

Then, with their bodies pierced, their second arms torn away from their regions, and their faces revealed, those serpent-arrows remained fixed upon Rāghava’s body with their arms interlocked. (Sētubandha 17–18)
The lordly serpents, their mouths set ablaze by the sparks of the fire of poison,
fall like iron rods— resembling arrows released from the drawing of a bow— that surpass even the stars at the edge of a flash of lightning. (Sētubandha 19)

Arrows, resembling fireflies emerging from the setting sun’s orb, fall across the sky— halfway through the heavens— which has been darkened by the great rākṣasa Māyandhara, like a black ocean. (Sētubandha 20)
The serpents, their coils split apart by the force of the arrows, become severed and fall upon their arms.
(Sētubandha 21) The young deer, their hearts shattered by the intense arrows, are bound; the gods, their pride humbled by the unseen rainbows, suffer;
and the monkeys wander with their mountain peaks bent down by the weight of the unobserved clouds. (Sētubandha 22)
The night-stalker licks the sky; the monkey host is pierced through the quarters by his unbroken heart;
though he is being split apart, the son of Daśaratha—who has fixed his eyes upon the sight of his enemy—is not broken.
He is like a reflection of the blazing fire of the submarine mare’s mouth, kindled by the fire of his own wrath.
The serpents merely avoid his arms, which have already gained their range over his limbs.

Encircled by those serpents, his arms—with their broad coils swelling from the pain of being gripped—became like sandalwood trees growing on the Malaya mountain, firm, motionless, and pure. (Setubandha 24–25)

Thus did the sons of Raghu act—light in their anger, which was rendered fruitless by mere bared lips, while the diamond-like hardness of their arms remained motionless, pierced by the arrows released from the drawn bow;
their bodies, though wounded by shafts, were still visible on the path of sight. (Sētu 26)
The sons of Raghu, their blood flowing from wounds inflicted by arrows seen and struck in the interval between the landing-stages, [proceeded].
(Sētubandha 27) With their pairs of thighs sewn together by arrows, they stood motionless and exhausted, their feet unable to move;
though their bodies were bound, the descent of the mountain was accomplished by the sons of Raghu. (Sētubandha 28)

Together with those gods, he fell upon the bow, which had its first-placed arrows failing and whose left hand was restrained by the impact of arrows discharged by invisible enemies; and then, at the rear of the surface of the celestial chariot that had suddenly lost its control, he leaped upward. (Setubandha 29)

Then Rāghava fell, shattering the bond of hope for the three worlds, casting a shadow over the strings of the lute that was wailing with a single mouthful of the poison of the wives of the gods. (Setu 30)
Like a forest elephant toward a nearby tree, he rushed toward Rāghava, who was tall as a lion’s goad;
and as the Lord of the Raghus fell, the son of Sumitrā followed him down like the mass of shade following a tree that has fallen from its upright position onto the ground. (Sētubandha 31–32)

As those chariots fell to the earth, their wheels turned upward with their rims facing the sky, their triangular frames remained for a long time with their flat surfaces turned upward, their weight causing them to sink so deeply that their fronts could not be discerned.
As if falling upon their hearts, they suddenly plunged into darkness as if falling into a swoon. (Sētubandha 33)
At Rāma’s fall, the three worlds became as if lifeless, like at the fall of the sun.
(Sētubandha 34) Then the monkey army, its faces turned toward the quarters of the sky now empty of Rāma’s protection, lost all vigor;
rendered motionless by fear, it could not even bear to look upon Rāghava though he had fallen. (Sētubandha 35)
The monkey army stood as if turned into a painting— dejected, its enthusiasm shattered, its minds agitated,
its hearts driven by despair, and with its eyes fixed upon Rāghava.
(Setubandha 36) Even though the Lord of the Raghus has fallen, the sight of him gives voice to the conversation of the monkey leaders.

The serenity of his face was maintained with fortitude by a great sigh of relief born of freedom from fear. (Sētubandha 37) But then, by the Lord of the Monkeys, whose eyes were like the waters of the ocean, the son of Daśāṇana was seen at his side in the sky, accompanied by his bow and having been dispatched on an errand. (Sētubandha 38)
Then Sugrīva, having rushed forth with his army of monkeys who were as fierce as the sons of Tāraka, entered Laṅkā while it was reeling in fear and remained there alone among the night-stalkers.
Having been informed by Indrajit of Rāghava’s death, the lord of the night-stalkers was delighted. (Setubandha 3.39)
Having found a means for the reunion with his father’s daughter, he was comforted and sighed a breath of relief.
(Sētubandha 40) Now, by the night-rangers, the fresh and momentary separation [from her] was perceived through the words brought from the Ten-faced One.
The daughter of Janaka was rendered unconscious, crying out with a voice faltering and broken by the three-fold agony.
Then Rāghava, his grief for Sītā momentarily cast aside as he gazed upon Sumitrā’s son who was fainting from exhaustion, began to lament for him. (Sētubandha 41–42)
He upon whose bow the entire triple world ascends with trepidation—he too has been slain by the Son of Sumitrā;
for there is nothing in this forest that does not come to pass through the transformation of destiny.
Or rather, the Son of Sumitrā has cast away his life for my sake, having accomplished his task.
"O noble one who has carried the burden of his arms in vain, I alone have lightened my own self.

(Sētubandha 44) Then he spoke sweet words to Sugrīva—words that revealed his inner resolve through his fortitude, and which were rendered profound by having suddenly overcome the state of death. (Sētubandha 45)

O steadfast one, you have carried out this task; likewise, the host of monkeys, their strength of arm directed toward the ocean, has performed this deed difficult to achieve even by the son of the Wind, whose fame was manifested through his own efforts.
This royal splendor of mine, which has instigated enmity among kinsmen, does not belong to Vibhīṣaṇa.
"Even my heart has not yet experienced the taste of the pain of an arrow's wound because of this sorrow. Therefore, go;
do not be bewildered. By that very bridge, look upon your circle of kinsmen before you realize the ripening of time’s suffering. (Setubandha 47–48)
Then the lord of monkeys, his arms tightly crossed over his chest in the agony of a face distorted by intense rage,
spoke this reply to the Lord of the Raghus without giving anything to the monkey: "Go [to him] who,
together with Lakṣmaṇa, has made a hero’s bed with a covering of fresh sprouts."
Bring the Lord of the Raghus here, who has dispelled the pain of the arrow-wound inflicted by the monkey-host;
and I too shall bring him whose bow was seized and drawn back at the sudden encounter, other than by the falling of a lightning bolt. (Setubandha 50, the final *kulaka*)
With his body exhausted by the weight of the earth, twisted and bent as it was cast down by his arms;
with his sword, the "Moonlight," its hilt held in a pair of hands supported upon his shoulder. (Sētubandha 51)
With chariots crushed by the trampling of his feet, their weapons falling away as they fled with faces turned toward the earth;
with his forearms shattered and rendered useless as he struggled with broken arms; and with his chest split open by a firm fist-strike from a hand falling like a thunderbolt—Sētubandha 52–53.
I shall make the Ten-faced one his head severed, dragged out, crushed, scattered, and shattered by the earth;
his heart split open and mangled by my claws, rendered fruitless and cold. Thus, this very day, when the Ten-necked one has been slain by me, I shall return to Kishkindha.
Janaka’s daughter looked upon the dying Rāghava as if he were still alive, or as if he were about to die only after a moment.
(Sētubandha 55) When Sugrīva was restrained by Vibhīṣaṇa with the words “These are poison-darting arrows,” the Lord of the Raghus began to recite the Gāruḍa mantra within his heart. (Sētubandha 56)

But now the surface of the earth has become such that Mount Suvela is being shaken by the ocean waves suddenly lashed up, and the corpses of Rākṣasas are scattered about by the force of the fierce winds. (Sētubandha 57) [Yugmaka]

And he beholds the path of the great seat of the Lord of Lakṣmī, placed upon its firm back where the feathers of its fresh plumage serve as soft eyelashes; a path where the great darkness is dispelled by the intense light of its golden down, and where the chest is revealed by the single feather released from the blow of Indra’s irresistible weapon. (Setubandha 58)

Rāma [beheld] Garuḍa, whose chest was adorned with a necklace of writhing serpents clinging to his throat. (Sētu 59) Then, when Garuḍa had descended and stood facing Rāma—who had offered his salutation—and both were visible, it could be discerned where those masses of arrows had gone, even though the bodies of both remained [intact]. (Sētu 60)

[124] Having released his arrow-fastenings, having discarded the grass used for binding, and being devoid of the exhaustion from the exertion, the Lord of the Raghus became as fierce as the elephant-slaying Garuḍa, possessing the mantras taught to him. (Sētubandha 61)
Then, hearing that Rāma was liberated from the bond of the arrow, the Lord of the Nishādas, suspecting the arrival of Garuḍa, cast the entire burden of battle upon Lakṣmaṇa.
Driven by rage, by chariot, or by his own prowess, he [advanced] together with the army of the Nishādas. (Setubandha 62)
Like an arm bearing a joyous smile, or like valor amidst the onset of enmity—Sētu 63.
Then that host of Rākṣasas, with their faces clouded by dust, stood upon the path where the submarine fire of the ocean’s end moves, like the wind-god Mārutāsuta. Sētu 64.
Then, when the conflict with the army of the one-eyed Rākṣasa, whose end was so terrible, had begun,
Dhūmrākṣa— intent on the slaughter of Akṣa— overwhelmed Māruti with his arrows.
Then, as his arrows struck against the hair-pits of [Hanumān] and became fruitless, he shook them off.
The poet laughs at the one who, having stepped upon and twisted the chariot, stands with his bow bent like a rainbow;
where the mace, hurled by the enraged Pavaṇaputra with arms as firm as diamond peaks, did not strike its mark, there the weapon lay shining haphazardly. (Sētubandha 66–67)
[The wrestling match],
wherein the lion’s throat is bent by the embrace grasped with the palm of his long left hand,
and wherein the sound of the lion roars as he circles within the chest while the life-force struggles to escape. (Setubandha 68)
With his hands hanging down as his weapons slipped from them, faltering due to the exertion of the moment,
Dhūmrākṣa— his life abandoned as he rose up like a blade of grass before the wind— was struck down.
When Dhūmrākṣa had fallen and the army of the night-stalkers was reduced to a mere remnant, [the battle ended].
The son of the Wind beholds Akampana, who is advancing as commanded by the ten-faced Rāvaṇa (Sētu 70).
Hanumān, confident on the chest of the [defeated] enemy, hurls him down, having cast off his multitude of weapons; his armor is shattered and scattered piece by piece (Sētu 71).
[125] Then,
commanded by the Ten-faced one and released from the blow of Hanumān’s fist,
he fell upon the face of Nīla, who was distressed at having missed the joy of battle and stood with hands outstretched. (Sētubandha 72)
Just as he was setting out, a black bee, released by a startled [elephant], fell upon Nīla’s chest, proclaiming it with a gushing flow of blood that pierced through his armor.
The monkey abandons the branch that has turned away from him, though it is fragrant with the scent of the celestial elephant. (Setubandha 73)
The bee clinging to the path of the cow’s hoofprints has extended its wing against the current toward the wish-fulfilling tree.
(Sētubandha 74) As the cloud thunders, the wind stands in the path of its arrival like a pillar of raindrops;
it causes the clusters of pearls and fruits to fall from the branches shaken by the wind. (Sētubandha 75)

Then, with his arms freed from the earth and a shower of pearls falling from his creeper-like moustache, he simultaneously struck the mountain peaks with his arrows and filled the sky with the monkeys, as blood flowed from his chest where the splintering branches had pierced it.
(Sētubandha 76) Simultaneously he fells the mountain peaks and simultaneously fills the vault of heaven with monkeys.

By him, a mass of rocks was released equally in the four directions, manifesting [as the bridge]. (Setu 77) The regions of the sky appear with masses of rocks shattered by the impact of falling trees and crumbling peaks, while mountain torrents are seen being severed as the mountains are crushed. (Setu 78)
With its thick mass of filaments scattered over its shoulders by the dust of mountain minerals,
the dark cloud appears in the sky like the twilight, its waters sprinkled with the glow of the evening sun.
(Setubandha 79) And then, at the edge of the sky, it is stilled as it turns back from the bow drawn for the descent [of the arrow].
The monkey appeared as if he were being held fast by the masses of arrows released at the very first;
then the night-stalker [Rāvaṇa] seized a mace that had rebounded from Nīla’s broad forehead, having been swiftly evaded by the force of its impact upon his chest. (Sētubandha 80–81)

And he seizes the black rock, which possesses a hardness as broad as his own expansive and powerful chest, and which bears the shadow of clouds clinging to its upper slopes like the smoke of a blazing fire. (Setubandha 82)
When the sun had risen far away and was no longer blue, having descended upon the rocky surface, the sky became day for a moment, while the earth became night with darkness firmly established.
Then, [the elephant] endured the deep blow out of devotion to the color of the blue gateway.
Split within by a blow, with his life-blood gushing from his throat, he fell to the surface of the earth.
(Sētubandha 84) Thus ends the fourteenth canto in the great poem *Daśamukhavadha* composed by the illustrious Pravarasena.
[The Five Comforts] Now,
when the lord of Prastha has been slain, he will experience the pressure of his arms as they quiver with fury at the slaughter of his kinsmen.
Daśagrīva advanced, filling the ten directions with his *huṃkāra* roars that met the fire [of Śiva’s eye].

(Setu 1) When he laughed so fiercely in his rage that it filled the ten directions from within the caves of his mouths, even his own retinue hid themselves within the pillars of their silence born of fear. (Setu 2)
He mounted a chariot whose rear seat was sinking under the weight of the feet of his retinue of Rākṣasas, and whose flight of restless horses was being checked by the charioteer;
[he entered] the middle of Laṅkā with a roar accompanied by a great clamor that shook the earth. (Sētubandha 3)
"Rāvaṇa has departed with his army and his city," so the monkeys cried out.
Then, emerging from the city, their faces covered in white ash as a sign of the intense grief for those slain, they shattered the monkey host that had abandoned its pride in battle. (Sētubandha 4–5)
Then the hosts of monkeys, their shoulders struck by the tips of the final tufts of mane curling at the mouths [of the lions],

watched Daśānana as he clung to the path along the broken [mountain]. Then they [the monkeys] were scattered, having been struck and crushed by the arrows discharged from the mouth of Dahavayaṇa (Dahamukha).
Having forgotten what was said, the son of Agni spoke with fear born of battle:
"Do not abandon the burden of combat! For the sake of this one, whose form half-emerges from the peak of Mount Malaya, the lord of monkeys shall snatch away your very life. (Sētubandha 7–8)
With a heart overcome by grief, he was addressed as "Daśānana" by the charioteer;
yet Rāma was not seen for so long with such great respect as when he was called her "beloved. (Setu 9) [p.
Then the Lord of the Night-dwellers, with his chariot overturned by the arrows discharged from Rāma’s bow,
abandoned his fleeing horses and turned back toward Laṅkā.
Thereupon, he was pursued by that [Rāvaṇa], whose fame was diminished and whose destruction was imminent, as he fled with his heroic stride abandoned.
The turning over [of the body] was performed by Kumbhakarṇa as he lay fast asleep without blinking.

He too, yawning with his head heavy from the turning-over caused by the *āyāla* (the demon), laughed for a long time and, having heard the light message regarding the slaying of Rāma... (Sētubandha 11–12).
The golden rampart of his body, its foundation the chariot of Rati crushed [by him], was like a girdle of molten gold slipped from the belly as it clung to the region of his thighs.
Beyond that rampart he had leaped, where the crocodiles were the struggling sea-monsters. (Sētubandha 13)
The ocean shores, with waters reaching only to the knees, became passable.

Then, as they beheld that [bridge], the hosts of monkeys—having turned back from their warlike activities, having descended from the mountains falling into their hands, and having crossed over—proceeded forward. (Sētu 14–15)
Then, having struck the entire monkey army with rocks, trees, iron clubs, mallets,
firm staffs, missiles, and maces, Rāvaṇa— drunk with blood— quickly pursued the monkeys and the elephants with his swift horses. (Sētubandha 16)
The enemy army, its strength shattered by the discharge of Rāma’s arrows, set out to flee.

Then, for both sides who had fought for a long time, the earth was first strewn with the sweat drenched by the arrows shot from Rāma’s bow, and afterwards with streams of blood gushing from their wounds. (Sētubandha 17–18)
One [arm], having blocked the mouth of the river, fell repeatedly like Mount Suvela;
the other, having regained its strength in the ocean, remained like a second bridge-post for the construction of the dam.
(Setu 19) Then, in the forefront of the battle, by him who had drawn back his bow and whose lion-maned tail was lashing about...
With his high, sky-reaching wheel, he severed Rāhu’s head as if it were Rāhu’s own discus;
with that [wheel] raised toward the heavens, its mouth-caverns filled with wind, [it roared]. (Setubandha 20)
Even with its peak shattered, Mount Trikuṭa still appears as if its lofty summit has risen four cubits higher.

(Sētubandha 21) And now that Kumbhakarṇa has fallen, the ocean—its crocodiles scattered and broken by those fleeing afar—seems to vomit forth the submarine fire from its very depths, its bosom heaving under the weight of its body. (Sētubandha 22)
Having heard of the destruction of Kumbhakarṇa, Daśānana,
his heart swelling with pride and burning with rage, laughs once more and shakes his multitude of faces.
Even from the distance between the pillars, she could not see the expanse of his chest;
only when he emerged from the door, filled the interior of the house with his broad chest uncovered, and stood up on his knees, did Śreṇya laugh and say, "It is Meghanāda! (Sētubandha 24–25).

Even when a son has accomplished a task as great as an act of daring, the father does not obtain the touch of a son— so dear to a son— from his own son alone. (Sētubandha 26) Why [do you grieve] for me, while holding back tears for the sake of a young son who is merely human?
He himself quickly destroys the glory of our Rākṣasa host;

he does not even recognize himself as one capable of bearing the burden of the three worlds—[a world] where the jewels of the raised serpents have been snatched away, the Nandana grove has been crushed, and the mountains overturned—just as [he does not recognize his own] self. (Sētu 27–28)
Shall I slay Rāghava, who has dried up the ocean with the mere tip of the spear at the front of battle?
Or shall I today cast all seven oceans into the mouth of the leaping submarine fire? (Setubandha 29) [Yugma]
With his head placed in the hands of the western charioteer of the Ten-faced one who had been informed [of his intent],
he caused the surface of the mountain to bend under the weight of the slow advance of his feet encased in armor;
(Sētu 30) the sunbeams were reflected by the lightning discharged from the clouds resting upon its peaks.
The sound of Rāma’s bow, drawn near him as he mounted his chariot for battle, resounded like the roar of the ocean.
Thus,
having restrained the ten-faced Rāvaṇa and having laid down the burden of the ocean's command, [the mountain remained].
The son of the Ten-faced One, mounted upon his chariot and surrounded by a retinue of Rākṣasas, [arrived]— Sētubandha 32.
He alone was the one who caused a great tumult at the city gate as the chariot rushed forward swiftly through the opening of the Ten-faced One’s front,
agitating the army of the monkeys— Sētubandha 33.
Then the son of Daśānana, his strength sapped by the monkeys who had first been struck down while their eyes were fixed upon Rāma, was repelled by the son of Añjana together with the monkey warriors;
[he was likewise repelled] by Nīla with a mountain peak, by Divija with a tree, and by Māruti with a slab of rock. (Setubandha 34)
Dāruṇa, together with Saṃnala, released a fragment of the peak of Mount Malaya.
Then Vibhīṣaṇa spoke to the son of Sumitrā, whose army of monkeys had been broken and whose departure toward Nīla had been thwarted: "Restrain Meghanāda! (Sētu 35–36).
Having heard of the slaying of Indrajit,

the Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa) angrily shed tears, even while his grandfather, the Grandfather of the Rākṣasas, was fighting with arrows that were neither made of wood nor iron, and had severed the head of Meghanāda by the hand of the Son of Sumitrā (Lakṣmaṇa). (Setubandha 37)

Like oil poured upon extinguished embers, it fell instantly with a loud hiss. (Sētubandha 38) And when Meghanāda was slain, Daśagrīva was struck down at that very moment by Fate, as if with two hands consisting of both wrath and despair, while he was turning about. (Sētubandha 39)
Having slain his kinsmen without exception, that Daśagrīva, though alone,
emerged like a world of rākṣasas— difficult to behold due to his many arms and possessing a terrifying mass of faces. (Sētubandha 40) [Yugma]
But now, the sun is obscured by the dense darkness of black clouds driven by the wind;
the mass of manes of the horses has been blown away by the rutting ichor of the aged Airāvaṇa;
and the western portion of the moon’s orb is stained by the dust raised by the wheels of the army. (Setubandha 41)
Having mounted his chariot, which was scorched by the mass of flames rising from the collapse of Dhanada’s city,
he was gazed upon even as he departed by the female *rākṣasīs*, whose hearts were filled with auspicious joy. (Setubandha 42)
As soon as tears welled up in his eyes, they formed a barrier;
then, with his mountain-cascade water poured from his palms, he quickly crossed the incomparable monkey army with his glances as if with arrows. (Sētubandha 43–44)
Even at Pāsāvaḍia, in the presence of Sevihiṣaṇa, whose retinue was formed by the monkey army, the arrow—
though composed of the essence of indignation because [the enemy] was wretched and grieving— leaps forth.
(Sētubandha 45) Furthermore, having endured the first blow, with arrows fixed in fury, it leaps forth.
Like a tree struck by lightning and thunder, Lakṣmaṇa was pierced in the chest (Sētu 46).
He too, his life further sustained by the mountain herbs brought by the son of the Wind-god, began to fight with those who had joined together as a single ocean of bows and arrows (Sētu 47).
Then Rāma also beheld the mountain peak, its clouds shattered by the blows of the horses' hooves,
and from which the fragrance of golden columns supporting the Vajrahara (Indra) as he stood upon it was wafting forth. (Sētu 48)
With its long shaft bent by the weight of the *mālatī* garlands held in the left hand,
with the tufts of its fly-whisks drooping as they rest upon the moisture from the breaking spray of the mountain peaks,
and appearing like a great white banner split by the sun’s rays scattered by the frost that resembles the moon— Sētubandha 49.
Like a celestial chariot falling from heaven toward the surface of the eastern ocean, [the mountain] appeared with its western slope uplifted.
Then Rāma, his face bright with the joy of being the first to see his mother,
was saluted by her as she bowed her head low out of great reverence for the gods.

And that armor of the Lord of the Three Worlds, its expanse revealed by the touch of the hand of the Daughter of the Mountain as she placed it upon his chest, with its fragrance streaming forth from within;
and that armor which brought a blissful touch to the eyes of Indra as they spread across all his limbs. (Sētubandha 52)

The broad earth, which had descended upon the chest of the Lord of the Raghus— once so slightly loosened by the touch of the hand of the Lord of Asuras and repeatedly trampled— now appears withered, as if languishing in separation from Śītā. (Setubandha 53)
Having mounted the chariot, Māyāvin fashioned a mechanical elephant [to challenge him] with all its limbs.
Then, having placed his hand upon the earth—which was pregnant with the bow that had just been broken—the son of Sumitrā, who was surrounded by the sons of Nīlaravi, spoke to Rāghava. (Sētu 54–55)
Rest your bow, its string slackened by the snout of the crocodile; soon you shall see the Ten-faced one ruined, like the sun’s son [Yama] upon the dark night.
Direct your wrath toward the heavy task, and abandon your indignation regarding the easy slaughter of the Ten-faced one.

He struck down the lofty bank of the river as a forest elephant [tramples] a level meadow. (Sētubandha 57) Is it not heard that the command of the Three-Eyed One was carried out by the gods, who, with a mere glance from the corner of their eyes, were capable of burning Tripura even though Rāghava was already fully prepared? (Sētubandha 58)
Then, his forehead crossed by the sea of wrath rising from the sight of the ten-faced one’s face, Rāghava, with his dark-blue eyes dilated in pride, replied to Lakṣmaṇa:
“My heart confirms the resolve you have expressed. (Setubandha 59)
But will my arm, having already slain the Ten-faced one, become a mere burden?

O Indrajit, do not carry away the Ten-necked one from the battlefield like a forest elephant seized by the mouth of a lion, for his death at the hands of the struggling Kumbha is unbearable. (Sētubandha 60–61)
Then, as he was cutting off the heads of those [monkeys] who had begun to flee,
a shower of arrows began to uproot the vanguard of the monkey army in the midst of the battle.
Then, while both [armies], possessing equal impetuosity, were being watched by the gods fleeing from the flight of arrows...

Then Rāma drew his bow, whose string was joined by the rays of the jewels in his earrings, for a battle between him and the Ten-faced one that was as grave as the death of an elephant. (Setubandha 63)
First, an arrow was released by the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, his kinsman, into the heart of Muktāphalaketu.

By that arrow, which fell with a roar, the Lord of the Raghus, though steadfast, was shaken in such a way that he made the entire triple world tremble as if it were not distinct from himself. (Sētubandha 64–65)
Even Rāvaṇa’s arrow, its armlet shattered by the successive impact of the blows from the forest of palm trees falling upon the mass of Daśagrīva’s arms, passed right through him.
Another arrow was fixed; another was suddenly drawn back to the ear and released. (Sētubandha 66)
The bow of the Lord of the Rākṣasas becomes equal [to Rāma’s], with its body made light by arrows;

yet Rāma’s bow is seen with arrows constantly departing from its joints, with the string fixed to the curved part at all times, with arrows being released perpetually, and its wide belly encircled by the string forever. (Sētubandha 67–68)
The left arm is stretched out while the right hand has fallen upon the region of the jaw;
and thus, the arrows aimed at the bows are seen in the intervals between them.
(Setu 69) By the arrow discharged by the Ten-faced One, [he struck] Rāma, who was already tormented by the constant grief of separation from Sītā.

Rāvaṇa’s heart was not known by Rāghava even though it was pierced by his arrow, for it remained steadfast and firm. (Sētubandha 70) The forehead of the Lord of the Rākṣasas, who had approached with a defiant spirit sent by the Lord of the Raghus, was split open, and his distinct frown-pattern was shattered. (Sētubandha 71)
Then, with their eyes filled by the streams of blood flowing from those who were fainting and agitated,
the multitude of faces repeatedly whirled about upon the tips of the arms. (Setu 72) Then,
the eyelashes became like a city consumed by the fire of eyes half-closed in the stupor of falling elephants...
He struck the arrow whose feathers were joined to the second side of his face, which was contorted with rage.
Then, filling the ten directions with thousands of rays resembling the fire of universal destruction,
that arrow fell back like the solar disc upon the path of Rāvaṇa’s mouth, which was like the mouth of Rāhu.
Rāvaṇa also, having proudly displayed his fortitude, beheld the Ten-faced one with his hand as if about to seize him, like a pond of blooming lotuses. (Sētubandha 75)

Rāma fixes his arrow; by the side of Vibhīṣaṇa, the fortune of the Rākṣasas turns back; and at that very moment, Sītā’s left eye throbs, portending the destruction of the Ten-faced one. The left eye of the night-stalker (Rāvaṇa) trembles, and the right eye of the Lord of the Raghus quivers.

The pair of eyes of Vibhīṣaṇa quivers, betraying his longing for the kingdom of his kinsman. (Sētubandha 77) As the bow, with its string fixed and bearing the weight of the child [Rāvaṇa] upon its belly, was being drawn, the clusters of tears shed by the wives of the gods were like the outpourings from the ports of Rāma’s arrows. (Sētubandha 78)
But then, by a single arrow from the Lord of the Raghus, that multitude of ten faces of the Ten-faced One—severed by Chandahāsa and already deprived of its leader—was struck down one by one.
Though severed, it remained formidable to the Ten-faced One because the weight of his throat had not yet been divided. (Setu 79)
The multitude of faces of the Lord of the Rākṣasas, who had emerged from beneath the earth after being released by the merchant, rose up like a mass of flames.

From that laughing Lord of the Rākṣasas at the head of the battle, a self [the arrow] issued forth toward him through all ten mouths, as terrifying as fire with its crests of flame. (Sētubandha 80–81)
When the Ten-faced one was slain and the universe was sighing on all sides,
Rāma, his brow furrowed, relaxed his speech and lowered his bow.
Unaware of the prowess of the Lord of the Night-dwellers, she [Sītā] was distressed by the breaking of her sleep.
Thinking, "He is my mother," the royal glory abandoned even the slain Rāvaṇa.
Then, in the heart of Vibhīṣaṇa, affection for his kinsman arose;
likewise, before the descendant of Daśaratha, a flood of tears was released by his eyes. (Sētubandha 83–84)
When Daśagrīva was slain, Vibhīṣaṇa, whose cry for immortality had been silenced, began to lament, his hope dashed by a sorrow exceeding even that of death:
"The very realm of Yama, which you beheld after conquering Death itself, has become a source of pleasure according to your own desire. (Sētubandha 85)

"How indeed will you appear before the lords of the earth, when that very same thing which is common to all other people has been disregarded by you alone through the instruction of the Lord of the Rākṣasas? (Sētubandha 8.6)

O King, if I am preeminent in righteousness, then who indeed could be ranked before me—except for Kumbhakarṇa alone, who in the heat of battle released [his foe] with equal composure? (Sētu 87) If I am preeminent in righteousness, then who indeed could be ranked before me—except for you, O King, who, though your kinsmen were equal in pleasure and pain, did not abandon me? (Sētu 88)

And he laughs like a mountain whose river-mouth is dried up by the heat of summer, its banks choked with tears flowing from the grief of his kinsmen’s slaughter, yet further intensified by the sorrow of Rāghava’s death. "O Lord, grant me leave; I shall fall at the feet of the Ten-faced one and Kumbhakarṇa. (Setubandha 89)
"Later, when he has gone to the other world, I shall kiss his head and my son Meghanāda.

(Sētu 90) Out of compassion for the cries of the terrified Vibhīṣaṇa, who had fallen to the ground in distress, Rāma, at the command of the Son of the Wind (Hanumān), also honored the Lord of the Rākṣasas. (Sētu 91)
And when the Ten-faced One was slain, Sugrīva, longing for the recovery of Janaka’s daughter, saw the interior of the ocean—which had witnessed his previous service—as if it were empty.
Having accomplished the task of the gods, he was dismissed by Rāghava in the presence of the host of monkeys. (Setu 92)
Having turned his chariot toward the rising spray of water scattered by the clouds, he was made to appear like a golden sacrificial staff by Mātali.
Having purified the son of Janaka as if in a fire, the Lord of the Raghus reached the city to fulfill Bharata’s devoted affection. (Sētubandha 93–94)

Herein concludes this poem titled *The Slaying of Rāvaṇa*, which— by means of the recovery of Sītā— produced joy for Rāma, is marked by passion, and dwells within the hearts of all people. (Setu 95) Thus ends the fifth canto, the Pañcaratha, in the great poem *The Slaying of the Ten-faced One* composed by Kālidāsa under the patronage of the illustrious Pravara-sena.

Laughing, he made a single handful of water with his left hand— which was opened by the grass on Mount Ghaṭīyoga and loosened by the salutation at twilight— and thus performed his own ritual offering of libations. (Setubandha 1) Even in a grave matter of war, those who are capable experience the aesthetic flavor only when they are at peace.
When the flower has borne fruit, it becomes the occasion for the bees.
(Sētu 2) Entering and turning back as they circle the groves and lakes, their paths traversing the sky, these [clouds] are like jewel-mountains with peaks as lofty as the clouds. (Sētu 3)

The coral sprout, with its shimmering luster, flashes like a flower of linked jewels; its tips are entwined by trees on revolving mountains that are pierced by the brilliance of fire. (Setubandha 4) The rivers flowing from within the mountain clefts carry along the bodies of fish that have been crushed smooth.

The arrows of Rāma, upon which the hoods of serpents clinging to his face were leaped over by his breaking anger, [fell]. (Sētubandha 5) Like the ocean being agitated and tossed by the clouds of the dissolution or by the winds of the doomsday, it was diminished and tasted by the arrows as if by the suns of the kalpa, while it was being measured out by the gods. (Sētubandha 6)

The riverbeds, their shells split open as the water was drawn away by Bāṇa’s arrows, are blooming with blossoming lotuses whose gem-filled centers are being crushed; yet the ocean, its face distressed by the pain arising from the upturned palms of his head, remains [unmoved]. (Setubandha 7)
At the feet of the son of Daśaratha, he fell like a tree cast down by the force of the wind.
(Sētu 8) Touched by the feet of the monkeys, the earth’s circumference—its waters of the ocean tossed up, its trees shaken, and its mountains trembling—moves and quakes. (Sētu 9)

The great mountains, where pairs of *kiṃnara*s are terrified by the falling of jagged, uneven rocky peaks, have their mountain torrents turned into cries of lamentation as they are uprooted by the monkeys. (Sētubandha 10)

The front of the bridge-foundation, with its mass of clouds scattered by the waters of the ocean tossed up by the mountain being dragged along, seems to fall forward as it is cut away by the chisel; even upon hearing the clamor of the great monkey army as the foundation is being bound, [the ocean trembles]. (Setubandha 11)
The heart of Daśānana instantly became agitated, terrified, and disordered;

[then] the moon, whose rays were like scattered necklaces, appeared like a breast in its fresh youth—its darkness-cloth removed by the sight of Rāma’s dark face at night, and bringing joy to the eyes. (Sētu 12–13)

The arrows of Rāma, released from the bow drawn by his hand— whose palm was rendered precious by the touch of Janaka’s daughter’s breasts— impetuously produce horripilation on the body of the Ten-necked One.
(Setubandha 14) Thus, there are additional *skandhaka* verses.
